notations: IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE

single_candidate_flags.why_uncertain: EC/AcceptancePolicy/DC formal spine may relate to the ideal-state-comparison-model lineage but no exact match confirmed.

sources.note: S0685's reframing of the whole pipeline: humans first hold/conceive an Ideal State I_t (the complete state of what is supposed to be known/true/valid), and Knowledge/Facts are produced by comparing observations against that ideal via reasoning, not by building an ideal state up from raw observations. Distinguishes the theoretical ideal I_t from our estimated hat I_t (hat I_t != I_t in general), reframes Knowledge as identified elements/relationships of the ideal state (K_t subset-or-approx I_t), places probability at the extraction of hat I_t from imperfect observations and logic at the ideal<->observed comparison, and raises 'where does the Ideal State come from?' (reality / human model / normative model / domain model / mathematical ideal / combination) as the most important unresolved problem, ahead of any Kernel definition.

rows.anchor: Human first has/conceives an Ideal State ... IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE. That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.
rows.statement: Major reorientation: humans do not build up an ideal state from arbitrary observations; instead a human first has/conceives an Ideal State and then evaluates reality against it, giving the pipeline IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE, substantially reversing the previously-used observation-first model.

lineage_claims.quote: That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.

rows.anchor: Ideal state ... The complete state of what is supposed to be known/true/valid for the thing at that point in time. ... all applicable rules; all required participants; ... I_t = Ideal Knowledge State at t ... O_t -- comparison with I_t --> K_t
rows.statement: Defines the ideal state I_t broadly as the complete state of what is supposed to be known/true/valid for a thing at time t; for an election system this would include all applicable rules, required participants, required conditions, valid relationships, required evidence, expected states, constraints, applicable laws, and known principles; every new piece of observed information O_t is evaluated against I_t, giving the extraction problem O_t --comparison with I_t--> K_t.

rows.anchor: Information that correctly describes some aspect of the ideal state is Knowledge. ... K_t subset I_t ... The ideal state itself may be unknown to us. ... I_t -- the theoretical ideal state, and hat-I_t -- our current extracted/estimated representation of it. Then: hat-I_t != I_t in general. That may actually explain your earlier statement: "We try our best but never achieve the best."
rows.statement: Refines 'information on the ideal state is knowledge' to 'information that correctly describes some aspect of the ideal state is Knowledge', giving K_t subset-or-equal I_t as the established/identified portion of the ideal state -- but the ideal state I_t itself may be unknown to us, so we must distinguish the theoretical ideal state I_t from our current extracted/estimated representation hat-I_t, with hat-I_t != I_t in general, explaining 'we try our best but never achieve the best'.
invariants: the estimated ideal state hat-I_t is never guaranteed to equal the true ideal state I_t

rows.anchor: P(x|O_{<=t},I_t^known) ... Probability is involved in extracting the ideal state from imperfect observations. Not: Knowledge=Probability. Instead: Probability models the uncertainty of our extraction of the ideal state.
rows.statement: Locates probability's role: for an ideal-state element x, given incomplete and overlapping observations O_1..O_n we estimate P(x|O_{<=t},I_t^known); probability is involved in extracting the ideal state from imperfect observations, not in defining Knowledge -- probability models the uncertainty of our extraction of the ideal state, not Knowledge itself.
invariants: probability attaches to the extraction of the ideal state, never to Knowledge or the ideal state itself

rows.anchor: System must have backup capability ... backup configuration exists ... If the applicable reasoning rules determine that the observation satisfies the criterion, we establish: F_t: "System has backup capability." ... the fact is not produced merely from the observation. It is produced by: Observation + Ideal State + Comparison Criteria + Reasoning.
rows.statement: Worked example of fact production: ideal state I_t requires 'system must have backup capability', observation O_t is 'backup configuration exists'; comparing O_t against I_t via applicable reasoning rules establishes fact F_t='System has backup capability' -- a fact is produced not merely from observation but from Observation + Ideal State + Comparison Criteria + Reasoning together.
invariants: a fact requires observation, ideal state, comparison criteria, and reasoning jointly -- never observation alone

rows.anchor: Logic = mechanism for comparing/deriving consequences from the ideal state and observed state. ... I_t: A and B and C. Observed: O_t: A,B,not-C. Logic gives: O_t does not entail I_t. Therefore the determination might be: F_t: "Current state does not satisfy the ideal state."
rows.statement: Defines logic's role as the mechanism for comparing/deriving consequences from the ideal state and observed state: given ideal state I_t=(A and B and C) and observed O_t=(A,B,not-C), logic determines O_t does not entail I_t, yielding determination F_t='Current state does not satisfy the ideal state'.

rows.anchor: P(A)=1, P(B)=0.9, P(C)=0.6, P(D)=0.2. Then our extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain. The probability is therefore attached to the extraction/determination, not necessarily to the underlying ideal state itself. That gives: I_t -> hat-I_t where hat-I_t is probabilistically estimated from available information.
rows.statement: Explains the origin of graded 0-to-1 values: if the ideal state requires A,B,C,D but observations only partially resolve them (P(A)=1,P(B)=0.9,P(C)=0.6,P(D)=0.2), the extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain -- this probability attaches to the extraction/determination I_t -> hat-I_t, not to the underlying ideal state itself.

rows.anchor: Where does the Ideal State come from? ... A. Given by reality I_t=Reality_t B. Given by human knowledge I_t=HumanModel_t C. Given by rules/laws/principles I_t=NormativeModel_t D. Given by the domain model I_t=DomainModel_t E. An ideal mathematical state I_t=I* F. Some combination I_t=f(Reality,Rules,Principles,Domain,HumanKnowledge). We should not assume which one it is.
rows.statement: Poses 'Where does the Ideal State come from?' as, in the author's opinion, the most important unresolved problem, with six unassumed candidate sources: given by reality (I_t=Reality_t), given by human knowledge (I_t=HumanModel_t), given by rules/laws/principles (I_t=NormativeModel_t), given by the domain model (I_t=DomainModel_t), an ideal mathematical state (I_t=I*), or some combination I_t=f(Reality,Rules,Principles,Domain,HumanKnowledge) -- explicitly: we should not assume which one it is.

rows.anchor: Knowledge = identified elements/relationships of an ideal state. And the current Knowledge state is K_t while the ideal state is I_t. The goal of knowledge extraction could therefore be: K_t -> I_t or more realistically: K_t approx I_t with the difference I_t - K_t representing what remains unknown, uncertain, or unextracted.
rows.statement: Resolves 'is Knowledge a collection of facts?' into a richer formulation: Knowledge = identified elements/relationships of an ideal state; with current knowledge state K_t and ideal state I_t, knowledge extraction aims at K_t -> I_t or more realistically K_t approx I_t, with the residual I_t - K_t representing what remains unknown, uncertain, or unextracted.

rows.anchor: "Every information on the ideal state of anything is knowledge." I would change "every information" to "every correctly determined proposition about the ideal state". ... "I believe the ideal state contains X." That is information about someone's belief, not necessarily Knowledge about the ideal state. ... "The document says X." ... Information about an ideal state != Knowledge of the ideal state.
rows.statement: Challenges the overbroad claim 'every information on the ideal state of anything is knowledge', proposing instead 'every correctly determined proposition about the ideal state'; example: 'I believe the ideal state contains X' is information about someone's belief, not Knowledge about the ideal state, and 'the document says X' is knowledge that the document says X, not knowledge that X is true. Preserves the distinction: Information about an ideal state != Knowledge of the ideal state.
invariants: information about a belief or a document's claim is never automatically knowledge of the ideal state itself

lineage_claims.target: the claim 'every information on the ideal state of anything is knowledge'
lineage_claims.quote: I would change "every information" to "every correctly determined proposition about the ideal state".

rows.anchor: IDEAL STATE -> (defines expected/relevant structure) -> OBSERVED REALITY -> INFORMATION -> EXTRACTION -> (evidence/uncertainty) -> COMPARISON (ideal <-> observed) -> LOGIC -> DETERMINATION -> FACTS -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> update over time. ... Probability primarily helps with the extraction from imperfect information, while Logic helps determine consequences and relationships.
rows.statement: Gives the full revised pipeline diagram: IDEAL STATE (defines expected/relevant structure) -> OBSERVED REALITY -> INFORMATION -> EXTRACTION (branching into evidence and uncertainty) -> COMPARISON (ideal<->observed) -> LOGIC -> DETERMINATION -> FACTS -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> update over time; probability primarily helps with extraction from imperfect information, logic helps determine consequences and relationships.

rows.anchor: before determination, we now need to investigate: What is the Ideal State? Because determination is: D_t = Compare(Observed_t, Ideal_t) and if we don't understand Ideal_t, we don't fully understand D_t. ... IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE
rows.statement: Revises the research direction: before determination can be understood, 'What is the Ideal State?' must be investigated, since determination is formalized as D_t=Compare(Observed_t,Ideal_t) and understanding D_t requires understanding Ideal_t; sets the research sequence as IDEAL STATE -> OBSERVATION -> EXTRACTION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT -> KNOWLEDGE, with Probability->uncertain extraction and Logic->comparison and consequence.

lineage_claims.target: the prior research direction of 'we need to understand determination'
lineage_claims.quote: I still believe that. But before determination, we now need to investigate: What is the Ideal State?

rows.anchor: the fundamental question for KnowledgeOS is not "How do we store Knowledge?" and not even "How do we extract Knowledge?" It may be: "How is an ideal state of Knowledge defined, and how does a system continuously determine its current relationship to that ideal state?" ... Knowledge becomes the currently justified representation of the relationship between them. I would now research Ideal State / normative state / complete state / target state / possible-world state / domain model / epistemic idealization across mathematics, epistemology, AI, systems theory, DDD, and philosophy before we touch the Kernel again.
rows.statement: States what may be 'the biggest discovery so far': the fundamental KnowledgeOS question may be neither 'how do we store Knowledge' nor 'how do we extract Knowledge' but 'how is an ideal state of Knowledge defined, and how does a system continuously determine its current relationship to that ideal state?'; Knowledge becomes the currently justified representation of the relationship between Ideal State and Observed State. Proposes researching Ideal State / normative state / complete state / target state / possible-world state / domain model / epistemic idealization across mathematics, epistemology, AI, systems theory, DDD, and philosophy before returning to Kernel definition.

rows.anchor: "Every information" you mean all possible information about the thing, not merely "some information." So your proposition is: I_t = the totality of all possible information about the object/domain at time t. And I_t may be infinite.
rows.statement: Reinterprets 'every information' as meaning ALL possible information about a thing, not merely some information: I_t is redefined as the totality of all possible information about the object/domain at time t, and I_t may be infinite -- a much stronger interpretation than given previously.

lineage_claims.target: the previous interpretation of I_t given in the immediately preceding document
lineage_claims.quote: That is much stronger than the interpretation I gave previously.

rows.anchor: O_t subset I_t or, more realistically, imperfect projections of I_t. The extraction process is therefore: I_t -> observable information -> extracted knowledge, with the extraction being imperfect because the underlying elements can overlap and the observation process cannot completely distinguish them.
rows.statement: A human/system cannot access all of the (possibly infinite) I_t, only observations O_t subset I_t or imperfect projections of it; extraction is I_t -> observable information -> extracted knowledge, imperfect because underlying elements can overlap and observation cannot completely distinguish them.

rows.anchor: K = the space of all possible information/knowledge elements ... I_t subset K is the complete/ideal information state relevant at that time. Then an observer A has only an extracted state: K_t^A subset I_t ... K_t^A != I_t in general.
rows.statement: Sharpens 'Knowledge is a state and subset of elements of the infinite Knowledge Space' into: K-script (the space of all possible information/knowledge elements), with I_t subset K-script being the complete/ideal information state relevant at time t; an observer A has only an extracted state K_t^A subset I_t (or a representation/projection of it), and because extraction is imperfect, K_t^A != I_t in general.
invariants: an observer's extracted state K_t^A is generally not equal to the ideal state I_t

rows.anchor: P(x in I_t | O_{<=t}^A). So probability describes the extraction uncertainty. ... Knowledge itself is not probability. Rather: Probability can describe the imperfect extraction of Knowledge from the ideal information state.
rows.statement: For an ideal-state element x in I_t that an observer cannot directly verify, the observer estimates P(x in I_t | O_{<=t}^A) given its observations -- probability describes extraction uncertainty, consistent with 'the elements overlap and only probability can extract them as separately as possible' (still to be tested as the right mathematical mechanism, but a coherent hypothesis). Knowledge itself is not probability; probability describes the imperfect extraction of Knowledge from the ideal information state.
missing: test of whether probability is always the right mechanism

rows.anchor: If I_t means all possible information, then we need to distinguish: possible information from true information and knowable information. ... whether your I_t means: 1. all logically possible information, or 2. all information that is actually true about the thing at t, or 3. all information that could in principle be known about the thing at t. I think this distinction is now the next critical question.
rows.statement: Raises the next critical question: since not every possible description of a system is true, I_t must be disambiguated among three readings -- (1) all logically possible information, (2) all information that is actually true about the thing at t, or (3) all information that could in principle be known about the thing at t; this distinction will determine the meaning of the 'infinite Knowledge Space' and what KnowledgeOS is trying to extract from it.
invariants: possible information, true information, and knowable information must be kept distinct

rows.anchor: I_t = the potentially infinite space of all relevant states/propositions/relationships at time t ... K_t (script) = Infinite Knowledge Space at t and I_t subset K_t (script) could represent an ideal state/configuration of the domain. But even I_t may itself be infinite. ... K_t = Pi_t(I_t) where Pi_t is the extraction/projection available to the observer.
rows.statement: If I_t can be infinite, it should not be modeled as a finite list of facts but as the potentially infinite space of all relevant states/propositions/relationships at t; introduces K-script_t (infinite Knowledge Space at t) with I_t subset K-script_t as an ideal state/configuration of the domain (itself possibly infinite), and the observer's actual accessible/extracted knowledge as K_t subset I_t or, more generally, K_t=Pi_t(I_t) where Pi_t is the observer's extraction/projection function.

rows.anchor: I_t={x_1,x_2,x_3,...}. We cannot observe all of them. ... construct an estimate hat-I_t from the observations. For an element x: P(x in I_t | O_{<=t},C_t) can express our uncertainty ... probability is increasingly looking like a mathematics of extraction from an incompletely observable/infinite state, rather than a definition of Knowledge.
rows.statement: With an infinite ideal state I_t={x_1,x_2,...} that cannot be fully observed, an estimate hat-I_t is constructed from observations O_{<=t}, and for an element x, P(x in I_t | O_{<=t},C_t) expresses uncertainty about membership; probability is increasingly a mathematics of extraction from an incompletely observable/infinite state, not a definition of Knowledge.

rows.anchor: "complete Knowledge" does not necessarily mean possessing an infinite list of everything. Completeness may instead mean: possessing the rules, structure and relationships necessary to answer every relevant question about the ideal state. ... I_t is ideal if it is sufficient to determine the answer to every admissible question at t. It does not require that every element be explicitly enumerated.
rows.statement: Redefines completeness operationally: if I_t is infinite, 'complete Knowledge' does not require an infinite explicit list of everything -- instead, I_t is ideal if it is sufficient to determine the answer to every admissible question at t, i.e. possessing the rules, structure and relationships necessary to answer every relevant question about the ideal state, without needing every element explicitly enumerated.
invariants: completeness of an ideal state means question-answering sufficiency, never explicit enumeration

rows.anchor: Infinite Knowledge Space K (script): the potentially unbounded universe of knowledge elements and relationships. Ideal state I_t: the state relevant to the domain/question space at time t. Extracted/observed state hat-I_t: what we can reconstruct from available information. Current Knowledge K_t: what has actually been determined/justified at t. ... K_t != hat-I_t != I_t subset K (script).
rows.statement: Establishes a four-level distinction, not automatically equal to each other: the Infinite Knowledge Space K-script (unbounded universe of knowledge elements/relationships), the Ideal state I_t (state relevant to the domain/question space at t), the Extracted/observed state hat-I_t (what can be reconstructed from available information), and Current Knowledge K_t (what has actually been determined/justified at t); K_t != hat-I_t != I_t subset K-script.
invariants: K_t, hat-I_t, I_t, and K-script are four distinct levels, never automatically equal

rows.anchor: What does it mean to have a complete or ideal state of an infinite Knowledge Space? ... 1. Explicit completeness -- impossible if the state is genuinely unbounded. 2. Structural completeness -- rules/relations are sufficient to derive answers. 3. Question-relative completeness -- sufficient to answer all questions in a defined question space. I suspect #2 and #3 will be much more important than #1 for KnowledgeOS.
rows.statement: Poses 'what does it mean to have a complete or ideal state of an infinite Knowledge Space?' and distinguishes three completeness notions: explicit completeness (impossible if genuinely unbounded), structural completeness (rules/relations sufficient to derive answers), and question-relative completeness (sufficient to answer all questions in a defined question space); hypothesizes that structural and question-relative completeness will matter far more than explicit completeness for KnowledgeOS. Connects Infinite state -> finite observations -> projection/extraction -> question-answerability, inviting comparison of measure theory, probability, logic, information theory, model theory, knowledge space theory, and epistemic logic -- not to decide what KnowledgeOS is, but to understand how a useful epistemic state is extracted from an effectively infinite space.
missing: proof that structural/question-relative completeness suffice in practice

rows.anchor: Nexus 2.69 is old ... I am not deriving that fact from the observation itself. O_t="Nexus version is 2.69." To determine that it is old, we need another piece of knowledge: I_t="The current/required version is 3.85." Then a human-defined comparison rule says: 2.69<3.85 therefore: Nexus 2.69 is old. This is exactly the ideal-state comparison mechanism.
rows.statement: Worked example exposing a flaw in the prior model: 'Nexus 2.69 is old' is not derived from the observation O_t='Nexus version is 2.69' alone; it also requires the reference/ideal state I_t='the current/required version is 3.85' and a comparison rule (2.69<3.85), yielding the determination 'Nexus 2.69 is old'. Three distinct facts are involved: Fact 1 (observation, F_1=2.69), Fact 2 (reference/ideal state, I_t=3.85), Fact 3 (determination, F_3=(2.69<3.85)) -- the third cannot be obtained from the first alone.
invariants: a determination fact requires both an observation and a reference/ideal state -- never the observation alone

lineage_claims.target: an implicit prior assumption that a determination could be derived from the observation alone
lineage_claims.quote: That example exposes an important flaw in how I described the previous model.

rows.anchor: The word "old" is not an intrinsic property of version 2.69. It is a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t. So if tomorrow the reference becomes 4.0, Old(2.69) remains true. But if the reference were somehow 2.0, Old(2.69) would be false.
rows.statement: Establishes that 'old' is not an intrinsic property of a value but a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t, whose truth depends entirely on the current reference (true if the reference rises to 4.0, false if the reference were 2.0) -- knowledge is often produced by comparing an observed state against a reference/ideal state, not by inspecting the observed state alone.
invariants: a relational property's truth value depends on the current reference state, not on the compared value alone

rows.anchor: K_t = Compare(O_t,I_t,R_t) where R_t contains the applicable reasoning/rules. For Nexus: O_t=2.69, I_t=3.85, R_t: "a version lower than the current required version is outdated." Therefore: K_t="Nexus 2.69 is outdated."
rows.statement: Formalizes the determination as K_t=Compare(O_t,I_t,R_t), where R_t is the applicable reasoning/rules; for Nexus, O_t=2.69, I_t=3.85, R_t='a version lower than the current required version is outdated', giving K_t='Nexus 2.69 is outdated'.

rows.anchor: The ideal state itself is Knowledge. Someone had to establish: 3.85 is the current/required version. That did not come from the comparison. It came from another chain of knowledge: Vendor releases 3.85 -> Human/system observes it -> Evidence -> Determination -> "3.85 is current/required" -> Ideal/reference state. So KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge.
rows.statement: The ideal/reference state is itself Knowledge, established through its own prior chain (vendor releases 3.85 -> observed -> evidence -> determination -> '3.85 is current/required' -> becomes the ideal/reference state); this reveals KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge -> (recursively) Updated Reference State -> ...
invariants: the reference/ideal state is never exempt from needing its own knowledge-establishment chain

rows.anchor: I previously said: Ideal State -> Observation -> Probability -> Knowledge. That is incomplete. Your Nexus example suggests: Reference/Ideal Knowledge + Observed State + Comparison Rules -> New Determination. And probability enters when either the observed state or the reference/ideal state is uncertain.
rows.statement: Corrects the previously stated pipeline 'Ideal State -> Observation -> Probability -> Knowledge' (declared incomplete) to 'Reference/Ideal Knowledge + Observed State + Comparison Rules -> New Determination', with probability entering specifically when either the observed state or the reference/ideal state itself is uncertain (e.g. 'we believe the current version is 3.85 with probability 0.9' and 'we believe the installed version is 2.69 with probability 0.99'), propagating an epistemic state to the determination under the chosen regime.

lineage_claims.target: the previously stated pipeline 'Ideal State -> Observation -> Probability -> Knowledge'
lineage_claims.quote: I previously said: ... That is incomplete.

rows.anchor: Many knowledge statements are not standalone facts. They are relationships between states. ... perhaps KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally think: Fact A, Fact B, Fact C but: Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.
rows.statement: Argues many knowledge statements are relationships between states (2.69<3.85; CurrentArchitecture!=RequiredArchitecture; ObservedState does-not-entail RequiredState) rather than standalone facts; proposes KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally model Fact A/Fact B/Fact C as independent items, but as Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.

rows.anchor: Descriptive ideal: What is the complete/correct state of the thing? Normative ideal: What should the state be according to rules, principles, requirements, laws, etc.? ... I_t^descriptive=current vendor version 3.85 and I_t^normative=version 3.85 is the required version. Those are different.
rows.statement: Introduces a critical research distinction between two kinds of 'ideal state': the descriptive ideal (what is the complete/correct state of the thing, e.g. current vendor version is 3.85) and the normative ideal (what should the state be according to rules/principles/requirements/laws, e.g. version 3.85 is the required version) -- these are different and KnowledgeOS may need to understand both; gives five worked domain examples of the ideal state (Nexus version, election validity conditions, approved software architecture, required governance state, required business process state).
invariants: descriptive ideal and normative ideal are never conflated

rows.anchor: What is the nature of the reference/ideal state against which observations are compared, and how is that reference state itself established? ... Knowledge -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge -> Updated Reference State -> ...
rows.statement: Sets the next research question: what is the nature of the reference/ideal state against which observations are compared, and how is that reference state itself established -- framed as necessary to understand the full recursive cycle Knowledge -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge -> Updated Reference State -> (repeat).

rows.anchor: There may be different reference states: I_t^business, I_t^architecture, I_t^security, I_t^legal, I_t^vendor, etc. Therefore the phrase "the ideal state" is dangerous. The more defensible formulation is currently: A reference/ideal state relative to a subject, purpose, context and point in time.
rows.statement: Corrects the singular phrase 'the ideal state' as dangerous, since there may be different reference states for different purposes (I_t^business, I_t^architecture, I_t^security, I_t^legal, I_t^vendor, etc.); the more defensible formulation is 'a reference/ideal state relative to a subject, purpose, context and point in time' -- e.g. 'the current version' and 'the required version' of Nexus are not necessarily the same statement.
invariants: there is no single universal ideal state -- every ideal/reference state is relative to a subject, purpose, context, and time

lineage_claims.target: the earlier singular usage of 'the ideal state' I_t as if there were one universal reference
lineage_claims.quote: Therefore the phrase "the ideal state" is dangerous.

rows.anchor: Fact = a determined proposition under specified conditions is a strong hypothesis. But we have not yet proven this definition across all types of knowledge. For example, purely descriptive facts may not require a normative reference state.
rows.statement: Proposes Fact = a determined proposition under specified conditions as a strong hypothesis (per the observation/reference/rule/determination chain, e.g. Nexus=2.69 vs required=3.85 vs 'below required is outdated' vs 'Nexus is outdated'), but explicitly notes it has not been proven across all types of knowledge -- purely descriptive facts may not require a normative reference state at all.
missing: proof the definition holds for purely descriptive facts

rows.anchor: We don't yet know whether Knowledge Space means: all possible propositions; all true propositions; all possible states; all possible information; all questions; all relationships; something more abstract. Therefore: K (script) is still a research concept, not a mathematical definition.
rows.statement: Acknowledges the infinite Knowledge Space K-script remains undefined at the element level: unresolved whether it means all possible propositions, all true propositions, all possible states, all possible information, all questions, all relationships, or something more abstract -- it remains a research concept, not a mathematical definition.

rows.anchor: whether there is one ideal state; whether there are multiple reference states; whether the ideal state is descriptive or normative; whether it can be infinite; whether it is itself Knowledge; how it is constructed; how we know that our model of it is adequate. So: Ideal State is still a research hypothesis.
rows.statement: Lists what remains unsolved about the Ideal State, currently the biggest unresolved issue: whether there is one ideal state or multiple reference states, whether it is descriptive or normative, whether it can be infinite, whether it is itself Knowledge, how it is constructed, and how adequacy of our model of it is known -- Ideal State remains a research hypothesis, not a solved concept.

rows.anchor: S_t = {(d_i,v_i)} ... A dimension is a distinguishable fact/aspect of a state ... An observation is an acquisition of information about some aspect/dimension of a state. ... Evidence: Information that supports or challenges a determination about a dimension's value. ... Determination: A conclusion produced from information, evidence, reference states, and applicable reasoning. Knowledge (Tentative): A time-dependent body of determined information about a state. The Ideal/Reference State: A reference against which observed values can be evaluated.
rows.statement: Consolidates six 'strong working hypotheses' into working definitions: a state at time t is S_t={(d_i,v_i)} (dimension-value pairs); a dimension is a distinguishable fact/aspect of a state; an observation is an acquisition of information about some dimension; evidence is information that supports or challenges a determination about a dimension's value; a determination is a conclusion produced from information/evidence/reference-states/reasoning; Knowledge (tentative) is a time-dependent body of determined information about a state; the ideal/reference state is a reference against which observed values are evaluated, possibly multiple (business/architecture/security/legal/etc.).

rows.anchor: Q5: What is the "ideal state"? ... Q6: Who establishes the ideal value? ... vendor specification? security policy? architecture decision? business requirement? law? expert judgement? What happens when they disagree? ... Q7: Is an ideal value necessarily a single value? What if acceptable versions are [3.80,3.85,3.90]?
rows.statement: Poses three unresolved questions about the ideal state: Q5 what is the ideal state (one universal state or multiple I_t^business/architecture/security/legal/...; what makes a state 'ideal' -- true/expected/required/desired/compliant reality or complete information); Q6 who establishes the ideal value (vendor spec, security policy, architecture decision, business requirement, law, expert judgement) and what happens when sources disagree; Q7 whether an ideal value is necessarily a single value or could be a set/range (e.g. acceptable versions [3.80,3.85,3.90] vs Version>=3.80). All marked Status: Undefined.

rows.anchor: Knowledge at Monday and knowledge at Tuesday are different epistemic states. ... K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. ... When a new dimension is discovered ... we gain knowledge. But the comparison with the previous state also reveals: The previous knowledge was less complete than today's knowledge. Even if the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty.
rows.statement: Knowledge at different times are different epistemic states, and a determination can be historically valid/obsolete/superseded/no longer applicable without deleting the historical record -- K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. Also: discovering a new dimension retroactively reveals that the PREVIOUS knowledge state was less complete than today's, even when the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty -- completeness assessment of past knowledge changes with later dimension discovery.
invariants: a knowledge trajectory is preserved, never overwritten, across time

rows.anchor: We still haven't formally defined Knowledge ... Knowledge is an evolving determination about an observed state, based on identified dimensions, their values, evidence, reasoning, relationships and temporal context. But we haven't established that this is the final definition. ... We haven't formally defined the "ideal state" ... Is it: the complete actual state? the complete possible description of the state? the theoretically complete set of dimensions and values? something else? This remains open.
rows.statement: Records two unsolved problems: (1) Knowledge still lacks a formal definition, with the current candidate being 'an evolving determination about an observed state, based on identified dimensions, their values, evidence, reasoning, relationships and temporal context' -- not established as final; (2) the ideal state I_t remains undefined -- unresolved whether it is the complete actual state, the complete possible description of the state, the theoretically complete set of dimensions and values, or something else.

rows.anchor: Reality/complete state versus: Observed/reconstructed state. But the exact relationship between them is still an open research problem. ... what it means for K_t to be correct relative to: information available at t; the underlying state; the reference state; applicable rules; later-discovered dimensions. This needs deeper epistemological and mathematical research. ... sets; dimensions; vectors/state spaces; relationships; probability; temporal structures; evidence; logical reasoning. But we haven't determined which mathematical structures are actually necessary.
rows.statement: Records three further unsolved problems: the exact relationship between the reality/complete state and the observed/reconstructed state remains open; correctness of K_t relative to available information, the underlying state, the reference state, applicable rules, and later-discovered dimensions is not formally defined, needing deeper epistemological and mathematical research; and among the candidate mathematical structures (sets, dimensions, vectors/state spaces, relationships, probability, temporal structures, evidence, logical reasoning), it has not been determined which are actually necessary -- named as where the independent mathematics research should continue.

rows.anchor: Knowledge starts with comparison, not accumulation. ... Knowledge_t = Comparison(ActualState_t, IdealState_t) ... Level 1 -- State difference: Actual != Ideal. Level 2 -- Meaning of the difference: acceptable/unacceptable/relevant/irrelevant. Level 3 -- Business determination: Action is required. ... Actual -> Difference -> Interpretation -> Determination.
rows.statement: Establishes the business principle 'Knowledge starts with comparison, not accumulation': the first business action is establishing a trusted reference and comparing it against actual system data, formalized as Knowledge_t = Comparison(ActualState_t, IdealState_t); a bare difference (e.g. 1 GB memory gap) is not self-interpreting, requiring three levels: Level 1 state difference (Actual != Ideal), Level 2 meaning of the difference (acceptable/unacceptable/relevant/irrelevant, requiring a business rule/context), and Level 3 business determination (action required) -- Actual -> Difference -> Interpretation -> Determination.
invariants: a raw state difference never by itself determines whether action is required -- interpretation via business rule/context is always required

rows.anchor: The reference itself has an epistemic history. We cannot simply store: RequiredVersion=3.85. We potentially need to know: Why do we accept 3.85 as the reference? ... Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. ... Trust is not the same as truth. ... Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance.
rows.statement: The reference/ideal state is itself knowledge requiring its own epistemic history: not merely RequiredVersion=3.85, but why 3.85 is accepted (who stated it, what evidence/justification, what trust rule, when valid, who accepted it, has it since changed), giving the recursive chain Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. Trust is not the same as truth: a trusted source's statement must preserve why it is trusted (Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance), not merely who said it.
invariants: a reference/ideal state is never stored as a bare value -- its own justification chain must be preserved
trust is never conflated with truth

rows.anchor: Priority(d | Context, Purpose, Decision) can be assigned to a dimension. ... the same dimension can have different priority at different times or in different contexts. ... Dimension+Value+Evidence+Reason+Direction+Priority+Time. ... And the conflict itself is knowledge. ... the ideal state may itself be multi-dimensional and internally constrained ... approaching something resembling a decision space, rather than a single ideal point.
rows.statement: Formalizes dimension priority as context-relative, Priority(d|Context,Purpose,Decision), never an intrinsic property (e.g. Priority(Security)>Priority(Cost) in one decision, reversed in another); proposes a richer per-dimension record Dimension+Value+Evidence+Reason+Direction+Priority+Time; restates conflict-itself-is-knowledge via a Decision/Security/Cost/Architecture conflict diagram feeding Human/Governance Decision; and extends the ideal state to be multi-dimensional and internally constrained (e.g. maximize security while staying within budget and remaining architecture-compliant), resembling a decision space rather than a single ideal point.
invariants: dimension priority is never an intrinsic property -- always relative to context/purpose/decision

rows.anchor: Reality timeline: S_t1 -> S_t2 -> S_t3 ... Knowledge timeline: K_t1 -> K_t2 -> K_t3 ... These timelines are not identical. ... Historical validity: Valid(K,t_determination). Current applicability: Applicable(K,t_now). Current completeness: Complete(K,t_now). These are not the same thing. ... Correct(K,t) is potentially different from Correct(K,t+delta t).
rows.statement: Introduces two non-identical timelines: the Reality timeline S_t1->S_t2->S_t3 (what actually happened) and the Knowledge timeline K_t1->K_t2->K_t3 (what was determined) -- a dependency can exist on the reality timeline while being absent from the knowledge timeline until discovered. Separates three temporal concepts that are not the same thing: historical validity Valid(K,t_determination) (was the determination defensible when made), current applicability Applicable(K,t_now) (does it still describe the current state), and current completeness Complete(K,t_now) (does current knowledge include all currently-known/relevant dimensions); correctness itself is time-indexed, Correct(K,t) potentially differing from Correct(K,t+delta-t).
invariants: the reality timeline and the knowledge timeline are never assumed identical
historical validity, current applicability, and current completeness are three distinct properties

rows.anchor: Historical knowledge ... Obsolete knowledge ... Superseded knowledge ... Incorrect knowledge ... these labels are not mutually exclusive. ... "historically valid" and "currently incorrect/obsolete" can coexist. ... K=(claim, determination time, evidence, context, status) and its status can evolve. ... KnowledgeOS should not delete or rewrite the previous knowledge state. Instead: K_t1 -> K_t2 with an explicit relationship: K_t2 supersedes/revises K_t1.
rows.statement: A superseded determination can simultaneously be historical knowledge (records what was determined then), obsolete knowledge (no longer represents current state), superseded knowledge (replaced by a newer determination), and incorrect knowledge (from the current perspective) -- these labels are not mutually exclusive; 'historically valid' and 'currently incorrect/obsolete' can coexist. Formalizes K=(claim, determination_time, evidence, context, status) with an evolving status field. KnowledgeOS should never delete or rewrite the previous knowledge state; instead K_t1 -> K_t2 with an explicit supersedes/revises relationship, preserving what was known, when, which dimensions, what evidence/reasoning, what determination, and what new information caused revision, so the evolution can be reconstructed.
invariants: a prior knowledge state is never deleted or rewritten, only explicitly superseded/revised while being preserved

rows.anchor: the ideal state exists independently of our knowledge. ... d_dependency in I_Mon even though humans do not know about it. So: Unknown dimension != Nonexistent dimension. ... Our observed state is only a projection. O_Mon = Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon). ... the missing dimension is not a missing part of reality. It is a missing part of our observation/extraction. ... Discovery does not create the dimension. It changes our knowledge of the dimension. ... dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.
rows.statement: Resolves an apparent reality/knowledge contradiction: the ideal state I_t exists independently of our knowledge of it -- a dependency dimension can already be an element of I_Mon (d_dependency in I_Mon) even though unknown, so unknown dimension != nonexistent dimension. The observed state is only a projection, O_Mon=Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon), so a missing dimension is a gap in observation/extraction, not in reality. Discovery therefore does not create the dimension -- it changes our knowledge of it: dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.
invariants: a dimension's existence in the ideal state never depends on the observer's knowledge of it
dimension discovery is always an epistemic event, never an ontological one

rows.anchor: Ideal State != Probability but: Knowledge Extraction about the Ideal State -> may involve probability. ... Reality/ideal state I_t. Observable information O_t. Knowledge K_t. So: I_t -> O_t -> K_t. ... Ideal observation O_t*=I_t (hypothetical). Actual observation O_t subset O_t*. ... K_t=I_t is generally impossible for a finite observer ... the gap is not simply I_t-K_t. There is an unknown portion of the gap.
rows.statement: Reaffirms Ideal State != Probability, but knowledge extraction about the ideal state may involve probability; formalizes three objects I_t (reality/ideal state) -> O_t (observable information) -> K_t (knowledge), where the first arrow is constrained by observation capability and the second by reasoning/evidence/rules/models/uncertainty. Distinguishes a hypothetical ideal observation O_t*=I_t (capturing all dimensions and values) from the actual observation O_t subset-of O_t* -- humans may never achieve the ideal observation even though the ideal state exists. Since I_t may have infinitely many dimensions, K_t=I_t is generally impossible for a finite observer, and even 'how close is K_t to I_t' is difficult since the gap I_t-K_t itself has an unknown portion (dimensions not yet known to exist).
missing: a way to bound or estimate the unknown portion of the gap
invariants: a finite observer can never achieve K_t=I_t when I_t has unboundedly many dimensions

rows.anchor: How can we determine whether the new information changes the ideal state, or merely changes our knowledge of the already-existing ideal state? ... state change versus knowledge change ... one of the most important unresolved questions ... a Kernel that cannot distinguish those two will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. ... hat-I_Tue != hat-I_Mon even if none of the previously known values changed. ... both state and observed model of the state can change ... they are not mutually exclusive explanations.
rows.statement: Distinguishes state change (the actual/ideal state I_t itself changes, e.g. Nexus is actually upgraded) from knowledge change (a previously-existing but unknown dimension is merely discovered) -- named one of the most important unresolved questions, since a Kernel unable to distinguish them will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. Formalizes that the observed ideal state must be recalculated purely from dimension-set expansion alone: if D_t subset D_{t+1}, then generally hat-I_t(D_t) != hat-I_{t+1}(D_{t+1}) even when every previously known dimension's value is unchanged -- the representation changed because the dimensional basis expanded, not because any value did. State change and dimension discovery can occur simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive explanations for why knowledge changed.
invariants: state change (reality) and knowledge change (discovery) are two distinct causes of Knowledge(t2)!=Knowledge(t1), never conflated

rows.anchor: Reality/actual state R_t. Complete conceivable description I_t* -- potentially infinite or inaccessible. Current reconstructed knowledge hat-I_t. So: hat-I_t != I_t* and potentially: I_t* != R_t if our conceptual model itself is incomplete.
rows.statement: Adds a third layer to the ideal-state terminology: reality/actual state R_t, complete conceivable description I_t* (potentially infinite or inaccessible), and current reconstructed knowledge hat-I_t -- giving hat-I_t != I_t* (our reconstruction never necessarily matches the complete conceivable description) and potentially I_t* != R_t (our conceptual model of what's conceivable may itself be incomplete relative to reality).
invariants: reality, the complete conceivable description, and the current reconstruction are three potentially-distinct levels

rows.anchor: Complete knowledge is impossible . this is not true but you try to catch the complete knowelge with your best but you will never reach that completeness becasue it is infinite. however you are better and better through this process.
rows.statement: A human correction rejects 'complete knowledge is impossible' as too absolute and reframes it as an asymptotic-approach model: complete knowledge K* exists as an ideal/reference point; because Ω is unbounded, no finite K_t reaches K*, but the process is one of continual improvement/approximation. Formalized as K_t -> K* as knowledge improves, while K_t ≠ K* for any finite t; improvement redefined as Quality(K_{t+1}) > Quality(K_t) (more relevant dimensions, better evidence, fewer unresolved contradictions, better-justified values, better semantic interpretation, fewer hidden assumptions, better coverage) rather than simply |K_{t+1}| > |K_t|, since a new dimension can reduce confidence in an existing determination.
invariants: K_t ≠ K* for finite t, assuming Ω is genuinely unbounded

rows.anchor: The ideal knowledge state of an observation consists of the dimensions that characterize that observation and the values/relationships associated with those dimensions. Because the dimension space may be unbounded, complete knowledge is treated as an ideal target rather than a finite endpoint. ... Seek (D*,V*) through iterative discovery and determination ... rather than Assume D_t=D*
rows.statement: States the document's final central hypothesis: the ideal knowledge state consists of the dimensions characterizing an observation plus their values/relationships; because the dimension space may be unbounded, completeness is an ideal target (K*, D*, V*) rather than a finite endpoint, and KnowledgeOS must continuously seek (D*,V*) through iterative discovery/determination rather than assuming D_t = D* — called 'the heart of the Infinite Knowledge Space model'.

rows.anchor: Complete knowledge is the ideal target. Under an unbounded knowledge-space hypothesis, a finite knowledge state cannot establish that it has exhausted the space merely because no further dimensions have yet been discovered. ... Discover dimensions -> Determine values -> Recalculate -> Search again ... This is knowledge expansion, not merely document ingestion.
rows.statement: Restates completeness as a search objective rather than an assumption: D_t ⊆ D*, K_t ⊆ K*, with a continuous cycle Discover dimensions -> Determine values -> Recalculate -> Search again, characterized as 'knowledge expansion, not merely document ingestion'.

rows.anchor: Reality/state R_t ... Ideal knowledge K^*(R_t) ... Current knowledge K_t(R_t) ... K_t(R_t)\subseteq K^*(R_t) ... K^*(R_t)\neq R_t ... knowledge about something is not identical to the thing itself.
rows.statement: Introduces a three-level formal distinction: Reality/state R_t (what actually exists), Ideal knowledge K*(R_t) (complete knowledge if all relevant dimensions/values were known), and Current knowledge K_t(R_t) (what is currently known), with K_t(R_t) ⊆ K*(R_t) and K*(R_t) ≠ R_t (even ideal knowledge about a thing is not identical to the thing).

rows.anchor: if Ω is genuinely infinite and unknown, we cannot generally calculate this distance. Therefore this is a conceptual convergence process, not necessarily a measurable metric. ... we cannot automatically claim: "We are 93.4% of the way to complete knowledge."
rows.statement: Warns that the convergence d(K_t,K*) toward the ideal is a conceptual process, not a measurable metric, when Ω is genuinely infinite/unknown; explicitly forbids claims like 'we are 93.4% of the way to complete knowledge' absent a known metric and denominator, though bounded domains can measure improvement.

rows.anchor: \lim_{t \to \infty} \text{Improve}(K_t) \to K^* ... But K^* may be unreachable if |\Omega|=\infty.
rows.statement: Restates the asymptotic-approach model using explicit limit notation: lim_{t→∞} Improve(K_t) → K*, while noting K* may be unreachable if |Ω| = ∞.

rows.anchor: R_t: Actual observed reality/state — what exists ... S^*_t: Ideal complete characterization of that state — what could be known ... K_t: Current justified knowledge representation — what we know ... K_t \rightarrow S^*_t while K_t \neq S^*_t and potentially S^*_t \subseteq \Omega
rows.statement: States the core unresolved gap of the whole research line as a three-object boundary problem: R_t (actual reality), S*_t (ideal complete characterization of that reality, a new notation distinct from prior K*), and K_t (current justified representation), with K_t → S*_t, K_t ≠ S*_t, and S*_t ⊆ Ω; states the Lord Lens gives the horizon Ω while the Zero Lens examines what prevents K_t from equalling S*_t.

rows.anchor: Is knowledge value determined by: number of dimensions? quality of evidence? confidence? completeness? relevance? consistency? explanatory power? decision usefulness? ... Knowledge itself does not care about priority. ... KnowledgeValue \neq DecisionPriority
rows.statement: States 'knowledge value' Value(K) is used repeatedly (knowledge increases/decreases) but never mathematically defined; lists eight candidate determinants (dimension count, evidence quality, confidence, completeness, relevance, consistency, explanatory power, decision usefulness) and formalizes KnowledgeValue ≠ DecisionPriority as a distinction requiring formalization.

rows.anchor: Truth(P)=1 while Determination(P)=? because nobody has discovered the evidence. This may be one of the most important foundational distinctions still missing.
rows.statement: Argues Truth and Determination must be kept formally separate: a proposition can be true (Truth(P)=1) in reality while our Determination(P)=? because nobody has yet discovered the relevant evidence — flagged as possibly the most important missing foundational distinction in the whole model.
invariants: Truth(P) can be 1 while Determination(P) is undetermined

rows.anchor: The quantification of the fact is the ideal value of that dimension of the observed state. ... V^*(d,O,C,t) versus \hat V(d,O,C,t) ... Knowledge Gap = V^*-\hat V
rows.statement: Formalizes a prior informal claim ('the quantification of the fact is the ideal value of that dimension') into ideal value V*(d,O,C,t) vs current estimated value V̂(d,O,C,t), with Knowledge Gap = V* − V̂ where the value space permits subtraction, connecting the ideal-state-comparison model to a concrete per-dimension gap quantity.

type_signature.domain: dimension d, observation O, context C, time t

rows.anchor: We therefore need four—not three—fundamental things ... N = Knower/Observer ... (N, R_t, S_t^*, K_t) ... O=(N,R,C,T,P) where N=observer/knower; R=observed reality/state; C=context; T=time; P=purpose/question.
rows.statement: Adds a fourth fundamental object N (Knower/Observer) to the previously three-object model (R_t reality, S*_t ideal state, K_t current knowledge), giving (N, R_t, S*_t, K_t); reformalizes 'observation' accordingly as O=(N,R,C,T,P) — observer, observed reality, context, time, purpose/question — rather than treating an observation as merely an object, while explicitly declining to accept the direct mapping 'Knower = KnowledgeOS/system' as an architecture decision.

rows.anchor: State=\{d_i:v_i\} is too simplistic. ... S_t = (D_t,V_t,R_t,C_t,T_t) ... A state is not merely a bag of values. It is a structured field containing distinguishable components and relationships.
rows.statement: Corrects the flat state model State={d_i:v_i} to a structured five-field tuple S_t=(D_t,V_t,R_t,C_t,T_t) (dimensions, values, relationships, context, temporal position), arguing a state is a structured field, not merely a bag of values.

rows.anchor:
Knowledge is not enough to determine action. ... Knowledge sufficiency 
eq Knowledge completeness ... Sufficiency(K_t,D,C) ... Completeness 
eq Confidence 
eq Sufficiency 
eq Priority ... This is one of the strongest results from this analysis.
rows.statement: Establishes Decision Sufficiency as a distinct new concept answering 'when does knowledge become sufficient for a decision?': Sufficiency(K_t,D,C) (is K_t enough to support decision D under context C?) is neither Completeness(K_t) nor Confidence nor Priority — a knowledge state can be incomplete yet sufficient for a specific decision, formalized as the four-way split Completeness ≠ Confidence ≠ Sufficiency ≠ Priority, explicitly named one of the strongest results of the analysis.

type_signature.domain: knowledge state K_t, decision D, context C

rows.anchor: Reasoning = deriving implications from known propositions according to explicit rules/models. ... Wisdom = understanding the broader structure, consequences and principles governing those determinations. ... reason and wisdom should not be collapsed.
rows.statement: Defines Reason as a justified transformation from premises/evidence to a conclusion via an explicit or declared logical/theoretical rule (inspectable/traceable), and distinguishes Wisdom as understanding the broader structure, consequences, and principles governing those determinations — stating the two must not be collapsed.

rows.anchor: Sattva/Rajas/Tamas ... I would not encode Sattva/Rajas/Tamas as literal KnowledgeOS statuses. But they reveal an important missing dimension: Knowledge Quality ... KnowledgeQuality \neq Truth ... KnowledgeQuality \neq Confidence
rows.statement: Introduces Knowledge Quality as a new missing concept (inspired by, but not implementing, the three Gunas), explicitly distinct from Truth and from Confidence — e.g. a highly biased source may still provide accurate information, so KnowledgeQuality ≠ Truth and KnowledgeQuality ≠ Confidence.

rows.anchor:
Trust 
eq Truth ... Trust 
eq Evidence ... TrustedSource(P)
ot\Rightarrow True(P) ... Trust influences the epistemic weight we assign to evidence; it does not determine reality.
rows.statement: Introduces Trust as a distinct epistemic concept separate from Truth and Evidence: a trusted source's claim does not thereby become true (TrustedSource(P) ⇏ True(P)); trust affects the epistemic weight assigned to evidence but does not determine reality — a distinction Zero should protect.

rows.anchor: Knower = system/consciousness. I would not accept that as an architecture decision. ... Observer and Knowledge Artifact must remain distinct. The system can record: Who observed this? without claiming: The system is the metaphysical Knower.
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects the mapping 'Knower = system/consciousness' as an architecture decision; the useful architectural abstraction instead keeps Observer and Knowledge Artifact strictly distinct — the system can record who observed something without claiming to itself be the metaphysical Knower.

rows.anchor: The object being observed and the process/actor observing it should not be conflated. ... separate bounded concepts such as: Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer ... rather than one giant Knowledge aggregate.
rows.statement: States a DDD architectural consequence: the observed object and the observing process/actor must not be conflated into one aggregate; proposes seven separate bounded concepts (Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer) rather than one giant 'Knowledge' aggregate.

rows.anchor: K_t = \langle D_t,V_t,R_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t,P_t,H_t \rangle ... this is still a candidate model, but it answers substantially more of our previous undefined questions. ... S_t^* = \langle D_t^*,V_t^*,R_t^*,C_t^* \rangle ... Gap_t=S_t^*-K_t ... we usually cannot calculate this gap completely.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate 8-field structures for current knowledge K_t=⟨D_t,V_t,R_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t,P_t,H_t⟩ (dimensions, values, relationships, evidence, reasoning/justification, context, provenance, epistemic/history state) and for the ideal state S*_t=⟨D*_t,V*_t,R*_t,C*_t⟩, defining Gap_t = S*_t − K_t while noting the gap generally cannot be fully calculated since S*_t itself is not fully known — explicitly marked candidate, not final.
missing: invariants, transitions, validity conditions for K_t

rows.anchor: We currently represent 127 recognized dimensions of Nexus. Of these, 109 have direct system evidence, 12 are supported by trusted external sources, and 6 remain unresolved. ... That is far more meaningful than: "We have 85% knowledge."
rows.statement: Gives a worked business-communication example: instead of answering 'how much do we know about Nexus?' with a single percentage, KnowledgeOS should answer with a structured breakdown (recognized dimension count, evidence-support breakdown, unresolved count, relationship coverage, count of areas where the dimensional model itself may be incomplete, and an explicit statement of decision-sufficiency vs completeness) — illustrating the practical payoff of the whole Lord+Zero+decision-sufficiency model.

rows.anchor: IdealState = Knower's perspective on Ω ... I would not accept this as our final definition. ... S_t^* = ideal characterization of the observed state versus N = observer/knower perspective. The Knower can observe or know the ideal state; it should not therefore be defined as the ideal state.
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects S0733's equation IdealState = Knower's perspective on Ω as conflating two things that must stay separate: S*_t (the ideal characterization of the observed state itself) and N (the observer/knower's perspective) — the Knower can know the ideal state without being defined as it.

lineage_claims.quote: I would not accept this as our final definition ... That conflates two things we now have reason to keep separate.

rows.anchor: Who or what can be a Knower? human? engineer? system? AI agent? sensor? external source? organization? governance body? ... Observer ... Source ... Interpreter ... Decision Owner ... Calling all of them "Knower" would destroy important business semantics.
rows.statement: Splits the overloaded philosophical 'Knower' concept into four architecturally distinct roles that must not be merged: Observer, Source, Interpreter, Decision Owner — illustrated with a pipeline (System observes -> AI Agent interprets -> Architecture Rule evaluates -> Architect decides), arguing collapsing all of these into one 'Knower' concept would destroy important business semantics.

rows.anchor: A correct determination is not automatically Knowledge. ... What additional property transforms a determination into Knowledge? Is it Determination + Provenance? Or Determination + Reason? Or Determination + Context + Evidence + Reason? ... We don't yet know.
rows.statement: Poses as still unresolved exactly what additional property must be added to a Determination to make it Knowledge (candidates: +Provenance, +Reason, +Context+Evidence+Reason, or requiring understanding of the field-observer relationship) — the correctness of a determination alone is not sufficient.

rows.anchor: legitimacy = non-attachment to outcomes. This is philosophically interesting but not sufficient for governance. ... Legitimacy = Authority + Evidence + Reason + Process + Scope ... true but unauthorized; well-evidenced but outside the person's authority; authorized but poorly evidenced. ... Truth \neq Legitimacy
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects S0731's 'Legitimacy = non-attachment to outcomes' as insufficient for governance, replacing it with Legitimacy = Authority + Evidence + Reason + Process + Scope; gives three worked counterexamples (true-but-unauthorized; well-evidenced-but-outside-authority; authorized-but-poorly-evidenced) to establish Truth ≠ Legitimacy.

lineage_claims.quote: This is philosophically interesting but not sufficient for governance.

rows.anchor: Does KnowledgeOS recommend action, authorize action, or execute action? Those are fundamentally different. This must remain outside the epistemic kernel unless explicitly governed. ... DecisionOwner ... DecisionAuthority ... KnowledgeOS should probably not silently decide.
rows.statement: Distinguishes recommending, authorizing, and executing action as fundamentally different capabilities that must remain outside the epistemic kernel unless explicitly governed; introduces DecisionOwner and DecisionAuthority as missing governance concepts, arguing KnowledgeOS should not silently decide.

rows.anchor: Is it a graph? propositions? dimensions + values? statements? models? semantic structures? evidence graphs? probability distributions? Until we define Representation(K_t) we cannot finalize the KnowledgeOS kernel.
rows.statement: Identifies the underlying representational data structure for K_t as the biggest remaining conceptual gap: is a 'representation' a graph, a set of propositions, dimensions+values, statements, a model, semantic structures, evidence graphs, or probability distributions — states the kernel cannot be finalized until Representation(K_t) is defined.

rows.anchor: Ontology | Reality, observation, state, dimension, value, relationship ... Decision | sufficiency, legitimacy, authority, ownership, action ... The next step should probably not be another philosophical book. ... formally define the KnowledgeOS ontology—starting with just six primitives: Observation, State, Dimension, Value, Evidence, Determination.
rows.statement: Collapses all accumulated open questions into eight foundational undefined domains (Ontology, Epistemology, Semantics, Logic, Infinite Space, Observation, Evolution, Decision) and issues a methodological pivot recommendation: stop consulting further philosophical sources and instead formally define six ontological primitives (Observation, State, Dimension, Value, Evidence, Determination), from which Knowledge, Reason, Probability, Confidence, Lord, Zero, and Decision can then be derived.

rows.anchor: Knower = the human who needs to understand and act upon an observation ... KnowledgeOS = a tool that increases the Knower's understanding ... I would not say: KnowledgeOS is the Knower. Nor: KnowledgeOS owns the knowledge. Instead: KnowledgeOS is an epistemic instrument for the Knower.
rows.statement: Resolves the ambiguous 'Knower' concept: Knower = the human who needs to understand and act upon an observation (not the KnowledgeOS system, and not owned by it); KnowledgeOS is explicitly an epistemic instrument FOR the Knower, helping answer 'what do I know, why, what don't I know, what could change my understanding.'

rows.anchor: Knowledge: What has been established about the observation. ... Understanding: The Knower's integrated comprehension of that knowledge, including relationships, reasoning, uncertainty and implications. ... KnowledgeOS: The tool that helps construct and present that understanding.
rows.statement: Establishes a three-way distinction between Knowledge (evidence-supported information/reasoning about an observation across dimensions/values/relationships/context), Understanding (the human Knower's integrated comprehension of that knowledge, including relationships, reasoning, uncertainty, implications), and KnowledgeOS (the system that helps construct/inspect/challenge/maintain that understanding) — KnowledgeOS(K_t) -> Understanding.

rows.anchor: Can we upgrade Nexus? ... KnowledgeOS should not simply answer: YES or NO. It should expose: WHAT WE KNOW / WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW / WHAT WE MAY NOT HAVE CONSIDERED / WHAT WE THINK / WHY / WHAT COULD CHANGE THE DETERMINATION / DECISION: Human / authorized owner.
rows.statement: Gives a concrete worked structured-answer template for a decision question ('Can we upgrade Nexus?') that a system must never answer with a bare YES/NO: it must expose what is known, what is not known, what may not even have been considered, the current provisional view and its reasoning, what could change the determination, and that the decision itself belongs to the human/authorized owner.

rows.anchor: Dhṛtarāṣṭra is not physically observing the battlefield himself. Sañjaya is the one providing the observation. ... Observed reality -> Observation capability -> Observer/source -> Information -> Knower ... observation does not necessarily require the Knower to be physically present at the observed state.
rows.statement: From Dhṛtarāṣṭra relying on Sañjaya's remote vision of the battlefield, derives that observation does not require the Knower to be physically present: a chain Observed reality -> Observation capability -> Observer/source -> Information -> Knower can mediate observation through an intermediary source.

rows.anchor: An observation is always made for a purpose within a context. ... Observation \neq Reality ... Observation = Reality \cap Context \cap Purpose \cap Observer
rows.statement: Formalizes a bounded-observation-context principle from Arjuna's specific request (not 'show me everything' but 'show me who I must fight'): Observation ≠ Reality; rather Observation = Reality ∩ Context ∩ Purpose ∩ Observer, compatible with the infinite-dimension model.

rows.anchor: Arjuna's knowledge increases. He sees the people. But paradoxically, his certainty about what to do decreases. ... More information \not\Rightarrow More decision certainty ... KnowledgeOS should therefore never equate information volume with decision quality.
rows.statement: Derives from Arjuna's crisis (more information about who he faces reduces, not increases, his certainty about what to do) the principle More information ⇏ More decision certainty, concluding KnowledgeOS must never equate information volume with decision quality — called one of the strongest observations in Chapter 1.

rows.anchor: The Knower's understanding of the ideal state can itself change after observing additional dimensions. ... Observation -> Knowledge -> Understanding -> IdealState_{t+1} ... The ideal state is not necessarily frozen.
rows.statement: Extends the ideal-state-comparison model with a feedback loop: Observation -> Knowledge -> Understanding -> IdealState_{t+1}, i.e. the Knower's own ideal-state model I_t is not frozen but can itself change as a consequence of new observation/knowledge/understanding, illustrated by Arjuna's changing sense of the desired outcome.
invariants: The ideal state is not necessarily frozen.

rows.anchor: Given what I now see, I cannot determine that fighting is the right action. ... Uncertainty about Decision \neq Uncertainty about Observation ... Knowledge about State and Knowledge about Decision
rows.statement: Distinguishes Uncertainty about Decision from Uncertainty about Observation: Arjuna is highly certain of the facts (these are his relatives) while being uncertain about the decision (whether to fight them), requiring KnowledgeOS to track Knowledge-about-State and Knowledge-about-Decision as separate epistemic dimensions.
invariants: Uncertainty about Decision ≠ Uncertainty about Observation

rows.anchor: O_{t+1} -> D_{new} -> K_{t+1} -> U_{t+1} -> I_{t+1} ... That is much more powerful than our original: Actual - Ideal = Knowledge ... KnowledgeOS is an evolving epistemic loop, not merely a comparison engine.
rows.statement: Formalizes the chapter's central candidate principle ('observation does not merely retrieve knowledge; it can change the Knower's model of the problem') as O_{t+1} -> D_new -> K_{t+1} -> U_{t+1} -> I_{t+1}, explicitly superseding the earlier simple comparison formula 'Actual - Ideal = Knowledge' with 'KnowledgeOS is an evolving epistemic loop, not merely a comparison engine.'

lineage_claims.target: the earlier 'Actual - Ideal = Knowledge' subtraction formula
lineage_claims.quote: That is much more powerful than our original: Actual - Ideal = Knowledge

rows.anchor: We should not say "KnowledgeOS is Sañjaya." We can say "KnowledgeOS performs a Sañjaya-like epistemic role for the human Knower." ... Battlefield/Dhṛtarāṣṭra/Sañjaya/Arjuna/Kṛṣṇa/Vyāsa's gift table
rows.statement: Proposes a full role-mapping analogy (Battlefield=observed reality/domain state; Dhṛtarāṣṭra=human Knower needing understanding; Sañjaya=KnowledgeOS; Arjuna=human participant/domain actor; Kṛṣṇa=guiding knowledge/higher reasoning lens; Vyāsa's gift=KnowledgeOS's ability to obtain/structure evidence beyond direct human observation), explicitly qualified as 'performs a Sañjaya-like role' rather than an identity claim, to keep the analogy useful without turning the Gita into an architecture spec.

rows.anchor: Observe -> Collect evidence -> Identify dimensions -> Structure statements -> Compare with ideal state -> Reason -> Expose uncertainty -> Expose missing dimensions -> Present understanding -> Human decides ... KnowledgeOS = Sañjaya-like epistemic intermediary, not simply KnowledgeOS=Sañjaya
rows.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS is more than a simple Sañjaya (who merely 'makes an inaccessible state observable'): it performs a full ten-step pipeline (observe, collect evidence, identify dimensions, structure statements, compare with ideal state, reason, expose uncertainty, expose missing dimensions, present understanding, human decides), formalized as KnowledgeOS = Sañjaya-like epistemic intermediary.

rows.anchor: Sañjaya reports. He doesn't become Dhṛtarāṣṭra. ... KnowledgeOS should report, explain, challenge and expose—but the human remains the owner of understanding and decision. ... KnowledgeOS \neq DecisionOwner
rows.statement: Uses the Sañjaya/Dhṛtarāṣṭra role separation to argue KnowledgeOS ≠ DecisionOwner: KnowledgeOS may report, explain, challenge, and expose, but the human remains owner of understanding and decision — pipeline KnowledgeOS -> Understanding -> Human -> Decision, consistent with the 'present both, warn the owner' rule.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is an epistemic intermediary between the observed world and the human Knower. It acquires and structures evidence, identifies dimensions and relationships, compares observations with the Knower's current ideal-state model, exposes uncertainty and missing knowledge, and provides the Knower with an understandable representation from which the human may make decisions.
rows.statement: Proposes a full candidate definition of KnowledgeOS as an epistemic intermediary between the observed world and the human Knower that acquires/structures evidence, identifies dimensions/relationships, compares against the Knower's ideal-state model, exposes uncertainty and missing knowledge, and provides an understandable representation for human decision-making — explicitly called a very strong candidate definition.

rows.anchor: Why do you believe this? Show me the evidence. What dimension is missing? What happens if this assumption is wrong? Compare it with the ideal state. What changed since yesterday? ... KnowledgeOS \neq Sañjaya as narrator ... Sañjaya + evidence system + reasoning system + Zero Lens + Lord Lens + interactive dialogue
rows.statement: Extends the Sañjaya analogy beyond passive one-way narration: the modern human Knower can interrogate KnowledgeOS interactively (why do you believe this, show me the evidence, what dimension is missing, what if this assumption is wrong, compare with the ideal state, what changed since yesterday), so KnowledgeOS ≠ Sañjaya-as-narrator but rather Sañjaya + evidence system + reasoning system + Zero Lens + Lord Lens + interactive dialogue.

rows.anchor: Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Knowledge_{battlefield}=\varnothing (directly observed) ... he does possess some prior/contextual information ... Dhṛtarāṣṭra has no direct knowledge of the current battlefield state and therefore requires an epistemic intermediary. ... Observer \neq Knower
rows.statement: Models Dhṛtarāṣṭra's blindness precisely: he has zero DIRECTLY-observed battlefield knowledge but does possess prior/contextual information (armies assembled, battle intended, parties known) — refining 'knows nothing' to 'has no direct knowledge, hence requires an epistemic intermediary'; formalizes Observer ≠ Knower with Sañjaya=Observer, Dhṛtarāṣṭra=Knower, KnowledgeOS=epistemic intermediary, resolving a previously open question.

rows.anchor: Reality(d)=v while Knowledge_{Dhṛtarāṣṭra}(d)=? ... Unknown_{Knower}(d) rather than Unknown_{Reality}(d) ... KnowledgeOS does not create the state, and it does not become the Knower. It reduces the gap between what exists in the observed state and what the human Knower can understand about that state.
rows.statement: States the capstone formalization: a dimension can have a perfectly definite value in reality (Reality(d)=v) while the Knower's knowledge of it remains unresolved (Knowledge_Knower(d)=?) — Zero must represent Unknown_Knower(d) as distinct from Unknown_Reality(d); concludes 'KnowledgeOS does not create the state, and it does not become the Knower. It reduces the gap between what exists in the observed state and what the human Knower can understand about that state.'

type_signature.codomain: reality value vs Knower's knowledge state

rows.anchor: Layer 1 — Sañjaya Layer: "What is the state?" ... L_S = State Knowledge ... Sañjaya Layer does not decide whether this is good or bad. It reconstructs the state. ... Layer 2 — Arjuna Layer: "What does this mean for me?" ... L_A = Understanding / Decision Knowledge
rows.statement: Proposes a two-layer KnowledgeOS architecture: the Sañjaya Layer L_S (State Knowledge — reconstructs the observed state as faithfully as possible, without judging it) and the Arjuna Layer L_A (Understanding/Decision Knowledge — determines what the state means given the Knower's purpose/ideal state); explicitly not two independent knowledge systems but two layers of processing with different responsibilities.

rows.anchor: Main question: What is happening? vs What does it mean? ... Can compare ideal state? Primarily no vs Yes ... Makes decision? No vs Supports human decision ... Owner: KnowledgeOS vs Human Knower
rows.statement: Gives a full comparison table distinguishing the two layers across seven axes (main question, focus, input, output, what each discovers, whether it can compare against the ideal state, whether it makes a decision, and who owns it) — Sañjaya layer cannot compare against the ideal state and does not decide; Arjuna layer can compare and supports the human decision but the human remains the ultimate owner.

rows.anchor: Sañjaya: Reality \rightarrow State Knowledge ... Arjuna: State Knowledge + Ideal State \rightarrow Understanding ... Understanding \rightarrow Human Decision
rows.statement: Formalizes the full pipeline: Sañjaya layer maps Reality to State Knowledge S_t; Arjuna layer maps (State Knowledge, Ideal State I_N) to Understanding via Compare(S_t,I_N); Understanding then feeds Human Decision.

rows.anchor: I would not make Krishna a third KnowledgeOS layer yet. Instead, Krishna can be treated as a lens / reasoning source / guidance mechanism operating on the Arjuna layer.
rows.statement: Makes an explicit architectural decision: Krishna is NOT a third KnowledgeOS layer but a lens/reasoning-source/guidance-mechanism operating on top of the Arjuna layer, keeping the layer count at two.

rows.anchor: LORD LENS -> SAÑJAYA LAYER -> ZERO LENS -> ARJUNA LAYER -> KRISHNA LENS -> HUMAN KNOWER -> learns -> Refines Ideal State -> SAÑJAYA AGAIN ... This is not a linear pipeline. It is an epistemic feedback loop.
rows.statement: Depicts the full architecture as a recursive epistemic feedback loop rather than a linear pipeline: Lord Lens -> Sañjaya Layer -> Zero Lens -> Arjuna Layer -> Krishna Lens -> Human Knower, who then refines the Ideal State and feeds back into Sañjaya again.
