rows.anchor: A two-layer epistemic system that first reconstructs knowledge about the observed state (Sañjaya Layer) and then transforms that state knowledge into contextual understanding for the human Knower (Arjuna Layer). ... the human remains outside the system as the ultimate Knower/owner of the ideal-state model and decision.
rows.statement: States the capstone candidate architecture principle: KnowledgeOS is a two-layer epistemic system (Sañjaya layer reconstructs state knowledge; Arjuna layer transforms it into contextual understanding), with the human always outside the system as owner of the ideal-state model and the decision; proposes testing this candidate architecture against Chapter 2, since that is where the actual Krishna-Arjuna knowledge-transfer process begins and can validate or refine the Arjuna-layer-as-Understanding claim.

rows.anchor: K_A(Reality) \neq K_B(Reality) ... KnowledgeOS must explicitly support the co-existence of multiple, potentially conflicting, knowledge representations of the same objective state, while clearly tracing their provenance.
rows.statement: Formalizes that different observers can have different knowledge states of the same reality, K_A(Reality) ≠ K_B(Reality), requiring KnowledgeOS to support co-existing, potentially conflicting knowledge representations of the same objective state while tracing their provenance — a multi-observer generalization beyond the single-Knower Unknown_Knower(d) formulation.

rows.anchor: Access \vDash Understanding ... More data or direct observation is not a solution. The system must distinguish between the raw data an observer has access to and the understanding they derive from it.
rows.statement: Formalizes 'physical presence does not guarantee understanding' as Access ⊭ Understanding (access does not entail understanding), a refutation of naïve realism: the system must keep raw data-access distinct from the derived understanding.

rows.anchor: Q_{new} \neq Q_{old} + New Info ... the process of inquiry generates new, deeper questions rather than just answering the original one.
rows.statement: Introduces an 'Inquiry Lifecycle' concept: new knowledge can change the question itself, formalized Q_new ≠ Q_old + New Info — the system must support inquiry that generates deeper/different questions, not merely answers to the original question.

rows.anchor: Sañjaya_K = (Observed, Inferred, Reported, Unknown, Conflicting, Unresolved) ... The system's raw output is not "truth"; it's a multi-faceted representation of epistemic status, preserving all its edges and ambiguities.
rows.statement: Formalizes the Sañjaya layer's output as a six-field epistemic-status tuple Sañjaya_K = (Observed, Inferred, Reported, Unknown, Conflicting, Unresolved), explicitly not a single truth value but a structure preserving every epistemic edge case.

rows.anchor: Q_t \xrightarrow{Inquiry} O_t(P) \xrightarrow{Reconstruction} S_t \xrightarrow{Comparison} I_t \xrightarrow{Understanding} U_t \xrightarrow{Knowledge Transfer} H_t \xrightarrow{Decision/Reflection} \{State Decision, Ideal State Revision (I_t \rightarrow I_{t+1})\}
rows.statement: Synthesizes all prior Chapter-1-derived principles into a single Core KnowledgeOS Epistemic Loop: a Knower's question Q_t drives purpose-driven observation O_t(P), reconstructed into State Knowledge S_t, compared against the Knower's Ideal I_t, yielding Understanding U_t transferred to the Human Knower H_t, who either makes a State Decision (ending the cycle) or revises the Ideal State (I_t->I_{t+1}, starting a new cycle) — explicitly confirmed as a feedback loop, not a linear pipeline.

type_signature.codomain: decision or revised ideal state I_{t+1}

rows.anchor: What is the role of the Krishna Lens when it acts as an "epistemic transformer" (diagnosing aśocyān anvaśocas tvam)? ... Chapter 2 is the ultimate test case.
rows.statement: Poses the Chapter 2 test agenda: what fundamental change occurs there, how the Arjuna Layer processes a profound epistemic shift, how Zero operates when an entire problem category (not just a value or dimension) is called into question, and what role the Krishna Lens plays as an 'epistemic transformer' — citing the specific Sanskrit phrase 'aśocyān anvaśocas tvam' as the diagnostic example to test.

rows.anchor: IdealState=f(Knowledge) ... I would not yet define ... as an established principle. ... I_{t+1}=Revision(I_t,U_t) ... I_N \neq I^* ... I_N = the Knower's current model of the ideal; I^* = the complete/ideal characterization that may lie beyond what the Knower can currently represent.
rows.statement: Rejects S0741's 'IdealState = f(Knowledge)' as premature, replacing it with I_{t+1} = Revision(I_t, U_t) (the Knower's ideal-state model may be revised as Understanding U_t grows) while explicitly preserving I_N ≠ I* (the Knower's current ideal model vs. the complete ideal characterization possibly beyond current representation) to keep the Lord Lens intact.

lineage_claims.quote: I would not yet define IdealState=f(Knowledge) as an established principle.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS \rightarrow Understanding_{Knower} ... rather than: KnowledgeOS \rightarrow Understanding \rightarrow Human ... The human isn't merely the recipient of understanding. The human is the subject in whom the understanding exists.
rows.statement: Corrects the pipeline 'KnowledgeOS -> Understanding -> Human' (which implies understanding is handed to a passive recipient) to 'KnowledgeOS -> Understanding_Knower' — the human is not downstream of understanding but the subject IN WHOM the understanding exists.

lineage_claims.quote: The human isn't merely the recipient of understanding. The human is the subject in whom the understanding exists.

rows.anchor: Ideal \leftrightarrow Observation \leftrightarrow Knowledge \leftrightarrow Understanding \leftrightarrow Ideal ... the result of understanding can change the Knower's understanding of the ideal. ... with Zero, Lord and Krishna lenses operating across the loop.
rows.statement: Replaces the linear 'Ideal -> Compare -> Answer' picture with a closed loop Ideal ↔ Observation ↔ Knowledge ↔ Understanding ↔ Ideal, since understanding's result can change the Knower's own conception of the ideal state, with Zero/Lord/Krishna operating across the whole loop rather than at one fixed stage.

rows.anchor: Test 1 — Does knowledge merely add dimensions? Or can it change the ontological model of the problem itself? ... Test 3 — Can Krishna Lens produce knowledge that changes the category of the question, rather than merely answering it? ... Test 6 — Does the Knower's ideal state remain stable, or can the very definition of "ideal" be transformed by deeper knowledge? That last question is probably going to be one of the most important architectural questions in Chapter 2.
rows.statement: Declares Chapter 1 'provisionally mined' (a testable hypothesis set, not proven truth) and sets six explicit falsification tests for Chapter 2: (1) can knowledge change the ontological model of the problem, not just add dimensions; (2) can the Arjuna Layer distinguish 'I don't know' from 'I have misunderstood what I am observing'; (3) can Krishna Lens change the category of the question rather than answer it; (4) can Zero operate when the missing element is a missing conceptual framework, not a missing fact; (5) can uncertainty be progressively reduced without pretending to reach completeness; (6) can the Knower's very definition of 'ideal' be transformed by deeper knowledge — flagged as probably the most important architectural question ahead.

rows.anchor: Information: Info = Raw_Data + Provenance ... Knowledge: Knowledge = Info + Meaning + Purpose ... Guiding Knowledge: K_Guide = f(State_Knowledge, Knower_Context, Ideal_State) ... Understanding: Understanding = Integration_Of(Knowledge) ... Decision Uncertainty: U_Dec = f(Unresolved_Meaning, Incomplete_Picture, Undefined_Goal) ... This is distinct from State_Uncertainty.
rows.statement: Formalizes a five-concept epistemic taxonomy: Information = Raw_Data+Provenance (descriptive, answers 'what/how' not 'why care'); Knowledge = Info+Meaning+Purpose (the Arjuna layer's currency, product of comparing State against Ideal); Guiding Knowledge K_Guide = f(State_Knowledge, Knower_Context, Ideal_State) (the Krishna Lens's output, prioritized/framed/actionable); Understanding = Integration_Of(Knowledge) (the final coherent internalized model); and Decision_Uncertainty U_Dec = f(Unresolved_Meaning, Incomplete_Picture, Undefined_Goal), explicitly distinct from State_Uncertainty — the specific uncertainty about what action to take.

rows.anchor: Information Increase \not\Rightarrow Decision Uncertainty Decrease ... the Krishna Lens is needed. It is not an information aggregator; it is an epistemic optimizer that prioritizes the right knowledge for the right purpose at the right time, thereby reducing U_Dec.
rows.statement: States the crucial invariant Information Increase ⇏ Decision Uncertainty Decrease as the formal justification for why the Krishna Lens exists: it is not an information aggregator but an 'epistemic optimizer' that prioritizes the right knowledge for the right purpose at the right time, specifically to reduce U_Dec.

rows.anchor: DDD (D): Domain Structure & Responsibility ... ensuring the Sañjaya Layer doesn't interpret, the Krishna Lens doesn't decide, and the Arjuna Layer doesn't overwrite objective reality. It maintains the integrity of the epistemic division of labor.
rows.statement: Gives the DDD Lens an explicit enforcement role: preventing the Sañjaya layer from interpreting, the Krishna Lens from deciding, and the Arjuna layer from overwriting objective reality — maintaining the epistemic division of labor across the whole architecture.

rows.anchor: The system must be stateful. It must remember Arjuna's U_t. ... The Krishna Lens must perform a gap analysis between U_t and I to determine the next most valuable piece of knowledge ... the goal of the system is not to produce a single definitive answer, but to support the Knower through a journey of understanding, reducing their uncertainty step-by-step until they are ready to act.
rows.statement: States four operational requirements for the 'progressive epistemic movement' idea: the system must be stateful (remembering U_t); Krishna must perform gap analysis between U_t and the ideal I to find the next most valuable knowledge; the system must adapt as I itself changes (the ideal-revision loop); and the system's goal is a step-by-step reduction of uncertainty toward readiness to act, not a single definitive answer.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS: \Omega \xrightarrow{Zero Lens} S_t \xrightarrow{Krishna Lens} A_t \xrightarrow{Krishna Lens} A_{t+1} \xrightarrow{...} A_n \xrightarrow{Knowledge Transfer} Knower's Decision ... KnowledgeOS's purpose is to reduce U_Dec for the Knower, guiding them toward readiness for action.
rows.statement: States a single unified KnowledgeOS equation consolidating the whole architecture: Ω (Lord) -> [Zero Lens] -> S_t (Sañjaya state knowledge) -> [Krishna Lens, iterated] -> A_t -> A_{t+1} -> ... -> A_n (Arjuna understanding, progressively advanced) -> Knowledge Transfer -> Knower's Decision; names the 'Sārathi Invariant' — KnowledgeOS's purpose is to reduce Decision_Uncertainty for the Knower, guiding them toward readiness for action.
invariants: KnowledgeOS's purpose is to reduce U_Dec for the Knower, guiding them toward readiness for action.

rows.anchor: I won't force Chapter 2 into our existing model. If Chapter 2 shows that something we called the "Arjuna Layer" is actually two different concepts, we'll split it. ... Chapter 1 gave us hypotheses. Chapter 2 is the experiment.
rows.statement: States an explicit falsification-first methodology for Chapter 2: track source facts, changes in Arjuna's knowledge state, changes in Krishna's role, and which Chapter-1 principles survive/need refinement/break; commits in advance to splitting or revising concepts rather than forcing the chapter into the existing model — 'Chapter 1 gave us hypotheses. Chapter 2 is the experiment.'

experiment.hypothesis: the Chapter-1-derived Sañjaya/Arjuna/Krishna/Zero/Lord architecture and its six falsification tests
experiment.setup: read Chapter 2 verse-by-verse against the six tests from S0743
experiment.assumptions: none frozen; the model may be split, revised, or extended
experiment.inputs: Bhagavad-gita As It Is, Chapter 2 text and Prabhupada purports
experiment.method: track S_t->U_t, U_t->U_{t+1}, I_t->I_{t+1}, Z_t->K_{t+1}, U_t->Action across the chapter
experiment.result: see subsequent contributions (all six tests reported 'fully validated')
experiment.interpretation: the architecture survived contact with a harder test case
experiment.limitations: validation is via lens-derived interpretation of a philosophical text, not an independent empirical trial
experiment.conclusion: the two-layer + Krishna/Zero/Lord model is provisionally retained and refined

rows.anchor: The Soul (ātman) is eternal. ... The Body is temporary. ... The Soul is immutable and indivisible. ... Duty (sva-dharma) is context-dependent. ... Results of action are not the measure of duty. ... The mind can be disciplined. ... The Krishna Lens is not a one-time correction. It is a guided tour through an epistemic landscape.
rows.statement: Gives a six-row worked example of progressive dimensional discovery (soul is eternal 2.12-13; body is temporary 2.18-22; soul is immutable/indivisible 2.23-25; duty is context-dependent 2.31-33; results are not the measure of duty 2.47-48; the mind can be disciplined 2.60-69), each introduced verse-by-verse and reframing prior understanding — validating the Krishna Lens as a sequenced 'guided tour', not a single correction.

rows.anchor: How do I avoid sin? -> How do I act in accordance with my eternal duty? ... Should I fight? -> What is my constitutional position as a living entity? ... Am I a killer? -> Am I the body, or am I the eternal soul? ... The system must be capable of changing the very category of the question it is answering.
rows.statement: Validates Test 3 (category-of-question change) with a three-row table showing Arjuna's original questions reframed into different-category questions (avoid sin -> act per eternal duty; should I fight -> what is my constitutional position; am I a killer -> am I body or soul), concluding the reframing mechanism requires a feedback loop where new understanding U_t revises the Ideal State I_{t+1}, which redefines the inquiry's purpose P.

rows.anchor: Family Loyalty | Replaced by the eternal soul's nature. ... Moral Purity | Replaced by duty (sva-dharma). Inaction is a greater sin than action. ... Personal Honor | Replaced by detachment from results. ... Goal of Life | Replaced by liberation (mokṣa). ... The system cannot assume a static, external "ideal state." The ideal is a dynamic model constructed by the Knower, and it evolves as understanding deepens.
rows.statement: Gives a concrete worked example of I_{t+1}=Revision(I_t,U_t): Arjuna's initial ideal state (family loyalty, moral purity, personal honor, avoiding sin) is systematically dismantled and rebuilt into a new ideal (soul's eternal nature, duty/sva-dharma, detachment from results, liberation/moksha) through Krishna's guidance, validating that the ideal state is dynamic, not static or externally fixed.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS's purpose is not to provide "truth." Its purpose is to guide the Knower from a state of paralyzing uncertainty to a state of informed readiness to act. ... It also positions the system as an epistemic guide (the Sārathi), not a final arbiter of truth.
rows.statement: Refines the system's stated purpose: KnowledgeOS's purpose is NOT to provide truth but to guide the Knower from paralyzing uncertainty to informed readiness to act — explicitly repositioning the system as an epistemic guide (the Sārathi) rather than a final arbiter of truth, sharpening the earlier 'Sārathi Invariant' wording.
invariants: KnowledgeOS's purpose is not to provide truth but to guide the Knower from paralyzing uncertainty to informed readiness to act.

lineage_claims.target: S0744's 'Sārathi Invariant' (KnowledgeOS's purpose is to reduce U_Dec...)
lineage_claims.quote: This is a more precise and powerful statement of our earlier model.

rows.anchor: 1. The two-layer model (Sañjaya/Arjuna) is structurally sound. 2. The Krishna Lens is not a "third layer" but a dynamic function (Knowledge + Guidance + Reframing) that operates on the Sañjaya Layer to generate the Arjuna Layer. 3. The Zero Lens and Krishna Lens are interdependent. 4. The ideal state is dynamic and subject to revision. 5. The ultimate goal of KnowledgeOS is "epistemic readiness"
rows.statement: States five concluding takeaways validated by the Chapter 2 test: the two-layer Sañjaya/Arjuna model is structurally sound; the Krishna Lens is a dynamic function (Knowledge+Guidance+Reframing) operating ON the Sañjaya Layer to GENERATE the Arjuna Layer (a slightly different framing than 'operating on the Arjuna layer' used elsewhere); Zero and Krishna are interdependent; the ideal state is dynamic; and KnowledgeOS's ultimate goal is 'epistemic readiness'.

rows.anchor: Sārathi frames the problem; human does not. I would change this. ... The Sārathi can challenge, reframe, expand, or propose a different perspective, but the Knower remains the owner of the problem, purpose and decision. ... Sārathi \rightarrow Propose/Reframe, not: Sārathi \rightarrow Own the Frame.
rows.statement: Second, titular correction: rejects the claim 'Sārathi frames the problem; human does not', replacing it with 'the Sārathi may propose, challenge, reframe or expand, but the Knower remains owner of the problem, purpose and decision' — Sārathi -> Propose/Reframe, never Sārathi -> Own the Frame; an important DDD boundary preserving Human Knower -> Ideal State ownership.
invariants: Sārathi may propose/reframe but never owns the frame

lineage_claims.target: a prior table entry 'Sārathi frames the problem; human does not'
lineage_claims.quote: I would change this.

rows.anchor: Function 1: Receive the Knower's uncertainty ... the Sārathi must know not only S_t ... but also U_t ... Function 2: Diagnose the actual problem ... Are you solving the right problem? ... Sārathi = Problem Diagnosis. But diagnosis is not decision ownership.
rows.statement: Derives two Sārathi functions from Chapter 2: (1) it must first understand both the observed state S_t AND the Knower's current understanding U_t before acting, rather than acting immediately; (2) it diagnoses the actual problem ('are you solving the right problem?'), which is more powerful than supplying another fact — but diagnosis is explicitly not decision ownership.

rows.anchor: SelectNextKnowledge(U_t,P_t) ... What is the next knowledge that will most improve the Knower's understanding? rather than: What additional information can I retrieve? ... D_t \rightarrow D_t + D_{new} ... D_{new} \rightarrow reinterpret(D_t) ... dimensional expansion and semantic re-evaluation.
rows.statement: Formalizes two further Sārathi functions: SelectNextKnowledge(U_t,P_t) — choosing the piece of knowledge that most improves understanding, not merely retrievable information — and dimensional expansion with semantic re-evaluation, D_t -> D_t+D_new followed by D_new -> reinterpret(D_t), consistent with the Chapter-1 recalculation principle.

rows.anchor: Sārathi: Knowledge \rightarrow Meaning \rightarrow Direction ... This is why Sārathi is a better architectural concept than merely "advisor." ... Sārathi Guidance \neq Uncertainty=0 ... Sārathi Guidance \rightarrow Relevant uncertainty reduced \rightarrow Actionable understanding
rows.statement: Formalizes two further Sārathi functions: connecting knowledge to the objective (Knowledge->Meaning->Direction, justifying 'Sārathi' over the weaker term 'advisor'), and reducing paralysis without promising zero uncertainty (Sārathi Guidance ≠ Uncertainty=0; rather Sārathi Guidance -> Relevant uncertainty reduced -> Actionable understanding).

rows.anchor: A charioteer does not merely explain the road. The charioteer helps the journey progress. ... the KnowledgeOS Sārathi role should have a notion of Progress. ... The Sārathi therefore operates longitudinally, not just as a one-time answer generator.
rows.statement: Adds a Progress function: the Sārathi should track longitudinal movement through a stage sequence (initial state -> uncertain -> missing dimension identified -> evidence acquired -> understanding improved -> decision confidence sufficient -> action -> observe resulting state), operating as an ongoing journey-companion rather than a one-time answer generator.

rows.anchor: K = \Omega ... because K_t \subset \Omega potentially forever. ... Knowledge Sufficiency for Current Action ... Not: Do we know everything? but: Do we know enough, with the remaining uncertainty explicitly understood, to proceed responsibly?
rows.statement: Refines the earlier 'complete knowledge' concept into a practical Knowledge-Sufficiency-for-Current-Action test: since K_t ⊂ Ω potentially forever, the relevant question is never 'do we know everything?' but 'do we know enough, with the remaining uncertainty explicitly understood, to proceed responsibly?' — flagged as one of the most important potential KnowledgeOS capabilities.

rows.anchor: Here is what we know. Here is what we don't know. Here is what changes if this assumption is false. Here are the consequences of the alternatives. Here is my recommended next inquiry. But: DecisionOwner = Human. The Sārathi can guide. The Arjuna/Knower decides.
rows.statement: States the final Sārathi function, preserving human agency: the Sārathi may state what is known, what is not known, what changes if an assumption is false, the consequences of alternatives, and a recommended next inquiry — but DecisionOwner = Human always; the Sārathi guides, the Knower decides.

rows.anchor: Krishna — Entity: Conceptual source/horizon represented through Lord Lens ... Sārathi — Role: Progressive knowledge, orientation, reframing, navigation ... Sañjaya — Role: State observation, evidence reconstruction, state reporting ... Arjuna — Role: Knower/actor: interpretation, decision, action
rows.statement: Gives a clean Entity-vs-Role separation table: Krishna is an Entity (conceptual source/horizon represented through the Lord Lens), while Sārathi, Sañjaya, and Arjuna are Roles (progressive-knowledge/orientation/reframing/navigation; state observation/reconstruction/reporting; and interpretation/decision/action respectively), plus Zero/Lord/DDD as cross-cutting lenses.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS = Sañjaya capability + Sārathi capability ... Sañjaya capability: Reality \rightarrow StateKnowledge ... Sārathi capability: StateKnowledge + IdealState + KnowerContext \rightarrow GuidedUnderstanding ... Human: GuidedUnderstanding \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow Action ... Reality_t \rightarrow Action \rightarrow Reality_{t+1}
rows.statement: Rejects treating KnowledgeOS as either 'Sañjaya' or 'Krishna' alone, formalizing it instead as the sum of two capabilities: Sañjaya capability (Reality->StateKnowledge) plus Sārathi capability (StateKnowledge+IdealState+KnowerContext->GuidedUnderstanding), with the Human taking GuidedUnderstanding->Decision->Action, and the resulting action changing reality (Reality_t->Action->Reality_{t+1}), starting the next observation cycle.

type_signature.domain: reality / (state knowledge, ideal state, knower context)

rows.anchor: Role: Warrior vs Charioteer ... Acts in battle: Yes vs No, as combatant ... Owns the action: Yes vs No ... Provides orientation: Receives vs Provides ... Executes the warrior's duty: Yes vs No
rows.statement: Gives a detailed eight-row responsibility comparison between Arjuna (Warrior: acts in battle, owns the action, makes the journey, receives orientation, executes duty) and Krishna-as-Sārathi (Charioteer: does not act as combatant, does not own the action, supports/navigates, provides orientation, does not execute the warrior's duty) — more precise than simply 'Krishna gives Arjuna knowledge.'

rows.anchor: Sārathi \neq Decision Maker ... Sārathi \neq Actor ... Sārathi = Guide of the Actor ... Sārathi: Knowledge \rightarrow Orientation \rightarrow Guidance ... Arjuna: Understanding \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow Action ... This preserves the distinction between guidance and agency.
rows.statement: Refines the previously 'too compressed' formula Krishna=Knowledge->Guidance->Action into Krishna->[assumes role]->Sārathi->[guides]->Arjuna, with Sārathi's internal process being Knowledge->Orientation->Guidance and Arjuna's being Understanding->Decision->Action; states Sārathi ≠ Decision Maker, Sārathi ≠ Actor, Sārathi = Guide of the Actor.

lineage_claims.target: the earlier 'Krishna = Knowledge -> Guidance -> Action' formula
lineage_claims.quote: I think this is now too compressed.

rows.anchor: Frames the problem | Yes (through the Krishna Lens) | No ... Provides knowledge | Yes | No ... Makes decisions | No | Yes ... Owns the action | No | Yes ... Is accountable for the outcome | No | Yes
rows.statement: Presents an eight-row System(Sārathi)-vs-Human responsibility table that explicitly assigns 'Frames the problem: Yes (through the Krishna Lens)' to the System — this is precisely the claim the same-batch S0746 later retracts ('Sārathi does not own the frame'; 'Sārathi -> Propose/Reframe, not Sārathi -> Own the Frame'), making this table an in-corpus contradiction later corrected rather than a stable position.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS \xrightarrow{provides} Guidance \xrightarrow{supports} Human Understanding \xrightarrow{enables} Human Decision \xrightarrow{results in} Human Action ... KnowledgeOS \not\Rightarrow Decision ... KnowledgeOS \not\Rightarrow Action ... It prevents the "Oracle" fallacy.
rows.statement: Formalizes the guidance/agency separation as a chain KnowledgeOS-provides->Guidance-supports->Human Understanding-enables->Human Decision-results in->Human Action, with explicit non-implications KnowledgeOS ⇏ Decision and KnowledgeOS ⇏ Action; argues this prevents an 'Oracle fallacy' (the system is not a dispenser of truth but a Sārathi supporting a journey the Knower must undertake), maintains human agency, clarifies the system's purpose as readiness rather than 'the right answer', and creates a clean DDD boundary.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS \neq Sārathi ... rather: KnowledgeOS assumes/implements the Sārathi role. ... Chariot | The Knower's journey through a decision/problem space
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS ≠ Sārathi but rather 'KnowledgeOS assumes/implements the Sārathi role', extending the Gita->KnowledgeOS mapping table with a new element: Chariot = the Knower's journey through a decision/problem space (alongside Krishna=knowledge source, Sārathi=role performed by KnowledgeOS, Arjuna=human decision owner, Battlefield=domain reality, Sañjaya=state-observation capability).

rows.anchor: It observes ... It exposes the current knowledge state ... It exposes Zero: What don't we know? And importantly: What don't we even know that we don't know? ... It applies the Lord Lens ... It guides inquiry ... It helps reinterpret ... It compares with the Knower's current ideal ... It progressively reduces relevant uncertainty: not U \rightarrow 0 but U_t \rightarrow U_{t+1}
rows.statement: Consolidates the Sārathi's functions into a ten-step list (observe [Sañjaya capability]; expose current knowledge state with evidence; expose Zero including unknown-unknowns; apply Lord Lens for undiscovered dimensions; guide inquiry toward the most worthwhile next investigation; help reinterpret existing dimensions when new ones appear; compare S_t against I_t; explain implications of the difference; progressively reduce relevant uncertainty U_t->U_{t+1}, never claiming U->0; help the Knower become ready to act), with KnowledgeOS ≠ DecisionOwner throughout.

rows.anchor: An assistant often behaves like: Question -> Answer. A Sārathi behaves more like: Current position -> Where are we? -> What do we know? -> What is missing? -> What matters? -> What should we investigate? -> What does the new knowledge change? -> Are we sufficiently understood? -> What are the possible actions? -> Human decides -> Action -> Observe the new state. That is an epistemic journey.
rows.statement: Contrasts a typical 'AI assistant' model (a single Question -> Answer step) with the Sārathi model, which is a twelve-step epistemic journey pipeline from current position through knowledge gaps, investigation, sufficiency assessment, action options, human decision, action, and observing the resulting state — argued to be a stronger conceptual model than 'AI assistant'.

rows.anchor: Human Knower = Destination/Objective Owner ... KnowledgeOS/Sārathi = Navigation Support ... If the Sārathi detects that the stated destination itself is based on an incomplete understanding, it can say: "Before we continue, I believe the objective itself needs examination." ... It may challenge the ideal state, but it does not silently replace it.
rows.statement: Formalizes the destination/navigation split (Human Knower=Destination/Objective Owner, KnowledgeOS/Sārathi=Navigation Support) with an explicit bounded exception: the Sārathi may flag that the stated destination/objective itself appears incompletely understood ('I believe the objective itself needs examination'), which is where Lord+Zero interact with the Sārathi role — but it may only challenge the ideal state, never silently replace it.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS: (K_t,I_t,U_t) \rightarrow GuidedInquiry \rightarrow (K_{t+1},I_{t+1},U_{t+1}) until Human Knower: Decision ... An epistemic Sārathi: a system that observes and reconstructs the state, exposes the boundaries of current knowledge, expands the inquiry horizon, progressively provides relevant knowledge and guidance, and accompanies the human Knower toward an informed decision—without taking ownership of the decision or action.
rows.statement: Formalizes the GuidedInquiry cycle (K_t,I_t,U_t) -> GuidedInquiry -> (K_{t+1},I_{t+1},U_{t+1}) repeating until the Human Knower decides, and gives the capstone definition of KnowledgeOS as 'an epistemic Sārathi' — a system that observes/reconstructs state, exposes knowledge boundaries, expands the inquiry horizon, progressively provides guidance, and accompanies the Knower toward a decision without owning it — explicitly stronger than 'AI engineering platform' or 'knowledge management system'.

rows.anchor: Zero reveals that we still haven't defined what "relevant" means. ... Knowledge itself does not care about priority. ... Knowledge = representation of known dimensions, values, relationships, and epistemic status ... Relevance = f(Knowledge, Purpose, Ideal, Context, Risk, Decision)
rows.statement: Identifies 'relevant' (as in 'reduces relevant uncertainty') as still undefined, and prevents it from silently becoming priority-weighted knowledge: Knowledge = representation of known dimensions/values/relationships/epistemic status (unweighted), while Relevance is a separate function Relevance = f(Knowledge, Purpose, Ideal, Context, Risk, Decision) — preserving the earlier discovery that knowledge itself does not care about priority.

type_signature.domain: knowledge, purpose, ideal, context, risk, decision

rows.anchor: For this decision, security is critical and documentation is secondary. That does not mean Security > Documentation in the knowledge model. It means: DecisionContext \rightarrow Priority/Weight/Constraint ... we need to separate: Knowledge from: Decision criteria. That is a major missing bounded concept.
rows.statement: Formalizes Knowledge≠Decision-Criteria as a missing bounded concept: a human declaring one dimension more decision-critical than another (e.g. security over documentation) does not make it more important in the knowledge model itself — it is a DecisionContext-derived Priority/Weight/Constraint layered on top of, not inside, the knowledge representation.

rows.anchor: Ontological completeness: Have we identified all dimensions that actually exist? ... \rightarrow \Omega ... effectively unreachable/undefined from the finite Knower's perspective. ... Knowledge completeness: D_i \rightarrow V_i ... Decision sufficiency: K_t + I_t + P_t + Context \rightarrow DecisionSufficiency? ... These must not be collapsed.
rows.statement: Restates and sharpens the completeness taxonomy into exactly three kinds that must not be collapsed: Ontological completeness (have all dimensions that actually exist been identified? tied directly to Ω, effectively unreachable for a finite Knower), Knowledge completeness (are the values of currently-represented dimensions sufficiently known?), and Decision sufficiency (K_t+I_t+P_t+Context -> DecisionSufficiency?, given purpose and ideal state, is available knowledge enough to responsibly decide?).
invariants: Ontological completeness ≠ Knowledge completeness ≠ Decision sufficiency

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is an epistemic Sārathi. It accompanies the human Knower through an evolving knowledge journey, reconstructing the observed state, preserving the epistemic status of knowledge, exposing what is known and what remains unknown or unresolved, expanding the inquiry horizon through candidate dimensions, progressively developing decision-relevant understanding, and enabling the Knower to determine whether the available knowledge is sufficient for the intended decision ... It does not claim that KnowledgeOS reduces uncertainty to zero. It makes uncertainty visible, structured and actionable.
rows.statement: Amends the capstone KnowledgeOS definition to make all the Zero corrections explicit: it reconstructs the observed state, preserves epistemic status, exposes known/unknown/unresolved, expands the inquiry horizon via candidate (not asserted) dimensions, develops decision-relevant understanding, and helps the Knower judge decision-sufficiency — without claiming to reduce uncertainty to zero, only to make it visible, structured and actionable.

lineage_claims.quote: I would preserve that, but make the hidden Zero conditions explicit

rows.anchor: 1 Observes S_t = Observe(Reality) ... 4 Exposes evidence of incompleteness Z(S_t) -> {Evidence_of_Incomplete_Model} ... 6 Guides inquiry K(S_t, Z(S_t), Decision_Context) -> {Next_Question} ... 11 Assesses Decision Sufficiency Sufficiency = f(K_t, I_t, P_t, Context, Risk)
rows.statement: Consolidates the Sārathi's functions (previously stated in prose across S0746/S0748/S0749) into a single eleven-row table each with an explicit formula — e.g. S_t=Observe(Reality); Z(S_t)->{Unknown,Unresolved,Conflicting}; Z(S_t)->{Evidence_of_Incomplete_Model} (replacing 'exposes unknown unknowns'); L(S_t)->{Candidate_Dimensions}; K(S_t,Z(S_t),Decision_Context)->{Next_Question} (inquiry guided by decision relevance, not just knowledge gaps); U_{t+1}=Reframe(U_t,K_new); Compare(S_t,I_t,Decision_Context)->U_t; and the new eleventh function, Sufficiency=f(K_t,I_t,P_t,Context,Risk) — assessing whether the Knower can decide responsibly.

rows.anchor: UNDERSTANDING (U_t = Compare(S_t, I_t) with Decision Context) ... Decision Sufficiency (Is K_t sufficient for this decision?) ... HUMAN KNOWER ... DECISION
rows.statement: Inserts 'Decision Sufficiency' as an explicit pipeline stage between Understanding and the Human Knower in the architecture diagram (Lord->Inquiry->Sañjaya->State Knowledge->{Zero,Evidence}->Sārathi->{Ideal State,Decision Context}->Understanding->Decision Sufficiency->Human Knower->Decision->Action), making the sufficiency check a first-class step rather than an implicit property of Understanding.

rows.anchor: This statement is now: Complete: It includes the missing concepts (relevance, decision context, sufficiency). Precise: ... Humble: It does not claim to reduce uncertainty to zero or to expose "unknown unknowns" directly. Operational: It provides a clear mandate for the system's behavior.
rows.statement: Self-assesses the revised capstone KnowledgeOS definition against four explicit criteria — Complete (includes relevance/decision-context/sufficiency), Precise (separates knowledge from relevance, uncertainty-reduction from epistemic progress), Humble (does not claim zero uncertainty or direct unknown-unknown exposure), and Operational (gives a clear behavioral mandate).

rows.anchor: Nexus version = 3.69 is information. ... The current version has a particular support/security relationship to the desired target, therefore these questions should be investigated before migration. is guiding knowledge. ... Information \neq GuidingKnowledge
rows.statement: Refines 'Krishna = Knowledge' into 'Krishna represents knowledge that is capable of becoming guidance', with a concrete example distinguishing bare Information ('Nexus version = 3.69') from GuidingKnowledge (a stated support/security relationship implying specific next investigative questions): Information ≠ GuidingKnowledge.

rows.anchor: K_L: (K_t,U_t,P_t,I_t,Z_t) \rightarrow (K_{t+1},U_{t+1},G_{t+1}) ... The important output isn't merely more knowledge. It is: GuidedUnderstanding
rows.statement: Defines the Krishna Lens's core function signature: K_L takes current knowledge, understanding, purpose, ideal state, and known epistemic gaps, and produces updated knowledge, updated understanding, and next-step guidance G_{t+1}; the salient output is GuidedUnderstanding, not merely additional knowledge.

rows.anchor: Krishna: \Omega \rightarrow InquiryPath(P,I,C) ... Not because Krishna knows that the chosen path is the only possible path, but because the Knower has an objective. ... The knowledge space may be infinite, but the Sārathi helps the Knower navigate a finite purposeful journey through it.
rows.statement: Connects Krishna to the infinite-space (Lord Lens) hypothesis: since Ω = {D_1,D_2,...,D_∞} and KnowledgeOS cannot search everything, Krishna provides direction via Purpose/Ideal-state/Context, formalized as Krishna: Ω -> InquiryPath(P,I,C) — not because that path is uniquely correct, but because the Knower has a specific objective; the knowledge space may be infinite while the journey through it remains finite and purposeful.

type_signature.domain: Ω, purpose P, ideal I, context C

rows.anchor:
Knowledge 
eq Understanding 
eq Guidance 
eq Decision ... KnowledgeOS may provide the first three, but not own the fourth.
rows.statement: Extends the Knowledge/Understanding split into a four-stage chain: Knowledge (what do we know?) ≠ Understanding (what does it mean?) ≠ Guidance (what should we examine next?) ≠ Decision (what will the human decide?); KnowledgeOS may provide the first three but must never own the fourth.

rows.anchor: DecisionReadiness ... relevant dimensions have been identified; relevant values have sufficient evidence; important conflicts are explicit; important unknowns are visible; implications are understood; the ideal state is sufficiently defined; remaining uncertainty is understood; the Knower accepts the remaining uncertainty; the Knower is able to make an informed decision. ... DecisionReadiness \rightarrow HumanDecision
rows.statement: Introduces DecisionReadiness (replacing the misleading 'KnowledgeComplete') as a nine-item checklist: relevant dimensions identified, relevant values sufficiently evidenced, important conflicts explicit, important unknowns visible, implications understood, the ideal state sufficiently defined, remaining uncertainty understood, the KNOWER ACCEPTS the remaining uncertainty, and the Knower is able to make an informed decision — the last two making explicit that readiness includes a subjective/acceptance component, not only an objective completeness measure; DecisionReadiness -> HumanDecision, never DecisionReadiness -> Decision directly.

rows.anchor: Zero: Detects absence / Identifies uncertainty / Exposes unresolved questions / Says "we don't know this" / Boundary detector ... Krishna: Responds to absence / Guides through uncertainty / Helps prioritize the next inquiry / Says "this is what we should understand next" / Navigation mechanism ... Zero = Epistemic Diagnosis ... Krishna = Epistemic Navigation
rows.statement: Gives a clean five-row Zero-vs-Krishna comparison table (detects vs responds to absence; identifies vs guides through uncertainty; exposes unresolved questions vs prioritizes next inquiry; 'we don't know this' vs 'this is what we should understand next'; boundary detector vs navigation mechanism), summarized as Zero=Epistemic Diagnosis, Krishna=Epistemic Navigation.

rows.anchor: KL(K_t,U_t,Z_t,I_t,P_t,C_t) \rightarrow (K_{t+1},U_{t+1},G_{t+1}) ... G_{t+1} \not\equiv Decision_{human} ... Lord: What else might exist? Zero: What is missing or unresolved? Krishna: What knowledge should guide us next? ... Sañjaya = What is the observed state? Sārathi = Guide the Knower through the knowledge journey. Arjuna = Understand, decide and act.
rows.statement: States the final formal Krishna Lens definition ('a lens for observing how knowledge becomes guidance for a Knower...while preserving uncertainty, provenance and human decision authority'), its six-argument function signature KL(K_t,U_t,Z_t,I_t,P_t,C_t)->(K_{t+1},U_{t+1},G_{t+1}), the critical invariant G_{t+1} ≢ Decision_human, and closes with what is called the cleanest formulation reached: Lord/Zero/Krishna as three questions and Sañjaya/Sārathi/Arjuna as three roles.

rows.anchor: Dhṛtarāṣṭra = Human Knower, remote/limited access ... Arjuna = Human Knower + Actor, directly involved ... the same KnowledgeOS can serve different Knower roles ... To know what is happening. ... To know what to do.
rows.statement: Splits the human Knower into two distinct positions the same KnowledgeOS must serve differently: Dhṛtarāṣṭra (remote/limited-access Knower, needing to know 'what is happening', served primarily by the Sañjaya role) and Arjuna (Knower+Actor directly involved and needing to know 'what to do', served primarily by the Sārathi role).

rows.anchor: Krishna = Knowledge within our Krishna Lens abstraction. KnowledgeOS is the system that makes that knowledge available and operational as guidance. ... Krishna is the knowledge; KnowledgeOS is the epistemic system through which that knowledge can be observed, structured, exposed and used to guide the Knower.
rows.statement: Re-settles the Krishna/KnowledgeOS relationship (rejecting 'Krishna = KnowledgeOS'): Krishna = Knowledge itself (within the Krishna Lens abstraction), while KnowledgeOS is the epistemic system that makes that knowledge observable, structured, exposed, and operational as guidance — Krishna is activated/made accessible through KnowledgeOS, not identical to it.

lineage_claims.quote: We should not say: Krishna = KnowledgeOS. Instead: Krishna = Knowledge

rows.anchor: Krishna is the ideal state at this observer state. ... I_t = f(K_r, Purpose, Context, Knower) ... rather than simply: Krishna = I_t ... This distinction protects the architecture from conflating knowledge of the ideal with the ideal itself.
rows.statement: Rejects an equation of Krishna with the Ideal State itself, replacing it with I_t = f(K_r, Purpose, Context, Knower) — the ideal state may be derived from or informed by Krishna-like knowledge K_r, but is not identical to it, protecting the architecture from conflating 'knowledge of the ideal' with 'the ideal itself'.

lineage_claims.target: an informal claim 'Krishna is the ideal state at this observer state'
lineage_claims.quote: I would refine this slightly.

rows.anchor: Ω \rightarrow K_{context} \rightarrow K_{accessible} \rightarrow Understanding ... The infinite knowledge space is not necessarily presented to the Knower as an undifferentiated infinity. Instead, knowledge becomes contextually accessible. ... The Sārathi provides the knowledge necessary for the current stage of the journey.
rows.statement: Introduces 'contextual manifestation': the infinite space Ω is not presented to the Knower as an undifferentiated infinity but becomes contextually accessible in stages, formalized as Ω -> K_context -> K_accessible -> Understanding, consistent with Krishna giving Arjuna knowledge piece by piece — the Knower does not need the entire infinite space at once.

rows.anchor: We do not collapse Krishna into KnowledgeOS. We do not collapse KnowledgeOS into the Knower. We do not collapse the Ideal State into Krishna. We do not collapse the Lord Lens into the Krishna Lens.
rows.statement: Closes with an explicit four-item non-collapse checklist for the whole architecture built this day: do not collapse Krishna into KnowledgeOS; do not collapse KnowledgeOS into the Knower; do not collapse the Ideal State into Krishna; do not collapse the Lord Lens into the Krishna Lens — keeping the architecture rigorous while philosophical exploration continues.

rows.anchor: Knowledge itself doesn't care about priority. ... we need to distinguish: Knowledge from: DecisionRelevance from: Priority. ... Who determines priority? ... threat; risk; business impact; legal obligation; security; human preference; governance; some combination. And who owns that determination? Still open.
rows.statement: States as genuinely open (not merely undefined) a three-way distinction between Knowledge, DecisionRelevance, and Priority, and the further question of what determines priority (threat/risk/business-impact/legal/security/preference/governance/combination) and who owns that determination.

rows.anchor: Yesterday's knowledge can become less complete when Tuesday reveals a dimension that existed yesterday but was unknown yesterday. But this does not necessarily mean yesterday's individual statements were false. ... KnowledgeState(t) ... Completeness(K,t) ... rather than simply declaring knowledge "correct" or "incorrect." This temporal epistemology is not fully solved yet.
rows.statement: States that temporal knowledge epistemology remains unsolved: yesterday's knowledge becoming less complete when a new dimension is discovered today does not make yesterday's individual statements false, requiring formal KnowledgeState(t) and Completeness(K,t) notions rather than a binary correct/incorrect judgment — flagged as not fully solved.

rows.anchor: Guidance \neq Truth ... We need epistemic status for guidance: Recommendation, Hypothesis, Inference, Warning, etc. This is not completely designed yet. ... Can the human override the Sārathi? ... We haven't defined the complete governance model for that.
rows.statement: States two open questions about guidance itself: (1) guidance can be wrong (Guidance ≠ Truth), requiring an undesigned epistemic-status typing for guidance itself (Recommendation/Hypothesis/Inference/Warning); (2) whether/how the human can override the Sārathi's guidance (agency says yes, but no governance model for the override interaction — e.g. system flags insufficient evidence, human accepts the risk and proceeds — has been defined).

rows.anchor: Where exactly does observation end and guidance begin? For example: "Dependency X exists and affects Y." Is that observation? Or interpretation? Or guidance? This is exactly where DDD and epistemic typing must eventually become precise.
rows.statement: Identifies an unresolved boundary between the two KnowledgeOS layers: it is unclear whether a compound statement like 'Dependency X exists and affects Y' counts as observation (Sañjaya), interpretation, or guidance (Sārathi) — flagged as exactly where DDD and epistemic typing must eventually become precise.

rows.anchor: Human Knower 🟢 Strong ... Knowledge sufficiency 🔴 Open ... Decision relevance 🔴 Open ... Priority/threat model 🔴 Open ... Temporal knowledge state 🔴 Open ... Guidance epistemic status 🔴 Open ... Stopping criterion 🔴 Open ... Lord ↔ Krishna relationship 🔴 Philosophically open
rows.statement: Presents a 25-row colour-coded scorecard of the whole architecture's maturity: ten items rated strong/green (Human Knower, Observer vs Knower, Sañjaya role, Sārathi role, KnowledgeOS=Sañjaya+Sārathi, Krishna Lens, Lord Lens, Zero Lens, infinite knowledge space, Knowledge≠information), three yellow/needs-formalization (dimension/value distinction, observation model, ideal-state model), and eleven red/open (knowledge sufficiency, decision relevance, priority/threat model, new-dimension recalculation, temporal knowledge state, guidance epistemic status, stopping criterion, human override, unknown-unknown representation, Lord↔Krishna relationship).

rows.anchor:
Reality 
eq Observation 
eq Dimension 
eq Value 
eq Knowledge 
eq Understanding 
eq Guidance 
eq Decision 
eq Action ... Sañjaya 
eq Sārathi 
eq Arjuna ... KnowledgeOS = Sañjaya + Sārathi ... Which of these concepts deserve to become actual KnowledgeOS domain objects, which are states, which are roles, which are relationships, and which should remain lens-level concepts?
rows.statement: Closes with a nine-term non-identity chain (Reality≠Observation≠Dimension≠Value≠Knowledge≠Understanding≠Guidance≠Decision≠Action) and Sañjaya≠Sārathi≠Arjuna as the day's substantial conceptual-vocabulary foundation, then pivots explicitly to the next required step: apply the DDD Lens to Chapter 1+2 to determine which of these concepts become actual domain objects, states, roles, relationships, or remain lens-level concepts only, before proceeding to Chapter 3.

rows.anchor: I_t=(D_t^I,V_t^I,R_t^I,C_t^I) ... \Delta_t(d)=Gap(X_t(d),I_t(d)) ... \Delta_t(d)\in\mathcal G_d ... there is no universal scalar distance between arbitrary knowledge states.
rows.statement: Formalizes the ideal state I_t=(D_t^I,V_t^I,R_t^I,C_t^I) with its own dimensions, desired values, relationships and constraints, and defines a per-dimension gap function Δ_t(d)=Gap(X_t(d),I_t(d)) ∈ G_d — each dimension has its own gap/metric structure (e.g. version numbers, booleans, probabilities differ), establishing there is no universal scalar distance between arbitrary knowledge states.

type_signature.domain: dimension d, actual value, ideal value

invariants: No universal scalar distance between arbitrary knowledge states

rows.anchor: Knowledge extent E(K_t) ... Decision utility/value U(K_t\mid P,I,C) ... E(K_{t+1})>E(K_t) while U(K_{t+1})<U(K_t) ... This resolves one of the most difficult issues we discussed.
rows.statement: Resolves 'when a new dimension is discovered, knowledge increases but the value of the state can decrease' by defining two independent functions: Knowledge extent E(K_t) (how much of the represented space is covered) and Decision utility U(K_t|P,I,C) (how useful that knowledge is for the current purpose), which can move in opposite directions: E(K_{t+1})>E(K_t) while U(K_{t+1})<U(K_t).

rows.anchor: Completeness(K)=\frac{|D^K|}{|\mathcal D|} ... this fails because: D may be infinite; we don't know the denominator; dimensions have different structures; knowledge can be incomplete in values, relationships, and semantics. ... C(K_t\mid R) ... where R is a declared reference scope. ... C(K_t\mid NexusMigrationScope)
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects a global completeness percentage Completeness(K)=|D^K|/|D| as mathematically indefensible (D may be infinite, the denominator is unknown, dimensions differ structurally, incompleteness can be in values/relationships/semantics too), replacing it with relative completeness C(K_t|R) with respect to an explicitly declared, bounded reference scope R (e.g. C(K_t|NexusMigrationScope)).

type_signature.domain: knowledge state K_t, reference scope R

invariants: Completeness requires a declared reference scope

lineage_claims.quote: But this fails because...

rows.anchor: \rho(d\mid P,C,I,T) ... \rho is not part of the knowledge itself. It is calculated from knowledge plus context. ... Knowledge \neq Relevance ... Knowledge \neq Priority ... \pi(d)=f(\rho(d),Threat(d),Impact(d),Constraints)
rows.statement: Formalizes Relevance ρ(d|P,C,I,T) as explicitly not part of knowledge itself but computed from knowledge plus context (Knowledge≠Relevance, Knowledge≠Priority), and derives Priority as π(d)=f(ρ(d),Threat(d),Impact(d),Constraints), allowing one dimension to be more urgent than another without claiming it constitutes 'more knowledge' — a major architectural separation, and a partial answer to the earlier open 'who/what determines priority' question.

type_signature.domain: dimension d, purpose, context, ideal, time

rows.anchor: Suff(K_t,I_t,P_t,C_t,D_t) ... Suff=1 when the knowledge satisfies the declared decision criteria and the remaining uncertainty is explicitly accepted/authorized. ... Suff = f(Coverage,Evidence,Conflict,Uncertainty,Risk,Relevance,IdealDefinition,DecisionContext) ... deliberately not reduced to one universal mathematical formula yet.
rows.statement: Formalizes Decision Sufficiency Suff(K_t,I_t,P_t,C_t,D_t), explicitly not requiring K_t=Ω: Suff=1 when knowledge satisfies the declared decision criteria AND the remaining uncertainty is explicitly accepted/authorized, conceptually decomposed as a function of Coverage, Evidence, Conflict, Uncertainty, Risk, Relevance, IdealDefinition, and DecisionContext — deliberately left as a domain-defined predicate rather than one universal formula.

rows.anchor: DR_t=DecisionReadiness(K_t,I_t,Z_t,P_t,C_t) ... DR_t=1 \not\Rightarrow Decision_t. The human still decides. ... K_{Tue}=Update(K_{Mon},d_{101},Evidence_{new}) ... S_{Tue}=Reconstruct(K_{Tue}) ... I_{Tue}=Reevaluate(I_{Mon},K_{Tue}) ... \Delta_{Tue}=Gap(S_{Tue},I_{Tue})
rows.statement: Formalizes Decision Readiness DR_t=DecisionReadiness(K_t,I_t,Z_t,P_t,C_t) with the explicit non-implication DR_t=1 ⇏ Decision_t (the human still decides), and operationalizes the Monday->Tuesday knowledge-evolution lifecycle as K_Tue=Update(K_Mon,d_101,Evidence_new) -> S_Tue=Reconstruct(K_Tue) -> I_Tue=Reevaluate(I_Mon,K_Tue) -> Δ_Tue=Gap(S_Tue,I_Tue).

rows.anchor: We should not overwrite Monday. ... K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,\Delta K) rather than: K_t \leftarrow overwrite ... What did we know when the decision was made? Formally: K(t_{decision})
rows.statement: Requires knowledge history to be immutable: K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,ΔK), never an in-place overwrite of K_t, giving KnowledgeOS temporal epistemic provenance and enabling the question 'what did we know when the decision was made?' to be answered formally as K(t_decision).

rows.anchor: Correct(s) ... Coverage(K) ... C(K\mid R) ... Correct(K_t)=1 does not imply Complete(K_t)=1 ... C(K_{Mon}\mid R_{Tue}) < C(K_{Tue}\mid R_{Tue}) because Tuesday revealed a dimension that was outside Monday's represented model.
rows.statement: Formally separates three properties that a flat 'correct/incomplete' label conflates: assertion Correctness(s), Coverage(K), and reference-relative Completeness C(K|R); Correct(K_t)=1 does not imply Complete(K_t)=1, illustrated by C(K_Mon|R_Tue) < C(K_Tue|R_Tue) even though Monday's individual statements remained correct.

rows.anchor: Krishna (Entity) | The source of knowledge. | Entity = Knowledge_Source ... Sārathi (Role) | The operational manifestation. | Role = f(Entity, Context, Relationship, Purpose) ... KnowledgeOS (System) | The system that makes knowledge operational. | System = Makes_Knowledge_Operational ... Entity \neq Role \neq System
rows.statement: Consolidates the day's Krishna/Sārathi/KnowledgeOS discussion into an explicit three-way non-identity: Entity (Krishna, the knowledge source) ≠ Role (Sārathi, the operational manifestation, Role=f(Entity,Context,Relationship,Purpose)) ≠ System (KnowledgeOS, which makes knowledge operational).

rows.anchor: Your understanding is the hypothesis. The lenses are instruments for examination, not proof.
rows.statement: States the governing methodological rule for all future phases of this research: the human's own conceptual understanding is the hypothesis under test; the Gita and the Lord/Krishna/Zero/DDD lenses are instruments for EXAMINING that hypothesis, never a source of proof for it.

rows.anchor: Step 1 — Your understanding ... Step 2 — Gita observation ... Step 3 — Lenses ... Step 4 — Mathematical interpretation ... Step 5 — KnowledgeOS implication ... Step 6 — Status: ESTABLISHED / HYPOTHESIS / SUPPORTED BY LENS / MATHEMATICALLY FORMALIZED / OPEN ... That prevents us from accidentally turning a philosophical interpretation into an architectural fact.
rows.statement: Defines a mandatory six-step procedure to be applied to every remaining research question: (1) state your own understanding informally; (2) check whether the Gita text gives a relevant observation; (3) apply the Lord/Krishna/Zero/DDD lenses strategically; (4) ask whether the concept can be represented rigorously; (5) determine what KnowledgeOS would need to represent or do; (6) classify the result under a five-level status taxonomy (ESTABLISHED, HYPOTHESIS, SUPPORTED BY LENS, MATHEMATICALLY FORMALIZED, OPEN) — explicitly to prevent a philosophical interpretation from silently becoming an architectural fact.

rows.anchor: 1. Observation 2. Dimension 3. Statement 4. Value 5. Knowledge 6. Known/Unknown Dimension 7. Epistemic Status 8. Evidence 9. Truth vs Knowledge 10. Ideal State 11. Actual-Ideal Gap 12. Uncertainty 13. Relevance/Priority 14. Sufficient Knowledge 15. Understanding 16. Guidance 17. Decision 18. Knowledge Evolution 19. Time 20. Mathematical Space
rows.statement: Proposes a specific 20-question research order to define the KnowledgeOS conceptual/mathematical model, deliberately ordered so that primitives (Observation, Dimension, Statement, Value) are settled before derived concepts (Knowledge, Epistemic Status, Evidence, Truth vs Knowledge, Ideal State, Gap, Uncertainty, Relevance/Priority, Sufficiency, Understanding, Guidance, Decision, Knowledge Evolution, Time), with the formal mathematical space (Ω,𝓕,μ) deliberately left as the LAST question, only after all conceptual questions are answered.

rows.anchor: A statement can be true but unknown. A statement can be believed but false. A statement can be unresolved. A statement can be supported by evidence but still uncertain. We need your understanding here before formalizing probability.
rows.statement: Poses Truth-vs-Knowledge as an open question preceding any probability formalization, illustrated with four asymmetric cases: a statement can be true but unknown; believed but false; unresolved; or evidence-supported yet still uncertain — the exact relationship between Truth and Knowledge is not yet defined.

rows.anchor: Is the ideal state itself part of knowledge? ... Can two humans have different ideal states for the same observation? ... Who defines it? Is it a state? Is it a set of constraints? Is it a set of desired values? Can it contain unknown dimensions? Can it change?
rows.statement: Poses the Ideal State's own formal status as still open, most sharply as 'is the ideal state itself part of knowledge?' and 'can two humans have different ideal states for the same observation?', alongside ownership, structure (state/constraints/desired-values), and whether it can contain unknown dimensions or change.

rows.anchor: Is the decision: Action? or: Choice of Action? or: Acceptance of uncertainty? This matters because Arjuna's movement from uncertainty to action is one of the central things we are studying.
rows.statement: Poses what a 'Decision' actually consists of as still open: is it the Action itself, the Choice of an action (prior to execution), or the Acceptance of remaining uncertainty (a precondition to acting) — flagged as mattering directly to the Arjuna case study of moving from uncertainty to action.

rows.anchor: I_t = Knowledge of the Ideal ... I^* = The actual ideal state (which may be beyond the Knower's current representation) ... I \neq Knowledge of I

unknown_candidate.why_uncertain: This file's I_t vs I* distinction predates (chronologically within the corpus) the batch-B0017 ideal-state-comparison-model registration but expresses essentially the same idea (theoretical ideal vs the Knower's representation of it); genuinely unclear whether the graph should treat this as the same object recurring or a separate independent derivation given the reconstruction is not fully chronological across batches.

rows.statement: Distinguishes the actual Ideal State I* from the Knower's current representation of it I_t, arguing Arjuna's model of the ideal (win the kingdom -> avoid killing family) changed, which does not by itself prove the ideal itself changed; Ideal != Knowledge-of-Ideal, mirroring Reality != Representation.

rows.anchor: State_t = (K_t, I_t, Q_t, C_t) ... I_t = (D_I, V_I, R_I, C_I) ... Compare(K_t, I_t) -> G_t
rows.statement: Introduces the complete System State as (KnowledgeState,IdealState,Question/Intent,Context), formalizes the Ideal State I_t=(IdealDimensions,IdealValues,IdealRelationships,Constraints), and defines Compare(K_t,I_t)->G_t as the set of gaps between current knowledge and the ideal.

rows.anchor: we must determine whether Ideal State means: the knowledge required to answer a question, the desired state of the world, the desired state of knowledge, the desired state of action, or some combination... We must not assume they are the same thing.
rows.statement: Opens Question 11 (Ideal State) with an explicit warning against assuming Ideal State is any one of: knowledge-required-to-answer-a-question, desired-state-of-the-world, desired-state-of-knowledge, or desired-state-of-action, without first determining whether these are the same object or must be modelled separately.

rows.anchor:
Goal 
eq IdealState 
eq Constraint 
eq DecisionCriterion
rows.statement: Adds a further distinction to the revised Q11 Ideal State: IdealState ≠ Goal (an Ideal Knowledge State describes what must be known, a Goal describes what someone wants to achieve, a Constraint describes what must/must not be true, a Decision Criterion describes what must be satisfied to decide) — these four must not collapse.

rows.anchor: \text{Knowledge Ātma}\neq K_t\neq I_t
rows.statement: Establishes three distinct concepts that must not collapse: Knowledge Ātma (who/what persists through knowledge-state changes), Knowledge State K_t (what is currently known/represented), Ideal State I_t (what should be known/understood/achieved for the current purpose) — Knowledge Ātma ≠ K_t ≠ I_t, called 'a very strong architectural separation'.

rows.anchor: Moksha\neq\text{achievement of one finite Ideal State}
rows.statement: Moksha ≠ K_t=I_t, because the Ideal State itself can evolve (I_0->I_1->I_2->...); Moksha is instead 'transcendence of the ordinary finite epistemic journey'. Formalizes a Moksha transition object M=(K_{T_M},T_M,𝒜_K,𝒦,Γ_M) where T_M is the transition point, K_{T_M} the knowledge state there, 𝒜_K the Knowledge Ātma, 𝒦 the Knowledge Space, and Γ_M the epistemic regime/condition defining Moksha: K_{T_M} 'is not merely large; it is epistemically transformed'.
invariants: Moksha ≠ achievement of one finite Ideal State

rows.anchor: \underbrace{\text{Ātma}}_{\text{Who knows}} \quad \underbrace{K_t}_{\text{What is known}} \quad \underbrace{I_t}_{\text{What should be known}}
rows.statement: Establishes a clean three-way separation Ātma ('who knows') / K_t ('what is known') / I_t ('what should be known'), judged much cleaner than identifying Ātma with the Knowledge State itself; repeats the caution that this is a KnowledgeOS mathematical/architectural abstraction inspired by Ātman, not a claim of having mathematically captured the metaphysical Ātman of the Gītā.

rows.anchor: Ātman should not be modeled as an "Ideal State" itself. It is better modeled as the invariant identity underlying changing states.
rows.statement: Rejects a proposed equation of Ātman with the Ideal State, offering instead 'Persistent Identity / Invariant Subject' ℐ with ℐ_{t+1}=ℐ_t while K_{t+1}≠K_t and I_{t+1}≠I_t in general, giving Identity ≠ Current State ≠ Ideal State — 'a very important refinement'. K_t = State(ℐ,t).

lineage_claims.target: a proposal that would equate Ātman with the Ideal State
lineage_claims.quote: Ātman should not be modeled as an "Ideal State" itself.

rows.anchor: Admit(P,\Pi_1) \neq Admit(P,\Pi_2)
rows.statement: Introduces admission policy Π_adm with Admit(P_c,E,C,Π_adm)->{Assertion|Reject|Defer|RequestMoreEvidence}; admission is purpose-dependent, Admit(P,Π_1)≠Admit(P,Π_2) (an exploration policy may allow Weak support, a production-migration policy may require Strong support) — connecting directly to the Ideal State theory: an assertion can exist with Σ_K=Weak while the Ideal State requires Σ_I=Strong, producing a discrepancy rather than an invalid assertion. Distinguishes Admission ('may this proposition exist as governed knowledge?', Candidate->Assertion) from Validation ('does this assertion satisfy a particular requirement?', Assertion×Constraint->ValidationResult): Admission ≠ Validation — an assertion can be admitted (e.g. during discovery) yet later FAIL a validation (e.g. a migration requiring verified version) WITHOUT being deleted; it 'remains useful historical knowledge'.

rows.anchor: 8 · IdealState → EpistemicContract → AcceptancePolicy → Committed (the formal spine)
rows.statement: IdealState first appears in 20260826-000839 (major clarification), immediately stress-tested the same hour by 20260826-001700 (an example exposing a flaw in the new model); 88 files thereafter. EpistemicContract first appears in Steps 023/024 (2026-08-27 16:23/16:25) — a LATE, Step-era formalization, not an early intuition (12 files). AcceptancePolicy first appears at Step 007 (2026-08-27 14:27), canonical host Step 008 (15:19), 4 files only — the concept v0.2's R-1 centers on is one of the corpus's narrowest. Committed (epistemic status) appears from Step 008 onward; the kernel-era string match (20260823-123630, 'What Is Being Committed To?') is a DIFFERENT sense (the kernel's commitment object) — a near-collision recorded with no lineage link.

rows.anchor: The IdealState
rows.statement: Describes the IdealState as the epistemic understanding the Knower would consider sufficient, changeable only by the Knower, a standard of sufficiency rather than a picture of the world (so the model needs no access to any ideal world); recounts its history as instructive and typical — introduced in the corpus 2026-08-26 at 00:08, broken by a worked example at 00:17, and repaired the same night, the discovery process attacking its own newest concept within the hour.

lexical.anchor: Human first has/conceives an Ideal State ... IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE. That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.

conceptual.anchor: What does it mean to have a complete or ideal state of an infinite Knowledge Space? ... 1. Explicit completeness -- impossible if the state is genuinely unbounded. 2. Structural completeness -- rules/relations are sufficient to derive answers. 3. Question-relative completeness -- sufficient to answer all questions in a defined question space. I suspect #2 and #3 will be much more important than #1 for KnowledgeOS.

formal.anchor: Human first has/conceives an Ideal State ... IDEAL STATE -> EXPECTATIONS/CRITERIA -> OBSERVATION -> COMPARISON -> DETERMINATION -> FACT/KNOWLEDGE. That is a substantially different model from the one I was using before.

governance.anchor: The object being observed and the process/actor observing it should not be conflated. ... separate bounded concepts such as: Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer ... rather than one giant Knowledge aggregate.

rationale_evidence.anchor: P(A)=1, P(B)=0.9, P(C)=0.6, P(D)=0.2. Then our extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain. The probability is therefore attached to the extraction/determination, not necessarily to the underlying ideal state itself. That gives: I_t -> hat-I_t where hat-I_t is probabilistically estimated from available information.
rationale_evidence.statement: Explains the origin of graded 0-to-1 values: if the ideal state requires A,B,C,D but observations only partially resolve them (P(A)=1,P(B)=0.9,P(C)=0.6,P(D)=0.2), the extracted representation of the ideal/current relationship is uncertain -- this probability attaches to the extraction/determination I_t -> hat-I_t, not to the underlying ideal state itself.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The word "old" is not an intrinsic property of version 2.69. It is a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t. So if tomorrow the reference becomes 4.0, Old(2.69) remains true. But if the reference were somehow 2.0, Old(2.69) would be false.
rationale_evidence.statement: Establishes that 'old' is not an intrinsic property of a value but a relational property: Old(2.69) iff 2.69 < ReferenceVersion_t, whose truth depends entirely on the current reference (true if the reference rises to 4.0, false if the reference were 2.0) -- knowledge is often produced by comparing an observed state against a reference/ideal state, not by inspecting the observed state alone.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The ideal state itself is Knowledge. Someone had to establish: 3.85 is the current/required version. That did not come from the comparison. It came from another chain of knowledge: Vendor releases 3.85 -> Human/system observes it -> Evidence -> Determination -> "3.85 is current/required" -> Ideal/reference state. So KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge.
rationale_evidence.statement: The ideal/reference state is itself Knowledge, established through its own prior chain (vendor releases 3.85 -> observed -> evidence -> determination -> '3.85 is current/required' -> becomes the ideal/reference state); this reveals KnowledgeOS has a recursive structure: Knowledge -> Ideal/Reference State -> Comparison -> New Knowledge -> (recursively) Updated Reference State -> ...

rationale_evidence.anchor: Many knowledge statements are not standalone facts. They are relationships between states. ... perhaps KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally think: Fact A, Fact B, Fact C but: Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues many knowledge statements are relationships between states (2.69<3.85; CurrentArchitecture!=RequiredArchitecture; ObservedState does-not-entail RequiredState) rather than standalone facts; proposes KnowledgeOS should not fundamentally model Fact A/Fact B/Fact C as independent items, but as Reference State <-> Observed State -> Comparison/Reasoning -> Determination.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge at Monday and knowledge at Tuesday are different epistemic states. ... K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. ... When a new dimension is discovered ... we gain knowledge. But the comparison with the previous state also reveals: The previous knowledge was less complete than today's knowledge. Even if the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty.
rationale_evidence.statement: Knowledge at different times are different epistemic states, and a determination can be historically valid/obsolete/superseded/no longer applicable without deleting the historical record -- K_Monday -> K_Tuesday must preserve the trajectory. Also: discovering a new dimension retroactively reveals that the PREVIOUS knowledge state was less complete than today's, even when the new dimension's value is known with 100% certainty -- completeness assessment of past knowledge changes with later dimension discovery.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The reference itself has an epistemic history. We cannot simply store: RequiredVersion=3.85. We potentially need to know: Why do we accept 3.85 as the reference? ... Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. ... Trust is not the same as truth. ... Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance.
rationale_evidence.statement: The reference/ideal state is itself knowledge requiring its own epistemic history: not merely RequiredVersion=3.85, but why 3.85 is accepted (who stated it, what evidence/justification, what trust rule, when valid, who accepted it, has it since changed), giving the recursive chain Evidence -> Justification -> Trusted Statement -> Reference State -> Comparison -> New Determination. Trust is not the same as truth: a trusted source's statement must preserve why it is trusted (Statement -> Reason -> Logic -> Justification -> Trust/Acceptance), not merely who said it.

rationale_evidence.anchor: the ideal state exists independently of our knowledge. ... d_dependency in I_Mon even though humans do not know about it. So: Unknown dimension != Nonexistent dimension. ... Our observed state is only a projection. O_Mon = Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon). ... the missing dimension is not a missing part of reality. It is a missing part of our observation/extraction. ... Discovery does not create the dimension. It changes our knowledge of the dimension. ... dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.
rationale_evidence.statement: Resolves an apparent reality/knowledge contradiction: the ideal state I_t exists independently of our knowledge of it -- a dependency dimension can already be an element of I_Mon (d_dependency in I_Mon) even though unknown, so unknown dimension != nonexistent dimension. The observed state is only a projection, O_Mon=Pi(I_Mon | Information_Mon), so a missing dimension is a gap in observation/extraction, not in reality. Discovery therefore does not create the dimension -- it changes our knowledge of it: dimension discovery is an epistemic event, not an ontological event.

rationale_evidence.anchor: How can we determine whether the new information changes the ideal state, or merely changes our knowledge of the already-existing ideal state? ... state change versus knowledge change ... one of the most important unresolved questions ... a Kernel that cannot distinguish those two will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. ... hat-I_Tue != hat-I_Mon even if none of the previously known values changed. ... both state and observed model of the state can change ... they are not mutually exclusive explanations.
rationale_evidence.statement: Distinguishes state change (the actual/ideal state I_t itself changes, e.g. Nexus is actually upgraded) from knowledge change (a previously-existing but unknown dimension is merely discovered) -- named one of the most important unresolved questions, since a Kernel unable to distinguish them will eventually corrupt the history of Knowledge. Formalizes that the observed ideal state must be recalculated purely from dimension-set expansion alone: if D_t subset D_{t+1}, then generally hat-I_t(D_t) != hat-I_{t+1}(D_{t+1}) even when every previously known dimension's value is unchanged -- the representation changed because the dimensional basis expanded, not because any value did. State change and dimension discovery can occur simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive explanations for why knowledge changed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Truth(P)=1 while Determination(P)=? because nobody has discovered the evidence. This may be one of the most important foundational distinctions still missing.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues Truth and Determination must be kept formally separate: a proposition can be true (Truth(P)=1) in reality while our Determination(P)=? because nobody has yet discovered the relevant evidence — flagged as possibly the most important missing foundational distinction in the whole model.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The object being observed and the process/actor observing it should not be conflated. ... separate bounded concepts such as: Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer ... rather than one giant Knowledge aggregate.
rationale_evidence.statement: States a DDD architectural consequence: the observed object and the observing process/actor must not be conflated into one aggregate; proposes seven separate bounded concepts (Observation, KnowledgeState, Evidence, Reasoning, Determination, Decision, Observer) rather than one giant 'Knowledge' aggregate.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Arjuna's knowledge increases. He sees the people. But paradoxically, his certainty about what to do decreases. ... More information \not\Rightarrow More decision certainty ... KnowledgeOS should therefore never equate information volume with decision quality.
rationale_evidence.statement: Derives from Arjuna's crisis (more information about who he faces reduces, not increases, his certainty about what to do) the principle More information ⇏ More decision certainty, concluding KnowledgeOS must never equate information volume with decision quality — called one of the strongest observations in Chapter 1.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Sañjaya reports. He doesn't become Dhṛtarāṣṭra. ... KnowledgeOS should report, explain, challenge and expose—but the human remains the owner of understanding and decision. ... KnowledgeOS \neq DecisionOwner
rationale_evidence.statement: Uses the Sañjaya/Dhṛtarāṣṭra role separation to argue KnowledgeOS ≠ DecisionOwner: KnowledgeOS may report, explain, challenge, and expose, but the human remains owner of understanding and decision — pipeline KnowledgeOS -> Understanding -> Human -> Decision, consistent with the 'present both, warn the owner' rule.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Role: Warrior vs Charioteer ... Acts in battle: Yes vs No, as combatant ... Owns the action: Yes vs No ... Provides orientation: Receives vs Provides ... Executes the warrior's duty: Yes vs No
rationale_evidence.statement: Gives a detailed eight-row responsibility comparison between Arjuna (Warrior: acts in battle, owns the action, makes the journey, receives orientation, executes duty) and Krishna-as-Sārathi (Charioteer: does not act as combatant, does not own the action, supports/navigates, provides orientation, does not execute the warrior's duty) — more precise than simply 'Krishna gives Arjuna knowledge.'

rationale_evidence.anchor: Frames the problem | Yes (through the Krishna Lens) | No ... Provides knowledge | Yes | No ... Makes decisions | No | Yes ... Owns the action | No | Yes ... Is accountable for the outcome | No | Yes
rationale_evidence.statement: Presents an eight-row System(Sārathi)-vs-Human responsibility table that explicitly assigns 'Frames the problem: Yes (through the Krishna Lens)' to the System — this is precisely the claim the same-batch S0746 later retracts ('Sārathi does not own the frame'; 'Sārathi -> Propose/Reframe, not Sārathi -> Own the Frame'), making this table an in-corpus contradiction later corrected rather than a stable position.

rationale_evidence.anchor: KnowledgeOS \xrightarrow{provides} Guidance \xrightarrow{supports} Human Understanding \xrightarrow{enables} Human Decision \xrightarrow{results in} Human Action ... KnowledgeOS \not\Rightarrow Decision ... KnowledgeOS \not\Rightarrow Action ... It prevents the "Oracle" fallacy.
rationale_evidence.statement: Formalizes the guidance/agency separation as a chain KnowledgeOS-provides->Guidance-supports->Human Understanding-enables->Human Decision-results in->Human Action, with explicit non-implications KnowledgeOS ⇏ Decision and KnowledgeOS ⇏ Action; argues this prevents an 'Oracle fallacy' (the system is not a dispenser of truth but a Sārathi supporting a journey the Knower must undertake), maintains human agency, clarifies the system's purpose as readiness rather than 'the right answer', and creates a clean DDD boundary.

aliases: Titelbaum Fundamentals of Bayesian Epistemology 1: Introducing Credences, extraction
