sources.note: A deep extraction from Titelbaum's Volume 1 (Introducing Credences), companion to this batch's own Volume-2 extraction (S2305/hpa-bayesian-epistemology-vol2), identifying EPISTEMIC STANDARDS as the single most important missing KnowledgeOS primitive. Central derivation: Titelbaum separates Total Evidence from Ultimate Epistemic Standards via a hypothetical prior Pr^H such that cr_i=Pr^H(.|E_i), giving K_t = F(E_t, S_t) rather than K_t=F(E_t) alone -- two agents with IDENTICAL total evidence can rationally reach different epistemic states because they have different standards (E_t^A=E_t^B does not imply K_t^A=K_t^B), motivating a new candidate element S^epi (Epistemic Response Standard/Interpretation Policy) explicitly distinct from Governance (Governance = what is permitted/required; S^epi = how evidence is interpreted/weighed). Proposes splitting the candidate Interpret kernel operator into Interpret(E,S)->M and Update(M,E,S)->K_{t+1} for kernel-experiment testing. Extends the Evidence tuple with acquisition context (Evidence=(Content,Source,Acquisition,Context,Time,Provenance)) motivated by Titelbaum's observation-selection-effect discussion (the fish-net sampling example: how evidence was obtained changes its epistemic meaning), proposing new candidate relations SelectionBias(e,H)/AcquisitionModel(e) belonging to the Evidence/Observation context model, not the kernel. Uses Titelbaum's credence-is-an-attitude-not-content distinction (credence attaches to an attitude toward a proposition, not to the proposition's content) to re-split the atomic knowledge tuple into a semantic layer c_i=(O,d_i,v_i,t) and an epistemic layer kappa_i=(E_i,S_i,Cr_i,Status_i,Provenance_i,Context_i,...), giving k_i=(c_i,kappa_i) -- KnowledgeContent != Confidence. Warns numerical credence can overstate precision (comparative confidence != a factually meaningful numerical difference) and proposes a non-numeric-friendly EpistemicAttitude type (Categorical|Comparative|Ranged|Quantitative|Unknown|Suspended) plus an epistemic-resolution concept Resolution(K), rather than assuming universal quantification. States ProbabilityCoherence != Truth != Knowledge (Titelbaum's five Bayesian core rules -- Non-Negativity, Normality, Finite Additivity, Ratio Formula, Conditionalization -- are norms on credences, not truth-establishing), proposing CoherenceValidation as only one of five validity dimensions: Validity = SemanticValidity AND EvidenceAdequacy AND InferentialCoherence AND Calibration AND PurposeAdequacy. Uses Conditionalization (Cr_{t+1}(H)=Cr_t(H|E)) as a genuine state-transition model for K_t->K_{t+1}, but notes strict Conditionalization over-commits (learned evidence becomes permanently certain), motivating Jeffrey Conditionalization and a generalized Update(K_t,E,mode)->K_{t+1} distinguishing hard/soft evidence, partial observation, revised interpretation, changed context, and conflicting evidence -- reinforcing the corpus's existing rejection of simplistic monotonic knowledge growth (EvidenceAccumulation != KnowledgeMonotonicity: F_t subset-of F_{t+1} can coexist with K_{t+1} revising/retracting prior conclusions). Formalizes a typed relevance relation Rel(E,H|C) with types SUPPORTS/REFUTES/IRRELEVANT/CONDITIONALLY_SUPPORTS/CONDITIONALLY_REFUTES/SCREENS_OFF/INDEPENDENT (drawn from Titelbaum's independence/positive-relevance/negative-relevance/conditional-relevance/screening-off apparatus), proposed as Knowledge-Space relation types, not kernel primitives -- reinforcing KnowledgeSpace != {claims} in favor of KS_t=(K_t,R_t), independently converging with the Davidson-derived relational Knowledge Space proposal but on a formal probabilistic basis. Uses Titelbaum's doxastically-possible-worlds apparatus to propose Zero(K_t,I_Q) as failure to eliminate all inquiry-relevant unresolved alternatives (explicitly marked as a KnowledgeOS-side derivation, not Titelbaum's own definition of Zero), and uses Titelbaum's Regularity discussion to give EpistemicZero != ProbabilisticZero != LogicalFalsehood, keeping Zero semantic rather than numeric. Extracts a standard-vs-state distinction ((K_t,S) rather than K_t alone, with S~=Pr^H potentially stable while evidence changes, backed by a cited Hypothetical Priors Theorem) suggesting K_t/S_t/Governance-constraints-G as three separate things. Uses Titelbaum's Objective-vs-Subjective-Bayesianism distinction (permissive cases: identical evidence, multiple rationally permissible credences) as independent theoretical support (alongside an earlier Davidson-derived finding) for Adequacy != Uniqueness (Adequate(K_1,Q) and Adequate(K_2,Q) can both hold for E,S_1->K_1 and E,S_2->K_2). Separates confirmation from determination (Evidence->Relevance->Confirmation does not automatically yield Confirmation->Determination; Support!=Determination; HighCredence!=Knowledge), and proposes making the Determine kernel operator explicitly inquiry-relative: Determine(K_t,Q,EC) iff Adequate(K_t,I_Q), replacing a context-free Determine(K_t). Adds an anti-double-counting principle from Titelbaum's independence/conditional-independence treatment (|E| != EpistemicStrength(E); EvidenceCount != EvidenceValue) and an intermediate relevance-before-value chain E->Relevance(E,H)->Confirmation(E,H)->CredenceChange(H)->InquiryAdequacy, refining the earlier expected-information-gain investigation objective to depend on Relevance(E,Q) rather than raw information quantity. Raises higher-order epistemic state (credences about one's own credences, MetaK_t) as a further candidate missing element, tied to Titelbaum's discussion of limited self-access to one's own mental state. Proposes testing, in the kernel-reduction experiment, whether RespondToEvidence and Maintain/ApplyEpistemicStandards decompose into existing operators (Interpret+Discriminate+Evaluate+Update) or are themselves required, explicitly anticipating the possible result that Epistemic Standards may be an essential SYSTEM component without being a primitive KERNEL operator -- a distinction the file calls exactly what the research needs. Closes with a seven-way non-collapse: Evidence != EpistemicStandards != Attitude != Representation != Confidence != Knowledge != Decision, and the temporal form K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E_{t+1},S_t^epi,C_{t+1},Q_{t+1}), explicitly allowing Claim_t in K_t but Claim_t not-in K_{t+1} as legitimate defeat/revision. Names Epistemic Standards as the single most important missing element exposed by this reading -- a genuine theoretical gap, not merely an architectural enhancement.

Re-registered in B0057 to satisfy this batch label-registration check; S2355 in this batch is a same-day (2026-09-01 22:50) follow-on Titelbaum-Vol-1 gap-analysis document that restates and substantially extends this same S_epi/evidence-vs-standards thread. relation_to_existing copied unchanged from the B0056 original proposal per cross-batch identity discipline.

rows.anchor: Epistemic Attitude_t = F(Total Evidence_t, Epistemic Standards). ... K_t = F(E_t,S_t). ... S^epi = Epistemic Response Standard / Epistemic Interpretation Policy. This must not be confused with Governance.
rows.statement: Central derivation: Titelbaum's hypothetical-prior formalism (cr_i=Pr^H(.|E_i)) shows an agent's epistemic attitude is a function of Total Evidence AND Epistemic Standards, not evidence alone, giving K_t=F(E_t,S_t); proposes S^epi (Epistemic Response Standard/Interpretation Policy) as a new KnowledgeOS candidate element explicitly distinct from Governance (Governance = what is permitted/required; S^epi = how evidence is interpreted/weighed).

rows.anchor: two agents possess the same total evidence but arrive at different credences because they have different epistemic standards. ... E_t^A=E_t^B does not imply K_t^A=K_t^B.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's same-evidence-different-standards cases to establish that identical total evidence does not entail identical epistemic states, proposing to split the candidate Interpret kernel operator into Interpret(E,S)->M and Update(M,E,S)->K_{t+1} for testing in the kernel-reduction experiment.

rows.anchor: Evidence = (Content, Source, Acquisition, Context, Time, Provenance). ... AcquisitionModel(e). ... how evidence was obtained can itself be epistemically relevant.
rows.statement: Extends the evidence tuple with acquisition context, motivated by Titelbaum's observation-selection-effect discussion (the fish-net sampling example, where knowing short fish could escape through net holes changes how the sample should be interpreted); proposes candidate relations SelectionBias(e,H)/AcquisitionModel(e) belonging to the Evidence/Observation context model rather than the kernel itself.

rows.anchor: A credence value is an attribute of an attitude, not part of the proposition's content. ... k_i=(c_i,kappa_i) ... c_i=(O,d_i,v_i,t) ... kappa_i=(E_i,S_i,Cr_i,Status_i,Provenance_i,Context_i,...)
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's credence-is-an-attitude-not-content distinction to re-split the atomic knowledge-claim tuple into a semantic layer c_i (object, dimension, value, time) and a separate epistemic layer kappa_i (evidence, standards, credence, status, provenance, context), yielding k_i=(c_i,kappa_i) and KnowledgeContent != Confidence.

rows.anchor: numerical credence can introduce more precision than is actually present. ... EpistemicAttitude = Categorical | Comparative | Ranged | Quantitative | Unknown | Suspended.
rows.statement: Warns against making a single numerical probability the universal epistemic representation, citing Titelbaum's classificatory/comparative/quantitative attitude distinctions, and proposes a non-numeric-friendly EpistemicAttitude type together with an epistemic-resolution concept Resolution(K) rather than assuming all knowledge is exactly quantified.

rows.anchor: ProbabilityCoherence != Truth != Knowledge. ... Validity = SemanticValidity AND EvidenceAdequacy AND InferentialCoherence AND Calibration AND PurposeAdequacy.
rows.statement: States that Titelbaum's five core Bayesian rules (Non-Negativity, Normality, Finite Additivity, Ratio Formula, Conditionalization) are norms on credences, not truth-establishing rules, yielding ProbabilityCoherence != Truth != Knowledge and proposing CoherenceValidation as only one of five independent validity dimensions (semantic validity, evidence adequacy, inferential coherence, calibration, purpose adequacy).

rows.anchor: Cr_{t+1}(H)=Cr_t(H|E) ... strict Conditionalization is not sufficient for KnowledgeOS ... Update(K_t,E,mode) -> K_{t+1} ... EvidenceAccumulation != KnowledgeMonotonicity.
rows.statement: Uses Conditionalization as a genuine mathematical state-transition model for K_t->K_{t+1}, but notes strict Conditionalization over-commits (learned evidence becomes permanently certain) and cites Jeffrey Conditionalization as the corrective, generalizing to Update(K_t,E,mode)->K_{t+1} that distinguishes hard/soft evidence, partial observation, revised interpretation, changed context, and conflicting evidence -- reinforcing EvidenceAccumulation != KnowledgeMonotonicity (F_t subset-of F_{t+1} coexisting with K_{t+1} revising/retracting prior conclusions).

rows.anchor: Rel(E,H|C) ... SUPPORTS / REFUTES / IRRELEVANT / CONDITIONALLY_SUPPORTS / CONDITIONALLY_REFUTES / SCREENS_OFF / INDEPENDENT ... KnowledgeSpace != {claims}. Instead: KS_t=(K_t,R_t).
rows.statement: Formalizes a typed relevance relation Rel(E,H|C) with seven relation types drawn from Titelbaum's independence/positive-relevance/negative-relevance/conditional-relevance/screening-off apparatus, proposed as Knowledge-Space relation types (not kernel primitives), independently converging -- on a formal probabilistic basis -- with an earlier Davidson-derived proposal that Knowledge Space is relational (KS_t=(K_t,R_t)) rather than a bag of claims.

rows.anchor: Zero(K_t,I_Q) as a condition concerning whether the current epistemic state sufficiently distinguishes the alternatives relevant to inquiry Q. ... This is not Titelbaum's definition of Zero. It is a KnowledgeOS derivation.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's doxastically-possible-worlds apparatus to propose Zero as 'failure to eliminate all inquiry-relevant unresolved alternatives' (illustrated by two viable connectivity hypotheses left undistinguished by current evidence), explicitly flagged as a KnowledgeOS-side derivation rather than Titelbaum's own concept.

rows.anchor: EpistemicZero != ProbabilisticZero != LogicalFalsehood. ... We should keep Zero semantic rather than identifying it with numerical probability.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's Regularity discussion (contingent propositions should not receive credence zero, yet Conditionalization can generate zero credences for evidence-inconsistent propositions) to argue Zero, as a KnowledgeOS gap/defect concept, must remain semantic and not be identified with numerical probability zero or logical falsehood.

rows.anchor: (K_t,S) where S represents epistemic standards. ... The Hypothetical Priors Theorem establishes that ... a common hypothetical prior [can represent a finite sequence of credence distributions]. ... K_t, S_t, and Governance constraints G are three different things.
rows.statement: Extracts a standard-vs-state distinction: alongside K_t, a stable epistemic-response-standard S (potentially equal to the hypothetical prior Pr^H, which can remain fixed while evidence changes, backed by a cited Hypothetical Priors Theorem) and governance constraints G are three genuinely separate things.

rows.anchor: permissive cases where agents with identical evidence can rationally arrive at different credences. ... Adequate(K_1,Q) and Adequate(K_2,Q) may both hold. ... Titelbaum provides independent theoretical support for Adequacy != Uniqueness.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's Objective-vs-Subjective-Bayesianism distinction (subjective Bayesianism permits multiple rationally acceptable credences for identical evidence) as independent theoretical support, alongside an earlier Davidson-derived result, for Adequacy != Uniqueness -- two different states can both be adequate for the same inquiry given different but equally rational epistemic standards.

rows.anchor: Evidence -> Relevance -> Confirmation does not automatically yield Confirmation -> Determination. Support != Determination. High Credence != Knowledge. ... Determine(K_t,Q,EC) iff Adequate(K_t,I_Q).
rows.statement: Separates confirmation from determination (evidential relevance producing confirmation does not automatically license determination; Support!=Determination; HighCredence!=Knowledge), and proposes replacing a context-free Determine(K_t) kernel operator with an inquiry-relative Determine(K_t,Q,EC) meaning 'determine whether K_t is sufficient to resolve inquiry Q under epistemic constraints EC', equivalent to Adequate(K_t,I_Q).

rows.anchor: |E| != EpistemicStrength(E) and EvidenceCount != EvidenceValue. ... E -> Relevance(E,H) -> Confirmation(E,H) -> CredenceChange(H) -> InquiryAdequacy.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's independence/conditional-independence apparatus to state an anti-double-counting principle (evidence item count is not the same as epistemic strength, since correlated or redundant items can masquerade as independent sources), and inserts a relevance-before-value chain refining the earlier expected-information-gain investigation objective to depend on Relevance(E,Q) rather than raw information quantity.

rows.anchor: higher-order credences -- credences about one's own credences ... MetaK_t.
rows.statement: Raises higher-order epistemic state (MetaK_t, credences about one's own credences) as a further candidate missing KnowledgeOS element, tied to Titelbaum's discussion of an agent's limited access to its own mental state.

rows.anchor: RespondToEvidence ... Maintain/ApplyEpistemicStandards ... Epistemic Standards may be essential to the KnowledgeOS system without being a kernel operator. ... essential system component vs primitive kernel operation.
rows.statement: Extends the kernel-reduction experiment's test list to include whether RespondToEvidence and Maintain/ApplyEpistemicStandards decompose into existing candidate operators (Interpret+Discriminate+Evaluate+Update) or require distinct primitives, explicitly anticipating the possible finding that Epistemic Standards could be an essential SYSTEM component without being a primitive KERNEL operator -- named exactly the kind of distinction the research needs.

rows.anchor: Evidence != Epistemic Standards != Attitude != Representation != Confidence != Knowledge != Decision. ... (E_t,S_t) -> K_t -> (E_{t+1},S_{t+1}) -> K_{t+1}. ... Claim_t in K_t but Claim_t not-in K_{t+1} can be legitimate.
rows.statement: Closes with a seven-way non-collapse chain (Evidence != Epistemic Standards != Attitude != Representation != Confidence != Knowledge != Decision) and the temporal transformation form K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E_{t+1},S_t^epi,C_{t+1},Q_{t+1}), explicitly allowing a claim present in K_t to be legitimately absent from K_{t+1} when new evidence defeats or revises it -- named the book's deepest contribution over merely 'adding Bayesian probability.'

rows.anchor: the single most important missing element exposed by Titelbaum is Epistemic Standards. ... That is a genuine theoretical gap, not merely an architectural enhancement.
rows.statement: States the file's bottom-line conclusion: Epistemic Standards is the single most important theoretical gap this reading exposes in KnowledgeOS -- the existing model has evidence, interpretation, inference, validation, K_t, Zero, inquiry and governance, but no explicit place for the mechanism determining how the same evidence gets epistemically evaluated.

rows.anchor: $$(E_t,S_t^{epi})\rightarrow A_t\rightarrow K_t$$ ... \(S_t^{epi}\) = epistemic response standards ... This is **not Governance**. Governance determines what a system is authorized or required to do. Epistemic standards determine how evidence is evaluated.
rows.statement: Restates and sharpens the core S^epi (Epistemic Response Standard) proposal: the compressed chain E_t -> K_t is replaced by (E_t, S_t^epi) -> A_t -> K_t, with S^epi explicitly distinguished from Governance (Governance = what is authorized/required; S^epi = how evidence is evaluated).
missing: a decision among the four candidate models (state/configuration/learned-state/emergent) for what S^epi actually is

rows.anchor: Model A -- standard as state K_t=(E_t,S_t^{epi},A_t,...) ... Model B -- standard as configuration ... Model C -- standard as learned state ... Model D -- standards emerge from kernel operations ... Titelbaum actually distinguishes **ongoing** standards from **ultimate** standards
rows.statement: Proposes four unresolved candidate models for the ontological status of the epistemic-standard object S^epi: (A) standard as part of the state K_t, (B) standard as external configuration outside K_t, (C) standard as a learned state updated via U_S(S_t,E_t), (D) standards emergent from kernel operations F(history,validation,experience); explicitly left undecided, motivated by Titelbaum's own ongoing-vs-ultimate-standards distinction.

rows.anchor: $$E_t=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$$ with each: $$e_i=(Content,Source,Acquisition,Time,Context,Provenance,Reliability,\ldots).$$
rows.statement: Proposes decomposing total evidence E_t into a set of individually structured evidence items e_i=(Content,Source,Acquisition,Time,Context,Provenance,Reliability,...), with the exact schema left [PROP], motivated by Titelbaum's total-evidence formalism.
missing: a fixed, ratified schema for the evidence-item tuple e_i

rows.anchor: $$AcquisitionContext(e)$$ as a first-class concept. ... Observation: port 8081 responds / Acquisition: remote TCP scan / Context: from host X / Time: t / Evidence: observation + acquisition conditions ... much stronger epistemically than: port = 8081
rows.statement: Proposes AcquisitionContext(e) as a first-class KnowledgeOS concept, arguing how evidence enters the system is epistemically relevant (Observation != Evidence != EpistemicInterpretation), illustrated by a worked Nexus example contrasting a bare fact ('port = 8081') with a fully contextualized evidence record (observation + acquisition method + source host + time).

rows.anchor: ### Semantic claim $$c_i=(O,d,v,t)$$ and: ### Epistemic assessment $$a_i=(c_i,E,S,Cr,Status,\ldots)$$ Then: $$K_t=\{(c_i,a_i)\}$$ ... $$Claim\neq Confidence$$ and: $$Confidence\neq Knowledge.$$
rows.statement: Restates (in near-identical form to a companion same-day extraction) the split of an atomic knowledge unit into a semantic claim c_i=(O,d,v,t) and a separate epistemic assessment a_i=(c_i,E,S,Cr,Status,...), giving K_t={(c_i,a_i)} as a candidate model and the two non-collapse principles Claim != Confidence and Confidence != Knowledge.

rows.anchor: $$Attitude(H)\in\{Categorical,Comparative,Interval,Quantitative,Unknown,Suspended,Conflict\}$$ is a candidate representation family.
rows.statement: Extends the earlier candidate EpistemicAttitude-type enumeration to a seven-member family {Categorical, Comparative, Interval, Quantitative, Unknown, Suspended, Conflict}, arguing against assuming a single universal point-probability representation of epistemic state, and noting this fits the corpus's existing knowledge-gap/conflict/unknown distinction.

rows.anchor: $$R\in\{Supports,Refutes,Irrelevant,Independent,ConditionallySupports,ConditionallyRefutes,ScreensOff\}.$$ These are candidates for **Knowledge Space relations**, not automatically kernel primitives.
rows.statement: Restates the typed relevance relation R_t(e,h|C) with a seven-member type vocabulary (Supports, Refutes, Irrelevant, Independent, ConditionallySupports, ConditionallyRefutes, ScreensOff), proposed as Knowledge Space relations rather than kernel primitives, derived from Titelbaum's relevance/independence/screening-off apparatus.

rows.anchor: $$EvidenceValue\neq EvidenceCount$$ and potentially: $$EvidenceValue(e_i,e_j)$$ for dependency. This is a direct statistical consequence of independence/conditional-independence structure.
rows.statement: Restates the anti-double-counting principle EvidenceValue != EvidenceCount using a worked example of two evidence reports copied from the same underlying source, arguing that |E|=2 does not mean evidence strength doubles, and that a pairwise dependency-aware value function EvidenceValue(e_i,e_j) may be needed.

rows.anchor: $$U(U(K,E_1),E_2)\neq U(U(K,E_2),E_1).$$ The book explicitly identifies this order dependence. ... Therefore we need to investigate: $$Update\ Order\ Sensitivity$$
rows.statement: Introduces update-order sensitivity as a new gap: Jeffrey Conditionalization updates can fail to commute (U(U(K,E1),E2) != U(U(K,E2),E1)), so KnowledgeOS cannot assume evidence items E1,E2 can always be treated as an unordered set, connecting this to the existing concern about temporal identity.
missing: an investigation of whether/how KnowledgeOS's own update operator is order-sensitive

rows.anchor: The Problem of Old Evidence: information obtained previously can nevertheless become relevant to a present epistemic problem. ... $$New\ epistemic\ relevance\not\equiv new\ raw\ observation.$$ An old fact can become newly relevant because: a new hypothesis is introduced; a new inquiry is asked; a new model becomes available; context changes; relationships among propositions change.
rows.statement: Introduces the Problem of Old Evidence as a KnowledgeOS-relevant gap: new epistemic relevance is not equivalent to new raw observation, since an old fact can become newly relevant when a new hypothesis, inquiry, model, context, or proposition-relationship is introduced -- offered as support for an inquiry-dependent KnowledgeOS model.

rows.anchor: $$K_t\models H.$$ That does not mean: $$H\in K_t$$ as an explicitly represented claim. Therefore we should distinguish: ExplicitKnowledge from DerivableKnowledge and potentially: OperationallyAvailableKnowledge.
rows.statement: Proposes a three-way distinction between ExplicitKnowledge (claims literally represented in K_t), DerivableKnowledge (K_t |= H without H being explicitly represented), and OperationallyAvailableKnowledge, derived from Titelbaum's logical-omniscience discussion, as a candidate refinement of Knowledge Space.
missing: formal definitions distinguishing the three knowledge-availability categories

rows.anchor: $$K_t:D_t\rightarrow A$$ where: $$D_t\subsetneq\mathcal L.$$ ... The system need not assign an epistemic value to every conceivable proposition. ... $$D_t\neq D_{t+1}$$ may be possible.
rows.statement: Proposes modelling K_t as a genuinely partial epistemic state (a function K_t:D_t -> A over a proper subset D_t of the full language, rather than a total function over all of L), with the further hypothesis that the domain D_t is itself dynamic (D_t != D_{t+1}), distinguishing State Value from State Domain and Inquiry Domain.
missing: a formal account of how the domain D_t itself evolves and how Inquiry Domain relates to it

rows.anchor: $$\mathcal{KS}_t=(K_t,R_t,D_t)$$ is worth investigating. Where: \(K_t\) = epistemic content/state; \(R_t\) = relations; \(D_t\) = represented domain.
rows.statement: Extends the previously-candidate relational Knowledge Space KS_t=(K_t,R_t) to a three-component KS_t=(K_t,R_t,D_t) by adding the represented domain D_t, still marked [PROP].
missing: justification for whether D_t needs to be a distinct third component versus derivable from K_t/R_t

rows.anchor: Evidence -> Support -> Assessment -> Determination -> Knowledge rather than: Evidence -> Knowledge. ... Suppose $$P(H\mid E)=0.85.$$ Is \(H\) determined? There is no context-free answer. ... $$Determine(K_t,Q,EC)$$ is much more defensible than: $$Determine(K_t).$$
rows.statement: Restates and re-argues (via a worked 0.85-credence example) that determination must be inquiry-relative: confirmation/support does not automatically yield knowledge, so Determine(K_t,Q,EC) is defended over a context-free Determine(K_t), reinforcing the existing I_Q and Zero(K_t,I_Q,EC) constructs.

rows.anchor: A credence of zero is a probabilistic attitude. It is not automatically: ignorance; a knowledge gap; contradiction; logical impossibility. ... our KnowledgeOS Zero should **not** be reduced to $$P(H)=0.$$ Instead: $$Zero(K_t,I_Q,EC)$$ remains a predicate about **epistemic adequacy**.
rows.statement: Restates and reinforces the principle that Zero must remain a semantic epistemic-adequacy predicate rather than being reduced to a probability of zero, noting Titelbaum's own discussion of cases where credence 1 does not amount to certainty as a supporting warning.

rows.anchor: $$\exists a\in Alt(K_t,Q)\text{ such that }a\text{ remains unresolved under }EC$$ or, for adequate determination: $$Alt_{relevant}(K_t,Q)\subseteq Resolved(K_t,Q,EC).$$ This is **our hypothesis**, not Titelbaum's definition.
rows.statement: Proposes, as an explicit KnowledgeOS-side (not Titelbaum-derived) research hypothesis, formalizing Zero via Titelbaum's doxastically-possible-worlds apparatus: Zero(K_t,I_Q,EC) holds iff some inquiry-relevant alternative a in Alt(K_t,Q) remains unresolved under EC, i.e. Alt_relevant(K_t,Q) is not a subset of Resolved(K_t,Q,EC) for adequate determination.
missing: a formal definition of Alt(K_t,Q) and Resolved(K_t,Q,EC)

rows.anchor: The core Bayesian rules do not determine one unique hypothetical prior. Multiple hypothetical priors can fit an agent's history. ... $$Evidence+constraints\not\Rightarrow unique\ epistemic\ state$$ in general. Therefore: $$\mathcal A(E,Q)=\{K_1,K_2,\ldots\}$$
rows.statement: Argues from Titelbaum's Objective/Subjective/extreme-Subjective Bayesianism distinction that evidence plus constraints does not in general yield a unique epistemic state, proposing that the correct representation of admissible states under (E,Q) may be a set A(E,Q)={K1,K2,...} of multiple simultaneously admissible states -- and that admissible alternatives are not automatically Conflict(K1,K2) but may instead be legitimate AlternativeInterpretations, motivating a status vocabulary of CONFLICT/ALTERNATIVE/UNKNOWN/UNDERDETERMINED/INCOMPATIBLE/UNVALIDATED.

rows.anchor: $$K_{t+1}=U_K(K_t,E_{t+1},S_t,C_t,Q_t)$$ $$S_{t+1}=U_S(S_t,E_{t+1},V_t)$$ where \(V_t\) might represent validation/learning. ... **KnowledgeOS does not only learn facts; it may learn how to respond to facts.**
rows.statement: Proposes a coupled dynamical system in which the knowledge state K_t and the epistemic-standard state S_t evolve via separate but interacting update functions U_K and U_S (the latter parameterized by a validation/learning signal V_t), summarized as the hypothesis that KnowledgeOS 'does not only learn facts; it may learn how to respond to facts' -- flagged as potentially one of the most important missing theoretical capabilities.
missing: a definition of the validation/learning signal V_t and of U_S

rows.anchor: Titelbaum explicitly defines higher-order credences as credences about one's own credences ... $$MetaK_t$$ about: what it currently accepts; how confident it is; why; what evidence supports it; what assumptions it used; what standards it applied; where it is uncertain; what it believes it should revise. ... $$K_t\neq MetaK_t$$
rows.statement: Introduces MetaK_t (higher-order epistemic state: knowledge about the system's own current acceptances, confidence, justifications, assumptions, standards, uncertainties and needed revisions) as distinct from K_t itself, derived from Titelbaum's higher-order-credence treatment, and connects it to explainability and deterministic assurance.

rows.anchor: ### Database expert: Has more relevant information. ### Analyst expert: Is better at evaluating relevance between propositions. ... $$Expertise\neq InformationVolume.$$ ... $$EpistemicAuthority(e,Q)$$ with separate dimensions: $$InformationAuthority$$ and: $$AnalyticalAuthority.$$
rows.statement: Introduces a database-expert vs analyst-expert distinction from Titelbaum (more information vs better relevance-evaluation) to argue Expertise != InformationVolume, proposing a two-dimensional EpistemicAuthority(e,Q) split into InformationAuthority and AnalyticalAuthority, explicitly connected to but not silently merged with the corpus's existing authority = provenance x standing research.
missing: reconciliation between this two-dimensional EpistemicAuthority and the existing authority=provenance x standing model

rows.anchor: The fire-alarm example ... Prior experience changes how a later signal is interpreted. ... $$Evidence\rightarrow Knowledge\rightarrow Epistemic\ Standards\rightarrow Interpretation\ of\ Future\ Evidence.$$ This may be a fundamental mechanism of epistemic learning.
rows.statement: Uses Titelbaum's fire-alarm example to argue evidence can change the standard by which later evidence is interpreted, proposing a feedback loop Evidence -> Knowledge -> Epistemic Standards -> Interpretation-of-future-evidence as a candidate fundamental mechanism of epistemic learning.

rows.anchor: Titelbaum treats decision theory separately from epistemic rationality ... $$K_t\rightarrow Decision\rightarrow Action$$ rather than: $$Action\in K_t.$$ ... it makes the candidate kernel operation `Select` suspicious. `Select` may belong to decision theory rather than the epistemic kernel.
rows.statement: Argues from Titelbaum's theoretical-vs-practical-rationality distinction that decision/action should remain strictly downstream of the epistemic state (K_t -> Decision -> Action, never Action in K_t), and on this basis explicitly casts doubt on Select as an epistemic-kernel primitive, proposing it may instead belong to a separate decision layer -- a candidate split of {Observe,...,Determine} (epistemic kernel) from {Evaluate options, Select, Act} (decision layer), marked [PROP] and requiring the kernel experiment to test it.
missing: the kernel experiment itself, to test whether Select belongs in the epistemic kernel or a decision layer

rows.anchor: ### Model M0 -- Evidence-only $$K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E)$$ ### Model M1 -- Evidence + standards ... ### Model M4 -- relational epistemic state $$K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E,S,C,Q,R).$$ Then construct controlled cases where E,C,Q are held constant while S changes.
rows.statement: Proposes a controlled-comparison experiment design over five competing update models M0-M4 (evidence-only; +standards; +standards+context; +standards+context+inquiry; +relational epistemic state), to be tested by holding E, C, Q fixed while varying S and checking whether observed K_t differences require the standards variable -- explicitly framed as a not-yet-executed research design.

experiment.hypothesis: Model M0 (evidence-only) is insufficient to explain observed epistemic-state differences; a distinct epistemic-standards variable S is required (models M1-M4).
experiment.setup: Five nested candidate update models M0..M4 differing in which of {E,S,C,Q,R} they take as arguments.
experiment.assumptions: A distance/comparison function d(K_i,K_j) between epistemic states exists.
experiment.inputs: Synthetic evidence sets E and varied standards/context/inquiry configurations, illustrated with a Nexus server discovery domain (OS/RAM/Port observations; hypotheses H1-H3 about operational/reachable/configured status; varied context, standards, inquiry, acquisition method).
experiment.method: Hold subsets of {E,C,Q} fixed while varying S (and separately C, Q, acquisition) and measure resulting K_t differences via sensitivity deltas Delta_K, Delta_E, Delta_S, Delta_C, Delta_Q.
experiment.interpretation: The purpose is not to prove one model correct but to determine which variables are functionally indispensable.
experiment.limitations: Design only; not executed in this document.

rows.anchor: For each candidate operator \(f_i\): $$\mathcal K=\{f_1,\ldots,f_n\}.$$ Remove it ... Can all required behaviors be reproduced? ... there is a second test: Can the missing behavior be reconstructed by composition of other operators without introducing hidden equivalent machinery? This prevents fake minimality.
rows.statement: Proposes a two-stage kernel-minimality criterion: (1) remove candidate operator f_i and test whether all required behaviours are still reproducible; (2) if so, additionally verify the missing behaviour is reconstructed by genuine composition of remaining operators rather than by introducing hidden equivalent machinery -- explicitly framed as a prevention of fake minimality claims, closely prefiguring the later executed protocol's semantic-smuggling test.

rows.anchor: Evidence / EpistemicAssessment / KnowledgeState / EpistemicStandard / Inquiry / Validation / Decision / Governance ... rather than putting them all into a single "Knowledge" aggregate.
rows.statement: Offers a preliminary DDD interpretation proposing eight separate bounded concepts (Evidence, EpistemicAssessment, KnowledgeState, EpistemicStandard, Inquiry, Validation, Decision, Governance) rather than one undifferentiated Knowledge aggregate, with a sketched relationship diagram (Evidence->Assessment->KnowledgeState, EpistemicStandard->Assessment, Inquiry->Determination, Validation->KnowledgeState, KnowledgeState->Decision, Governance->Authorization), explicitly marked conceptual DDD rather than implementation architecture.
missing: implementation-level architecture for the eight proposed bounded concepts

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is a system for controlled epistemic state transformation. ... $$(E_t,S_t,C_t,Q_t,EC_t)\rightarrow K_t$$ and: $$(K_t,E_{t+1},S_{t+1},Q_{t+1},EC_{t+1})\rightarrow K_{t+1}.$$ The key object is therefore not merely the claim. It is the **state transition under epistemic constraints**.
rows.statement: States a revised 'theoretical center of gravity' rejecting both 'KnowledgeOS is a system that stores knowledge' and 'a Bayesian knowledge engine', proposing instead 'KnowledgeOS is a system for controlled epistemic state transformation', formalized as (E_t,S_t,C_t,Q_t,EC_t) -> K_t and (K_t,E_{t+1},S_{t+1},Q_{t+1},EC_{t+1}) -> K_{t+1}, with the key object being the state transition itself rather than any individual claim.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS needs to model not only what it knows, but how it is disposed to respond to evidence. ... $$(K_t,S_t^{epi})\xrightarrow{E,Q,C,EC}(K_{t+1},S_{t+1}^{epi})$$ is the candidate epistemic dynamics. I would **not yet canonize this equation**.
rows.statement: States the file's deepest closing result: KnowledgeOS must model not only what it knows but how it is disposed to respond to evidence, yielding the coupled candidate dynamics (K_t,S_t^epi) --E,Q,C,EC--> (K_{t+1},S_{t+1}^epi}, explicitly held as the strongest current candidate model but not yet canonized.

rows.anchor: We need controlled worlds where: E_1=E_2 but: S_1^{epi}!=S_2^{epi}. Then measure: K(E,S_1,Q,C)!=K(E,S_2,Q,C). If so, the experiment establishes: K!=f(E) under the tested model. ... A factorial design would be ideal ... 2^4=16 conditions ... central question becomes: Does epistemic state depend on standards independently of evidence?
rows.statement: Proposes a dedicated controlled/factorial experiment (2 evidence levels x 2 epistemic standards x 2 contexts x 2 inquiries = 16 conditions) to empirically isolate the causal/functional contribution of E, S^epi, Q and C to the resulting knowledge state K, holding pairs equal and varying the others, to test whether K genuinely depends on epistemic standards independently of evidence -- directly operationalizing the Titelbaum-derived S^epi hypothesis and judged more important than another large random ablation run.

rows.anchor: $$K_t=\Phi(E_{\leq t},S_t,Q_t,C_t,R_t)$$ with: $$K_{t+1}=U(K_t,e_{t+1},S_{t+1},Q_{t+1},C_{t+1}).$$ ... $$Decision_t=D(K_t,Q,Objective,Authorization).$$ This gives a much cleaner separation: Epistemic system -> Decision system -> Governance/Authorization.
rows.statement: Restates the file's provisional overall mathematical model: K_t = Phi(E_{<=t},S_t,Q_t,C_t,R_t), K_{t+1}=U(K_t,e_{t+1},S_{t+1},Q_{t+1},C_{t+1}), with Zero(K_t,I_Q,EC) as a predicate, Determine(K_t,Q,EC) as a judgment/transition of unknown primitive status, and Decision_t=D(K_t,Q,Objective,Authorization), giving a three-layer separation Epistemic system -> Decision system -> Governance/Authorization.

rows.anchor: A doxastic attitude is an attitude **toward** a proposition; it is not the proposition itself. Therefore I think KnowledgeOS needs a missing theoretical layer: **Epistemic Assessment** between evidence and Knowledge State.
rows.statement: Identifies the single largest finding of the reading: KnowledgeOS risks collapsing Evidence -> Assessment -> Knowledge into a bare Evidence -> K_t, whereas Titelbaum's doxastic-attitude-toward-a-proposition framing motivates introducing an explicit missing theoretical layer, Epistemic Assessment, between evidence and the Knowledge State.

rows.anchor: $$A_t = \text{Epistemic Assessment State at }t$$ with something like: $$A_t(h)=\langle attitude,\ strength,\ warrant,\ status\rangle$$ where `strength` **need not be numerical**. Thus: $$E_t \rightarrow A_t \rightarrow K_t$$
rows.statement: Formalizes the Epistemic Assessment State A_t(h)=<attitude, strength, warrant, status> (with strength explicitly not required to be numerical), giving E_t -> A_t -> K_t as the corrected pipeline, with the DDD consequence that Evidence, Epistemic Assessment, and Knowledge State should be separate conceptual responsibilities.
missing: a fixed, ratified schema for A_t(h)

rows.anchor: $$Support(E,H\mid S,C)$$ distinct from: $$Assessment(H\mid E,S,C)$$ and distinct again from: $$KnowledgeStatus(H)$$
rows.statement: Argues Justification != Confidence and Evidence-Hypothesis-Support != Agent-Confidence, since strong support does not itself dictate a specific numeric confidence (that additionally depends on the epistemic standard/regime); introduces three distinct relations Support(E,H|S,C), Assessment(H|E,S,C), and KnowledgeStatus(H) that must not be conflated.

rows.anchor: The book explicitly describes ultimate standards as a function: $$S: \text{Bodies of Evidence}\rightarrow \text{Attitudes}$$ and then uses a hypothetical prior merely as one Bayesian representation of that function. **The hypothetical prior is not the theory.**
rows.statement: Clarifies that Titelbaum's ultimate epistemic standard is a function from bodies of evidence to attitudes, of which the hypothetical-prior construction is merely one Bayesian representation, not the theory itself; introduces S_t^epi (epistemic standard at t) and S* (ultimate/evidence-independent standard), with A_t = Assess(E_t, S_t^epi, Q_t, C_t).

rows.anchor: $$(E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t)\rightarrow A_t$$ ... `Determine` ... should probably become: $$Determine(E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t)\rightarrow \mathcal A_Q$$ where $$\mathcal A_Q=\text{set of admissible determinations}.$$ Then: $$|\mathcal A_Q|=1$$ means **epistemically unique determination**.
rows.statement: Generalizes Determine from Determine(K_t,Q)->Answer to Determine(E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t) -> A_Q, a SET of admissible determinations, with |A_Q|=1 meaning epistemically unique determination and |A_Q|>1 meaning the evidence does not uniquely determine the answer under the permitted standards -- since Titelbaum shows identical total evidence with differing standards can license different conclusions, and even the Bayesian core rules alone do not force a unique rational response.

rows.anchor: A downstream system may nevertheless choose: $$a^\star=a_2.$$ That is **selection**, not determination. So: $$Determine \neq Select$$ ... `Select` should remain **outside the epistemic core unless independently proven otherwise**.
rows.statement: Argues that when multiple epistemically admissible determinations A_Q={a1,a2,a3} exist, a downstream system choosing one (a* = a2) performs selection, not determination -- supporting Determine != Select and the kernel experiment's suspicion that Select may belong to a neighbouring decision context; recommends, as a strong [INF] hypothesis (not yet architecture), that Select remain outside the epistemic core unless independently proven otherwise.

rows.anchor: the mechanism by which information was acquired can itself be part of the evidence. ... $$\boxed{Qualify(Observation,AcquisitionContext,Source,Method,Policy,Context)\rightarrow EvidenceStatus}$$
rows.statement: Using Titelbaum's fish-net/Monty-Hall acquisition-mechanism discussion, gives Qualify a deeper signature than Qualify(O,P)->E: Qualify(Observation, AcquisitionContext, Source, Method, Policy, Context) -> EvidenceStatus, illustrated by a worked '31 GB RAM' example showing the bare number is not the full epistemic object once source/method/environment/timestamp/reliability-assumptions are included.

rows.anchor: $$E_t^{total}$$ and: $$E_{t,Q}^{relevant}$$ with: $$E_{t,Q}^{relevant}\subseteq E_t^{total}.$$ But the projection must be **derived**, not confused with the actual evidence state. So: $$Relevant(E_t,Q,C,S)\rightarrow E_{t,Q}^{relevant}$$
rows.statement: Distinguishes total evidence E_t^total from relevant evidence E_{t,Q}^relevant (a derived subset via Relevant(E_t,Q,C,S) -> E_{t,Q}^relevant, not to be confused with the actual evidence state), on the grounds that most total evidence may be irrelevant to a particular inquiry while probabilistic relevance relations are non-monotonic -- connected explicitly to the existing Inquiry model.

rows.anchor: something can be relevant unconditionally but become irrelevant once another fact is known. ... $$Relevant(E,H\mid B,C,S)$$ where B is background information. ... A fact does not possess a permanently fixed epistemic relevance independent of inquiry/context.
rows.statement: Refines Relevant(E,H) (too crude) into a background-conditioned Relevant(E,H|B,C,S), from Titelbaum's screening-off/conditional-independence treatment, supporting with a stronger mathematical basis the existing idea that the Knowledge Gap is inquiry-relative: a fact has no permanently fixed epistemic relevance independent of inquiry and context.

rows.anchor: a representation that is too coarse can omit relevant distinctions ... whether updating works correctly can depend on the richness of the language used to represent the agent's possibilities. Therefore: $$RepresentationAdequacy$$ is a missing KnowledgeOS concept. ... $$AdeqRep(L,Q,E,C)$$ must hold before we trust: Infer, Validate, Determine, Zero.
rows.statement: Introduces RepresentationAdequacy AdeqRep(L,Q,E,C) as a missing KnowledgeOS concept from Titelbaum's Monty-Hall representation-richness discussion: a representation language can be too coarse to support correct updating, and adequacy of representation (not mere existence of a representation) must hold before Infer, Validate, Determine or Zero can be trusted -- suggested as a possible explanation for part of the Interpret-vs-Represent instability found in the kernel experiment.

rows.anchor: Two logically equivalent propositions may have the same possible-world extension while remaining distinct propositions. ... $$SemanticEquivalence\neq Identity$$ and: $$CurrentStateEquality\neq HistoricalIdentity.$$ ... Therefore **semantic deduplication must not erase epistemic history**.
rows.statement: Extends the existing historical-identity discipline via Titelbaum's warning against identifying a proposition with its possible-world extension: SemanticEquivalence != Identity and CurrentStateEquality != HistoricalIdentity, illustrated with two semantically-equivalent-but-provenance-distinct claims ('Nexus listens on TCP 8081' vs 'Port 8081 is open for Nexus'), concluding semantic deduplication must not erase epistemic history (provenance, timestamp, source, justification, interpretation path can differ).

rows.anchor: a conditional credence $$cr(P\mid Q)$$ is an attitude toward an **ordered pair of propositions**, not a proposition containing a numerical value. ... $$Assessment(P\mid Q)$$ is a different semantic object. ... $$A: (Claim,Condition,Context)\rightarrow Assessment.$$
rows.statement: Argues, from Titelbaum's conditional-credence-as-attitude-toward-an-ordered-pair treatment, that KnowledgeOS should not model conditional assessment as an ordinary proposition ('if Q then confidence(P)=0.8') but as a distinct semantic object Assessment(P|Q), giving a richer assessment type A: (Claim, Condition, Context) -> Assessment relevant to scenario reasoning, alternative worlds, conditional validation, counterfactual analysis, and challenge generation.

rows.anchor: infinitely many hypothetical priors can fit the same observed credence history. That means: $$History_t\not\Rightarrow unique\ Standard.$$ ... Define: $$S_1\sim_t S_2$$ iff $$\forall E\in\mathcal E_{\le t},\quad S_1(E)=S_2(E).$$ Then the data identify only an equivalence class: $$[S]_t$$
rows.statement: Presents what it calls the strongest mathematical result of the reading: Titelbaum's Hypothetical Priors Theorem guarantees existence but not uniqueness of a representing standard, so a finite observed history identifies only an equivalence class [S]_t of epistemic standards (via S1 ~_t S2 iff they agree on all evidence up to t), not one unique standard -- a classical statistical identifiability problem directly relevant to the kernel experiment's Q-11/Q-14 concerns.

rows.anchor: $$S_t^{ongoing}\neq S^\star.$$ A candidate transition is: $$S_{t+1}^{ongoing}=U_S(S_t^{ongoing},E_{t+1})$$ ... the deeper model may be: $$(E_t,S_t,A_t,K_t)\rightarrow (E_{t+1},S_{t+1},A_{t+1},K_{t+1})$$ Knowledge can change not only because the system learned new facts, but because its **way of evaluating evidence changed**.
rows.statement: Restates and formalizes the ongoing-standard vs ultimate-standard distinction (S_t^ongoing != S*), with an update rule S_{t+1}^ongoing = U_S(S_t^ongoing, E_{t+1}), proposing the deeper KnowledgeOS state model (E_t,S_t,A_t,K_t) -> (E_{t+1},S_{t+1},A_{t+1},K_{t+1}) in which knowledge can change either because new facts were learned or because the way of evaluating evidence changed.

rows.anchor:
$$ProbabilisticCoherence
ot\Rightarrow EpistemicAdequacy$$ This reinforces a KnowledgeOS principle already emerging from Freedman: $$FormalConsistency
eq Validity$$ and: $$ModelCoherence
eq Knowledge.$$
rows.statement: States ProbabilisticCoherence does not imply EpistemicAdequacy (agents satisfying the same probability axioms and update rules can still hold wildly different attitudes given the same evidence), reinforcing a Freedman-derived principle that FormalConsistency != Validity and ModelCoherence != Knowledge, proposed as a formal anti-collapse constraint.

rows.anchor: $$Confidence \not\equiv Probability$$ and more importantly: $$AssessmentSpace\neq [0,1]^{Claims}$$ as a universal KnowledgeOS assumption. A more general theoretical object is: $$\mathcal A(c)$$ where an assessment might be: accepted; rejected; deferred; uncertain; ordinal; comparative; interval-valued; probabilistic; distributional.
rows.statement: Argues numerical confidence should be optional rather than fundamental: Confidence is not equivalent to Probability, and AssessmentSpace should not be universally assumed to be [0,1]^Claims; proposes a general assessment object A(c) whose value may be accepted/rejected/deferred/uncertain/ordinal/comparative/interval-valued/probabilistic/distributional, explicitly connected to the primitive-granularity problem discovered in KR-2026-09-01.

rows.anchor: $$Authority_{epi}=(EvidenceAdvantage,\ AssessmentCompetence,\ Domain)$$ because: more evidence != better reasoning. And this must remain distinct from: $$Authority_{gov}$$ which means authorization to make decisions.
rows.statement: Refines the coarse Authority = Provenance x Standing model into a three-component epistemic authority Authority_epi = (EvidenceAdvantage, AssessmentCompetence, Domain), kept distinct from Authority_gov (authorization to make decisions), giving a DDD split of Epistemic Authority (Evidence Authority, Assessment Authority) from Governance Authority (Decision/Authorization power), proposed to resolve existing authority ambiguities in the corpus.

rows.anchor: $$\mathfrak E_t=(E_t,S_t,A_t,K_t,Q_t,C_t,H_t)$$ ... Evidence qualification $$O_t\xrightarrow{Qualify}E_t$$ ... Assessment $$A_t=\mathsf{Assess}(E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t)$$ ... Knowledge commitment $$K_t=\mathsf{Commit}(E_t,A_t,W_t,P_t,H_t)$$
rows.statement: Proposes a consolidated seven-component research-model state E_t=(E_t,S_t,A_t,K_t,Q_t,C_t,H_t) (qualified evidence, standard, assessment, committed knowledge, inquiry, context, history) with three composed operations -- evidence qualification O_t --Qualify--> E_t (with E_t = f(O_t,Source,Method,Provenance,Context,Policy)), assessment A_t = Assess(E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t), and knowledge commitment K_t = Commit(E_t,A_t,W_t,P_t,H_t) where W_t is warrant/validation and P_t provenance -- explicitly marked as a research model, not canon.
missing: formal definitions of Assess and Commit

rows.anchor: $$Zero(K_t,E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t,I_Q,EC)$$ ... the gap becomes: $$\Delta_Q=D(\mathsf{Adequacy}(K_t,S_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t),I_Q)$$ with: $$Zero\iff \Delta_Q=0$$ only after the adequacy relation itself has been defined.
rows.statement: Refines Zero from Zero(K_t,I_t,EC) to a seven-argument Zero(K_t,E_t,S_t,Q_t,C_t,I_Q,EC), since adequacy depends on evidence, standard, inquiry and context, not only stored K_t, with the gap Delta_Q = D(Adequacy(K_t,S_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t), I_Q) and Zero iff Delta_Q=0 only once Adequacy itself is defined; explicitly states this reinforces the kernel experiment's conclusion that Zero should be a predicate rather than automatically an operator.
missing: a formal definition of the Adequacy relation

rows.anchor: The kernel reduction was attempting to minimize **operations**, while the deeper missing objects are partly **state dimensions and relations**. ... the question 'Is Interpret or Represent primitive?' may be premature. The deeper question is: **Which semantic carriers must exist before operator minimality is even well-defined?**
rows.statement: Reinterprets the kernel-reduction experiment's DetectGap/Qualify findings as evidence that the experiment attempted to minimize operations before separating the underlying state dimensions/carriers (Observation, Qualification, Evidence, Standard, Assessment, Validation, Knowledge, with Inquiry selecting the relevant projection); reframes 'is Interpret or Represent primitive' as premature relative to the deeper question 'which semantic carriers must exist before operator minimality is even well-defined', explicitly connecting this to the experiment's own Q-14.

rows.anchor: P-T01 -- Assessment Separation Claim!=Assessment!=Knowledge. P-T02 -- Evidence Qualification Observation!=Evidence. P-T03 -- Standard Dependence Assessment=f(Evidence,Standard,Inquiry,Context). P-T04 -- Non-Uniqueness Evidence!=>unique Assessment. P-T05 -- Standard Non-Identifiability History_t!=>unique Standard.
rows.statement: Consolidates the file's first five numbered research hypotheses (P-T01 Assessment Separation: Claim!=Assessment!=Knowledge; P-T02 Evidence Qualification: Observation!=Evidence, requiring qualification under acquisition/source/context conditions; P-T03 Standard Dependence: Assessment=f(Evidence,Standard,Inquiry,Context); P-T04 Non-Uniqueness: evidence does not imply a unique assessment absent a standard/contract guaranteeing it; P-T05 Standard Non-Identifiability: history does not imply a unique standard), explicitly marked [PROP], not canon.

rows.anchor: P-T06 -- Total-Evidence Principle ... P-T07 -- Acquisition-Mechanism Principle ... P-T08 -- Representation Adequacy ... P-T09 -- Semantic Identity Separation ... P-T10 -- Epistemic/Practical Separation Determine!=Select ... P-T11 -- Assessment-Representation Plurality ... P-T12 -- Epistemic Authority Decomposition EvidenceAuthority!=AssessmentAuthority!=GovernanceAuthority.
rows.statement: Consolidates the file's remaining seven numbered research hypotheses (P-T06 Total-Evidence Principle: assessment must respect total evidence via a relevance projection; P-T07 Acquisition-Mechanism Principle: meaning depends partly on how evidence was acquired; P-T08 Representation Adequacy: insufficient representation can invalidate determination; P-T09 Semantic Identity Separation: semantic equivalence != record identity; P-T10 Epistemic/Practical Separation: Determine != Select unless proven otherwise; P-T11 Assessment-Representation Plurality: assessment is not equivalent to numeric probability; P-T12 Epistemic Authority Decomposition: EvidenceAuthority != AssessmentAuthority != GovernanceAuthority), explicitly marked [PROP], not canon.

rows.anchor: I would **not** currently add: $$K_t=P_t(\cdot)$$ or: $$K_{t+1}=K_t(\cdot|E)$$ to KnowledgeOS. ... this previous direction: "Credences are the KnowledgeOS epistemic state" should be **rejected**. ... $$Bayesian\ credence\text{ is one possible formal representation of }Assessment.$$
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects importing K_t = P_t(.) or K_{t+1}=K_t(.|E) (identifying knowledge with a probability measure/its conditional update) into KnowledgeOS as too strong, rejecting the direction 'credences are the KnowledgeOS epistemic state'; the correct research interpretation is that Bayesian credence is one possible formal representation of Assessment, not identical to Knowledge.

rows.anchor: Knowledge State is no longer the place where all epistemic machinery is hidden. ... And I would rank the first four as **blocking gaps** for the next KnowledgeOS theoretical phase: Evidence -> Epistemic Standards -> Assessment -> Knowledge. Until these four are formally separated, another large-scale operator-minimality experiment risks optimizing the wrong abstraction level.
rows.statement: Concludes that Knowledge State should no longer be the place where all epistemic machinery is hidden, ranking the four-stage separation Evidence -> Epistemic Standards -> Assessment -> Knowledge as a blocking gap the next KnowledgeOS theoretical phase must resolve before another large-scale operator-minimality experiment is run, since doing so risks optimizing the wrong abstraction level.

rows.anchor: different bodies of belief/premises can yield materially different numerical judgments from the same observed data. ... (E,S,M,Q,C) -> Assessment ... Good gives an independent reason: the same evidence can legitimately lead to different assessments because the underlying body of beliefs/premises differs.
rows.statement: Provides an independent statistical justification (from Good's contingency-table discussion) for the Titelbaum-derived Epistemic Standards hypothesis: Assessment = f(Evidence, Standards, Model, Context, Inquiry), since different bodies of belief/premises can legitimately yield different numerical judgments from the same observed data -- strengthening the S^epi hypothesis into a cross-source finding, still marked [PROP].

lexical.anchor: Epistemic Attitude_t = F(Total Evidence_t, Epistemic Standards). ... K_t = F(E_t,S_t). ... S^epi = Epistemic Response Standard / Epistemic Interpretation Policy. This must not be confused with Governance.

conceptual.anchor: $$AcquisitionContext(e)$$ as a first-class concept. ... Observation: port 8081 responds / Acquisition: remote TCP scan / Context: from host X / Time: t / Evidence: observation + acquisition conditions ... much stronger epistemically than: port = 8081

formal.anchor: Evidence = (Content, Source, Acquisition, Context, Time, Provenance). ... AcquisitionModel(e). ... how evidence was obtained can itself be epistemically relevant.

operational.anchor: ### Model M0 -- Evidence-only $$K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E)$$ ### Model M1 -- Evidence + standards ... ### Model M4 -- relational epistemic state $$K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E,S,C,Q,R).$$ Then construct controlled cases where E,C,Q are held constant while S changes.

governance.anchor: A downstream system may nevertheless choose: $$a^\star=a_2.$$ That is **selection**, not determination. So: $$Determine \neq Select$$ ... `Select` should remain **outside the epistemic core unless independently proven otherwise**.

rationale_evidence.anchor: two agents possess the same total evidence but arrive at different credences because they have different epistemic standards. ... E_t^A=E_t^B does not imply K_t^A=K_t^B.
rationale_evidence.statement: Uses Titelbaum's same-evidence-different-standards cases to establish that identical total evidence does not entail identical epistemic states, proposing to split the candidate Interpret kernel operator into Interpret(E,S)->M and Update(M,E,S)->K_{t+1} for testing in the kernel-reduction experiment.

rationale_evidence.anchor: permissive cases where agents with identical evidence can rationally arrive at different credences. ... Adequate(K_1,Q) and Adequate(K_2,Q) may both hold. ... Titelbaum provides independent theoretical support for Adequacy != Uniqueness.
rationale_evidence.statement: Uses Titelbaum's Objective-vs-Subjective-Bayesianism distinction (subjective Bayesianism permits multiple rationally acceptable credences for identical evidence) as independent theoretical support, alongside an earlier Davidson-derived result, for Adequacy != Uniqueness -- two different states can both be adequate for the same inquiry given different but equally rational epistemic standards.

rationale_evidence.anchor: $$EvidenceValue\neq EvidenceCount$$ and potentially: $$EvidenceValue(e_i,e_j)$$ for dependency. This is a direct statistical consequence of independence/conditional-independence structure.
rationale_evidence.statement: Restates the anti-double-counting principle EvidenceValue != EvidenceCount using a worked example of two evidence reports copied from the same underlying source, arguing that |E|=2 does not mean evidence strength doubles, and that a pairwise dependency-aware value function EvidenceValue(e_i,e_j) may be needed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: $$U(U(K,E_1),E_2)\neq U(U(K,E_2),E_1).$$ The book explicitly identifies this order dependence. ... Therefore we need to investigate: $$Update\ Order\ Sensitivity$$
rationale_evidence.statement: Introduces update-order sensitivity as a new gap: Jeffrey Conditionalization updates can fail to commute (U(U(K,E1),E2) != U(U(K,E2),E1)), so KnowledgeOS cannot assume evidence items E1,E2 can always be treated as an unordered set, connecting this to the existing concern about temporal identity.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The Problem of Old Evidence: information obtained previously can nevertheless become relevant to a present epistemic problem. ... $$New\ epistemic\ relevance\not\equiv new\ raw\ observation.$$ An old fact can become newly relevant because: a new hypothesis is introduced; a new inquiry is asked; a new model becomes available; context changes; relationships among propositions change.
rationale_evidence.statement: Introduces the Problem of Old Evidence as a KnowledgeOS-relevant gap: new epistemic relevance is not equivalent to new raw observation, since an old fact can become newly relevant when a new hypothesis, inquiry, model, context, or proposition-relationship is introduced -- offered as support for an inquiry-dependent KnowledgeOS model.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Evidence -> Support -> Assessment -> Determination -> Knowledge rather than: Evidence -> Knowledge. ... Suppose $$P(H\mid E)=0.85.$$ Is \(H\) determined? There is no context-free answer. ... $$Determine(K_t,Q,EC)$$ is much more defensible than: $$Determine(K_t).$$
rationale_evidence.statement: Restates and re-argues (via a worked 0.85-credence example) that determination must be inquiry-relative: confirmation/support does not automatically yield knowledge, so Determine(K_t,Q,EC) is defended over a context-free Determine(K_t), reinforcing the existing I_Q and Zero(K_t,I_Q,EC) constructs.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The core Bayesian rules do not determine one unique hypothetical prior. Multiple hypothetical priors can fit an agent's history. ... $$Evidence+constraints\not\Rightarrow unique\ epistemic\ state$$ in general. Therefore: $$\mathcal A(E,Q)=\{K_1,K_2,\ldots\}$$
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues from Titelbaum's Objective/Subjective/extreme-Subjective Bayesianism distinction that evidence plus constraints does not in general yield a unique epistemic state, proposing that the correct representation of admissible states under (E,Q) may be a set A(E,Q)={K1,K2,...} of multiple simultaneously admissible states -- and that admissible alternatives are not automatically Conflict(K1,K2) but may instead be legitimate AlternativeInterpretations, motivating a status vocabulary of CONFLICT/ALTERNATIVE/UNKNOWN/UNDERDETERMINED/INCOMPATIBLE/UNVALIDATED.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Titelbaum treats decision theory separately from epistemic rationality ... $$K_t\rightarrow Decision\rightarrow Action$$ rather than: $$Action\in K_t.$$ ... it makes the candidate kernel operation `Select` suspicious. `Select` may belong to decision theory rather than the epistemic kernel.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues from Titelbaum's theoretical-vs-practical-rationality distinction that decision/action should remain strictly downstream of the epistemic state (K_t -> Decision -> Action, never Action in K_t), and on this basis explicitly casts doubt on Select as an epistemic-kernel primitive, proposing it may instead belong to a separate decision layer -- a candidate split of {Observe,...,Determine} (epistemic kernel) from {Evaluate options, Select, Act} (decision layer), marked [PROP] and requiring the kernel experiment to test it.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Evidence / EpistemicAssessment / KnowledgeState / EpistemicStandard / Inquiry / Validation / Decision / Governance ... rather than putting them all into a single "Knowledge" aggregate.
rationale_evidence.statement: Offers a preliminary DDD interpretation proposing eight separate bounded concepts (Evidence, EpistemicAssessment, KnowledgeState, EpistemicStandard, Inquiry, Validation, Decision, Governance) rather than one undifferentiated Knowledge aggregate, with a sketched relationship diagram (Evidence->Assessment->KnowledgeState, EpistemicStandard->Assessment, Inquiry->Determination, Validation->KnowledgeState, KnowledgeState->Decision, Governance->Authorization), explicitly marked conceptual DDD rather than implementation architecture.

rationale_evidence.anchor: A downstream system may nevertheless choose: $$a^\star=a_2.$$ That is **selection**, not determination. So: $$Determine \neq Select$$ ... `Select` should remain **outside the epistemic core unless independently proven otherwise**.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues that when multiple epistemically admissible determinations A_Q={a1,a2,a3} exist, a downstream system choosing one (a* = a2) performs selection, not determination -- supporting Determine != Select and the kernel experiment's suspicion that Select may belong to a neighbouring decision context; recommends, as a strong [INF] hypothesis (not yet architecture), that Select remain outside the epistemic core unless independently proven otherwise.

Define: $$S_1\sim_t S_2$$ iff $$\forall E\in\mathcal E_{\le t},\quad S_1(E)=S_2(E).$$ Then the data identify only an equivalence class: $$[S]_t$$
rationale_evidence.statement: Presents what it calls the strongest mathematical result of the reading: Titelbaum's Hypothetical Priors Theorem guarantees existence but not uniqueness of a representing standard, so a finite observed history identifies only an equivalence class [S]_t of epistemic standards (via S1 ~_t S2 iff they agree on all evidence up to t), not one unique standard -- a classical statistical identifiability problem directly relevant to the kernel experiment's Q-11/Q-14 concerns.
