conceptual.anchor: KnowledgeEntity has stable identity ... Assertion (Value Object) ... ObservationEvent (Domain Event) ... KnowledgeAggregate ... a strong DDD fit

formal.anchor: W\rightarrow O\rightarrow R\rightarrow A\rightarrow K

operational.anchor: Falsification test 1: R_1=R_2, R_1\equiv_{exact}R_2, but if created at different times O_1\neq O_2. PASS.

rationale_evidence.anchor: AssertionIdentity separate from KnowledgeObjectIdentity ... identity of an Entity is not the same as equality of its attributes
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues two knowledge objects with the same assertion but different provenance are different knowledge records referring to the same proposition, requiring AssertionIdentity separate from KnowledgeObjectIdentity — explicitly analogized to the DDD principle that entity identity differs from attribute equality.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Candidate A: Atma(K)=Identity(A) ... A-identity alone is insufficient
rationale_evidence.statement: Candidate definition A (Atma(K)=Identity(assertion)) is rejected: two knowledge records with the same proposition but different evidence would become identical, losing epistemic distinction.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Candidate B: Atma(K)=Identity(E) ... E-identity alone is insufficient
rationale_evidence.statement: Candidate definition B (Atma(K)=Identity(evidence)) is rejected: two independent evidence items for the same knowledge would become different Atmas, useful for evidence but not for knowledge identity.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Candidate C: K=(A,C,V,P,S) ... much closer ... but provenance may change without changing the underlying knowledge proposition
rationale_evidence.statement: Candidate definition C: K=(Assertion,Context,Validity,Provenance,Status) is 'much closer' but still conflates identity with mutable provenance, motivating a further split into CoreKnowledgeIdentity vs KnowledgeRecordIdentity.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K_t=Fold(Observations_{0..t},Rules) ... analogous to event sourcing
rationale_evidence.statement: Frames knowledge-state construction as event sourcing: K_t = Fold(Observations_0..t, Rules), letting K_t be reconstructed from InitialState and Events.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Alice observes Nexus 3.69, Bob independently observes Nexus 3.69 ... SameKnowledgeMeaning can coexist with DifferentKnowers
rationale_evidence.statement: Worked example: Alice and Bob independently observe the same fact — Knower(Alice)≠Knower(Bob), O_A≠O_B, E_A≠E_B, yet they may support SameAssertion, so SameKnowledgeMeaning can coexist with DifferentKnowers — 'exactly the distinction our architecture requires.'

rationale_evidence.anchor: Exact representation identity Hash(R) ... Observation identity structured event ID ... Assertion identity canonical serialization+hash ... all ordinary computation
rationale_evidence.statement: Lists the core identity layers (exact representation identity via Hash(R), observation identity via structured event ID, assertion identity via canonical serialization+hash, knowledge record identity via stable ID+version, provenance via graph relations, temporal validity via interval evaluation) as 'all ordinary computation.'

sources.note: Step 214's operational data structure implementing step 213's F/D/P/U discipline: a per-step 10-field ledger record and 15-field practical schema, an Evidence Lineage Graph (ELG), the Negative Knowledge concept, the 'late naming' phenomenon, a context-relative Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions) validity model, a semantic-preservation condition for cross-context evidence transfer, an eight-value non-linear KState enum, and a knowledge-continuity model K_t=(CurrentKnowledge,HistoricalKnowledge,Uncertainty).

rows.anchor: EL_i=(Step,Artifact,Observation,Fact,Derivation,Decision,Architecture,Invariant,Evidence,Status) ... EL=∪_i EL_i
rows.statement: Defines the Evidence Ledger as a per-step 10-field record EL_i=(Step,Artifact,Observation,Fact,Derivation,Decision,Architecture,Invariant,Evidence,Status), with the overall ledger EL as the union across all steps, turning step 213's F/D/P/U discipline into a working data structure.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 214 turns that distinction into a working ledger.

rows.anchor: Observation -> Fact -> Derivation -> Architectural Principle -> Invariant ... Invariant -> Implementation -> Test -> Evidence
rows.statement: States the ledger's two-directional fundamental chain (forward: Observation->Fact->Derivation->Architectural Principle->Invariant; feedback: Invariant->Implementation->Test->Evidence->New Knowledge), diagrammed as the architecture's epistemic feedback loop.

rows.anchor: Knowledge_t != Knowledge_{t+1} ... The fact that H_2 is better does not mean H_1 never existed
rows.statement: States that the ledger must preserve chronology (when a belief was held), not only its content, since a later, better hypothesis H2 does not erase the historical fact that an earlier hypothesis H1 was held -- essential to reconstructing the real engineering journey rather than a retrospectively idealized one.

rows.anchor: Calendar chronology ... Engineering chronology ... Epistemic chronology ... The code may exist before the architectural concept has been named
rows.statement: Distinguishes three non-identical chronologies (calendar: when it happened; engineering: what was built before what; epistemic: when it was understood), illustrated by Implementation->Observation->Understanding, where code can precede the naming of its own underlying architectural concept.

rows.anchor: implementation -> repeated problem -> experiment -> pattern recognized -> concept named ... The later name should not be projected backward as though it had been consciously designed from the beginning
rows.statement: Names the 'late naming' phenomenon: a pattern can exist implicitly in the implementation before it is given a formal concept name, and warns against projecting the later name backward as if it had been consciously designed from the start, since that would distort the history.

rows.anchor: | Field | Purpose | ... Rejected alternative | What was not chosen |
rows.statement: Gives a practical 15-field Evidence Ledger schema (Step ID, Artifact, Date/sequence, Observation, Fact, Interpretation, Derived principle, Decision, Rejected alternative, Architectural consequence, Invariant, Verification, Evidence status F/D/P/U, Confidence, Open question).

rows.anchor: What we rejected ... as by: What we selected ... That rejection itself is architectural knowledge
rows.statement: Argues architecture is defined as much by what was rejected as by what was selected (e.g. Alternative A rejected because SemanticLoss(A)>0), justifying a dedicated 'Rejected alternative' ledger field as architectural knowledge in its own right.

rows.anchor: NegativeKnowledge ... knowledge about approaches, assumptions, transitions or interpretations that have been demonstrated to be unsuitable under specified conditions ... different from failure
rows.statement: Introduces NegativeKnowledge as knowledge about approaches/assumptions/transitions/interpretations demonstrated unsuitable under specified conditions, distinguished from mere failure -- a failure becomes useful (negative) knowledge only once its cause ('why it failed') is understood.

rows.anchor: Experiment=(Hypothesis,Setup,Observation,Result,Interpretation,Consequence) ... Result -> Knowledge
rows.statement: Defines a six-field experimental-lineage record (Hypothesis, Setup, Observation, Result, Interpretation, Consequence) intended to let the eventual book demonstrate the scientific/engineering nature of the work.

rows.anchor: A hypothesis says: X may be true ... An invariant says: X must remain true ... Hypothesis -[evidence]-> Pattern -[validation]-> Invariant. Not every hypothesis becomes an invariant
rows.statement: Distinguishes hypothesis (X may be true) from invariant (X must remain true) and defines the promotion pipeline Hypothesis->(evidence)->Pattern->(validation)->Invariant, explicitly noting not every hypothesis is promoted.

rows.anchor: Observed(H) does not imply Universal(H) ... AllAI -> InconsistentCode [is unwarranted from one tested workflow]
rows.statement: States a statistical-discipline guardrail: evidence for H under tested conditions (Observed(H)) must not be generalized to Universal(H), illustrated by a prompt-strategy-specific inconsistency finding that must not be generalized to all AI.

rows.anchor: Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions) ... Valid(C) should really mean: Valid(C | Context,Conditions)
rows.statement: Proposes representing every conclusion as Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions) so that validity is always conditioned (Valid(C|Context,Conditions) rather than bare Valid(C)), framed as a connection between DDD and statistical reasoning; extends this to bounded knowledge (Knowledge_A != Knowledge_B across DDD bounded contexts, requiring an explicit ubiquitous-language-guarded translation when a concept crosses a context boundary).

rows.anchor: p(C_A) => p'(C_B) ... where p' is the explicitly defined interpretation in the target context. If that implication does not hold, the contract may introduce semantic loss
rows.statement: Defines a semantic-preservation condition for cross-context evidence transfer: a property p holding in context C_A after transformation T to C_B must imply the target-context-defined interpretation p' holds in C_B, or the contract introduces semantic loss; states evidence for a claim in one context does not automatically establish it in another without an explicit Mapping and evidence the property survives translation.

rows.anchor: ELG=(V,E) ... V=Artifacts∪Facts∪Observations∪Hypotheses∪Decisions∪Principles∪Invariants ... substantially richer than a conventional requirements traceability matrix
rows.statement: Defines the Evidence Ledger as a graph ELG=(V,E) with seven node types (artifacts, facts, observations, hypotheses, decisions, principles, invariants) and seven edge types (supports, contradicts, derives, motivates, rejects, implements, verifies), explicitly positioned as richer than a conventional requirements traceability matrix.

rows.anchor: C_1 <-[contradicts]-> C_2 ... We should not immediately delete one. Instead record: Contradiction(C_1,C_2) ... Sometimes the contradiction disappears once context is made explicit
rows.statement: Treats contradiction as a first-class graph edge to be recorded rather than resolved by deletion; investigating Context(C_1) vs Context(C_2) can dissolve an apparent contradiction, and more generally an apparent contradiction (ModelA accurate vs inaccurate) can resolve into conditional coherence once Context/Population/Time/Purpose dimensions are introduced -- framed as contradiction potentially revealing a missing dimension.

rows.anchor: Generation != Adjudication ... Candidates -> Evidence -> Adjudication -> AcceptedKnowledge
rows.statement: Applies the contradiction-as-evidence principle to AI-generated competing interpretations: rather than declaring one AI output true and another false, treats {AI_1,AI_2} as an explicit candidate knowledge set requiring adjudication, architecturally separating Generation from Adjudication via Candidates->Evidence->Adjudication->AcceptedKnowledge.

rows.anchor: KState in {Observed,Hypothesized,Derived,Corroborated,Contested,Rejected,Accepted,Deprecated} ... should not automatically be treated as a single linear lifecycle ... Accepted + Contested
rows.statement: Defines an eight-value knowledge-item epistemic state (Observed/Hypothesized/Derived/Corroborated/Contested/Rejected/Accepted/Deprecated), explicitly not a single linear lifecycle -- states may coexist, e.g. Accepted+Contested when knowledge is operationally accepted but still scientifically disputed; reiterates the anti-Boolean discipline (verified=true is insufficient; use KnowledgeState+Evidence+Context+Time).

rows.anchor: UnderlyingPrinciple != CurrentManifestation ... The analogy helps us ask better architecture questions. It does not prove them
rows.statement: Applies a Gita chapter-4 analogy (enduring knowledge vs changing manifestation) to DomainInvariant!=CurrentRuntimeState and HistoricalKnowledge!=CurrentRepresentation, explicitly bounding the analogy as interpretive/heuristic ('helps us ask better questions, does not prove them').

rows.anchor: S_{t+1} does not contain all information about S_t ... S_{t+1} ⊉ S_t ... CurrentState + HistoricalRecord -> HistoricalUnderstanding
rows.statement: Formalizes the 'new state does not know old state' principle as S_{t+1} not-superset-of S_t in general, requiring an additional historical mechanism H_t; concludes CurrentState alone is insufficient and CurrentState+HistoricalRecord is needed for HistoricalUnderstanding, distinguishing CurrentState, HistoricalRecord, and HistoricalInterpretation as three different things.

lineage_claims.target: earlier 'Chapter 4' history-preservation observation referenced in steps 212-213
lineage_claims.quote: We can now express your earlier insight more rigorously.

rows.anchor: K_t=(CurrentKnowledge_t,HistoricalKnowledge,Uncertainty_t) ... Update does not necessarily erase prior knowledge ... KnowledgeVersion [distinct from] KnowledgeState ... Git commit != current working tree
rows.statement: Defines a knowledge-continuity model K_t=(CurrentKnowledge_t,HistoricalKnowledge,Uncertainty_t) with K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_{t+1}), where Update may supersede/qualify/contradict/preserve/deprecate rather than erase prior knowledge; proposes distinguishing KnowledgeVersion from KnowledgeState by analogy to a git commit vs the current working tree, again explicitly flagged as analogy not proof.

rows.anchor: 1. Problem 2. Observation 3. Experiment 4. Failure/Contradiction 5. Insight 6. Abstraction 7. Architecture 8. Verification 9. Remaining uncertainty
rows.statement: Proposes a nine-part chapter template for the eventual book (Problem, Observation, Experiment, Failure/Contradiction, Insight, Abstraction, Architecture, Verification, Remaining uncertainty), argued to be much stronger than presenting only the final architecture, letting the reader follow Why->How->What->Evidence rather than only What.

rows.anchor: No architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it ... No evidence should be interpreted outside its demonstrated context without an explicit derivation
rows.statement: States Step 214's core theorem-like principle and its dual as candidates for the book's 'methodological constitution': no architectural claim should exceed its evidentiary support, and no evidence should be interpreted outside its demonstrated context without an explicit derivation.

rows.anchor: EL(S_1...S_182) rather than continuing blindly to S_215, S_216 ... Let the evidence tell us where the natural conceptual boundaries are
rows.statement: Previews Step 215: rather than continuing to add theory (S215, S216, ...), retrospectively construct the Evidence Ledger for Steps 1-182, tagging each with F/D/P/U and its actual architectural contribution, producing a step-range x contribution-type matrix from which the book's real chapter boundaries should be discovered rather than decided in advance -- explicitly to prevent the book from becoming a retrospective justification of a theory.

lineage_claims.quote: The next step should be retrospective reconstruction.

rows.anchor: each file's tail contains the agenda for the next step
rows.statement: Structural observation, load-bearing for the whole verification: each file in the 208-215 band ends with the agenda section for the *next* step (e.g. the file titled 'Step 208' ends with a '# Step 209' section at line 1423 onward), so the band is a chain of overlapping documents and every 'Step N' agenda exists in two places (as the prior file's tail and the next file's own opening).

rows.anchor: The band is a five-deep chain of deferral
rows.statement: Step 215 produces a 14-code type taxonomy (glossary), a 20-column header list (text fence), a 5-row placeholder matrix (28/40 cells '...'), a 3-phase workflow, and a closing pointer to Step 216 -- i.e. FORWARD POINTER, not an artifact. Verbatim deferral chain: 212->213 ('the next stage should be an evidence-driven reconstruction'); 213->214 ('create the first Evidence Ledger'); 214->215 ('the next step should be retrospective reconstruction'); 215->216 ('Step 216 should not be another theoretical step... it should be the actual execution of the reconstruction'); 216->? ('we should not yet write another architectural theory step', out of scope). Four consecutive files each announce that the *next* file will do the empirical work; the audit announced in Step 212 has not begun by the end of Step 215.

rows.anchor: The three files that announce empirical work ... DO NOT BREAK THE PATTERN
rows.statement: Decisive verdict: Step 212 'Architecture Gap Discovery', Step 213 'Evidence-First Reconstruction' and Step 214 'Build the Evidence Ledger' each announce empirical work and each performs none -- zero shell commands, repository reads, file paths, commit hashes, test-runner output, directory listings, or tool invocations in any of the eight files. The corpus's prior 465-file/207-step record of zero empirical acts is extended, unbroken, to 215 steps and 473 files. Each of the three files states its own non-execution explicitly: Step 212 Section 212.32 ('No evidence => Unknown') then assigns no status to any row; Step 213 Section 213.3 ('each artifact is evidence') then opens no artifact; Step 214 Section 214.1 defines a 10-tuple ledger then records no ledger entry. Under TEST SPECIFIED != TEST EXECUTED, all 15 invariants I1-I15 and all 15 gaps G-01-G-15 remain at 'specified'.

rows.anchor: Does Step 214 cite Step 109? NO — prior EvidenceLedger already existed
rows.statement: Probe (f): grep of Step 214 for '109' finds only a false-positive ('prior' inside another word); zero citation. Prior art confirmed: Step 109 Section 109.69 ('Evidence Ledger') already defines a 6-column schema (ID | Claim | Evidence | Type | Strength | Status) with four fabricated example rows E-001..E-004. Step 214, titled 'Build the Evidence Ledger', does not cite Step 109 and re-mints the ledger schema from scratch (a 10-tuple in Section 214.1, a 15-field table in Section 214.6) rather than extending Step 109's schema -- described as an ES-005.4-style 'never a copy' violation transposed into the research corpus.

rows.anchor: A file titled 'Build the Evidence Ledger' builds no ledger, and produces strictly fewer ledger rows than the uncited step that mandated one 105 steps earlier
rows.statement: Row-count comparison: Step 109 Section 109.69 produced 0 real rows and 4 fabricated example rows (4 total). Step 214 ('Build the Evidence Ledger') produces 0 real rows and 0 fabricated rows (0 total) -- machine-counted across its three tables: a 15x2 field glossary, an 8x2 self-assessment table, and an 8-column matrix header with zero data rows. Step 109's 4 rows were fabricated examples; Step 214's 0 rows are not even that -- a genuine regression relative to the uncited prior step.

rows.anchor: PREVIOUS DEPENDENCY: ZERO individual prior steps (one range, Steps 1-182); LATER RESPONSE: Steps 214 and 215 both build on F/D/P/U
rows.statement: Step 213 cites zero individual prior steps by number, only the Steps-1-182 range (in the Step-214 preview). Later response in scope: Step 214 Section 214.1 operationalizes F/D/P/U into the 10-tuple EL_i; Step 215 Section 215.4 adopts F/D/P/U as its second classification axis.

rows.anchor: FORMAL OBJECTS: EL_i 10-tuple; EL=union of EL_i; NegativeKnowledge; Hypothesis != Invariant; ELG=(V,E); KState 8-valued
rows.statement: Step 214 ('Build the Evidence Ledger') boxes Fact!=Derived!=Proposed!=Unknown; defines the ledger row EL_i=(Step,Artifact,Observation,Fact,Derivation,Decision,Architecture,Invariant,Evidence,Status) and boxes EL=union_i EL_i; boxes Observation->Fact->Derivation->Architectural Principle->Invariant and Invariant->Implementation->Test->Evidence; boxes 'NegativeKnowledge'; defines Experiment=(Hypothesis,Setup,Observation,Result,Interpretation,Consequence) and Hypothesis-[evidence]->Pattern-[validation]->Invariant with Observed(H)⇏Universal(H); defines Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions) and Valid(C|Context,Conditions); defines the Evidence Lineage Graph ELG=(V,E) with node classes Artifacts/Facts/Observations/Hypotheses/Decisions/Principles/Invariants and edges supports/contradicts/derives/motivates/rejects/implements/verifies; a contradiction relation C_1<->C_2; KState in {Observed,Hypothesized,Derived,Corroborated,Contested,Rejected,Accepted,Deprecated}; a knowledge-continuity triple K_t=(CurrentKnowledge_t,HistoricalKnowledge,Uncertainty_t); and boxes 'no architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it' and 'no evidence should be interpreted outside its demonstrated context without an explicit derivation'.

rows.anchor: PREVIOUS DEPENDENCY: 1 (Step 213); Step 109 is NOT cited despite being the prior EvidenceLedger
rows.statement: Step 214 cites Step 213 by number ('up to Step 213, we established...') but does not cite Step 109, the prior corpus step that already specified an Evidence Ledger (see the dedicated Step 214 vs Step 109 finding). Later response in scope: Step 215 adopts F/D/P/U and expands the 10-tuple to a 20-column schema without reconciliation.

rows.anchor: EVOLUTION VERDICT: PARTIALLY_RESOLVES/UNRESOLVED — 'the schema is designed well, the ledger is not built'; DEFINITION VERDICT: CLEAR on new terms, CONTRADICTORY on arity
rows.statement: NegativeKnowledge is precisely defined ('knowledge about approaches, assumptions, transitions or interpretations that have been demonstrated to be unsuitable under specified conditions' -- the crucial qualifier 'under specified conditions' makes it the best-scoped definition in the band), and Hypothesis ('X may be true') vs Invariant ('X must remain true') with its evidence/validation pipeline is excellent. Against this, the ledger is specified three times in one file at three different arities (Section 214.1's 10-tuple, Section 214.6's 15-field table, and the line-1095 8-column matrix header), and KState (8 values) vs Step 213's F/D/P/U (4) vs Step 212's Status (5) are three unmapped status vocabularies -- Section 214.23 correctly warns these should not be treated as one linear lifecycle since states may coexist (e.g. Accepted+Contested), which makes KState set-valued and hence not substitutable for the single-valued Status of Step 212.

rows.anchor: DERIVATION VERDICT: VALID_WITH_ASSUMPTIONS in the body; the one defect is Section 214.33's self-assessment violating Section 214.32's own boxed rule eight lines later
rows.statement: Sections 214.11-214.12's Observed(H)⇏Universal(H) with a worked over-generalization example is correct and well executed, and Sections 214.16-214.17's semantic-preservation condition p(C_A)⇒p'(C_B) is correctly typed (it demands p', an explicitly-defined target-context interpretation, not p itself -- more careful than most treatments). No first invalid inference in the body, but Section 214.33's self-assessment table ('Risk of overclaiming | Explicitly controlled') is a claim about the corpus's overclaiming risk, supported by zero evidence, made eight lines after Section 214.32's own boxed rule 'no architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it' (Contradiction #9).

rows.anchor: COMPUTABILITY: EL=union of EL_i over an empty index set — 'the emptiest formal object in the band, and it is boxed'; 0 ledger rows produced
rows.statement: EL_i and EL=union_i EL_i are DEFINED, but EL is a union over an empty index set, i.e. EL=empty-set; ELG=(V,E) is DEFINED with 0 nodes/0 edges; Experiment 6-tuple is DEFINED with 0 experiments recorded; KState is DEFINED but assigned to 0 items; K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_{t+1}) is DEFINED but Update is never specified. Table audit: Section 214.6 (15x2 glossary, 30 cells), Section 214.33 (8x2 self-verdicts, 16 cells), and the line-1095 header (8 columns, 0 data rows) together produce 0 ledger rows -- fewer than the uncited Step 109's 4 fabricated example rows. TEST VERDICT NOT_EXECUTED.

rows.anchor: STATISTICAL VERDICT: VERY STRONG (contradiction-as-missing-covariate is the most sophisticated statistical move in the band); MEASUREMENT VERDICT: mostly correct
rows.statement: Section 214.20's treatment of apparent contradiction as a missing covariate ('introduce Context, Population, Time, Purpose; then we may discover Accurate(ModelA|Context_1) but not Accurate(ModelA|Context_2)') is exactly right Simpson's-paradox reasoning correctly applied to knowledge claims -- the most sophisticated statistical move in the entire band. Section 214.13's Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions) correctly makes every claim conditional, the right statistical form. Measurement: KState is nominal, explicitly declared non-linear and co-occurring -- correctly refuses to impose an order; Valid(C|Context,Conditions) and S_{t+1} not-superset-of S_t are correctly typed; but SemanticLoss(A)>0 (Section 214.7) is a comparison on the undefined loss quantity, the fourth occurrence of the Section 208.10 defect in the band, and Section 214.33's verdict labels (Strong, Very strong, Explicitly controlled) are nominal labels arranged as if ordinal with no rubric or anchors.

rows.anchor: DDD VERDICT: STRONG (bounded knowledge; Translation_{A->B} as the Anti-Corruption Layer obligation; KnowledgeVersion vs KnowledgeState with the git analogy correctly self-limited)
rows.statement: Section 214.14's 'bounded knowledge' (Knowledge_A != Knowledge_B) is a legitimate, productive transposition of the bounded-context idea to knowledge itself; Section 214.15's insistence on an explicit Translation_{A->B} is correctly identified as the Anti-Corruption Layer/Context Map obligation; Section 214.17's p(C_A)⇒p'(C_B) is the correct formal statement of what a translation must preserve; Section 214.29's KnowledgeVersion vs KnowledgeState distinction, with the git-commit-vs-working-tree analogy and its own immediate self-limit ('the analogy is useful, but again it is an analogy, not proof of the architecture'), is well handled. Deficiency: no bounded context is named, and Translation_{A->B} is instantiated for zero pairs.

rows.anchor: UL NOTES: NegativeKnowledge and Adjudication well-minted, the anti-Boolean principle restated a fourth time, E now overloaded with three more bindings; WHAT SURVIVES / DOES NOT SURVIVE
rows.statement: NegativeKnowledge and Adjudication are both well-minted with precise scope; Section 214.24 restates the anti-Boolean principle (verified=true is insufficient) for the fourth time in the band (after Sections 208.16, 211.16, 211.25) -- the corpus is now repeating its own good ideas without noticing. E is additionally bound in this file to the ledger (EL, ELG), to evidence increments (E_{t+1} in Update(K_t,E_{t+1})), and to graph edges (ELG=(V,E)) -- three more bindings. Survives: NegativeKnowledge; Hypothesis != Invariant with the transformation pipeline; Observed(H)⇏Universal(H); Claim=(Proposition,Context,Conditions); the contradiction-as-missing-dimension insight (the band's best statistical insight); contradiction as a first-class edge; Generation != Adjudication; KState as explicitly non-linear and co-occurring; the three chronologies; the late-naming warning; 'no architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it' (the band's best principle, stated in the file that violates it in its own verdict table). Does not survive: the title; EL=union_i EL_i (empty); the 10-tuple as *the* schema (three competing arities in one file); Section 214.33's verdict table.

rows.anchor: ASSUMPTIONS / HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS — the ledger's precondition (artifact accessibility) is known-unmet at the time the ledger is specified
rows.statement: Stated: every significant step has a retrievable artifact; chronology is recoverable; contradictions are worth preserving. Hidden: that the artifacts are accessible to whoever fills the ledger -- Step 215's Step-216 preview says explicitly they are not yet available ('once they are available here...'), meaning the ledger's precondition is known-unmet at the time the ledger is specified; that 'significant step' is decidable (Step 215 Section 215.2 later concedes StepCount != KnowledgeCount without giving a criterion); that Update preserves the ledger's invariants (Update is never specified). Undefined symbols: Update(.,.), p' (the target-context interpretation -- the whole content of Section 214.17 rests on it and it is never constructed for any p), Uncertainty_t, Confidence codomain, SemanticLoss(A), and every one of ELG's seven named edge predicates.

rows.anchor: The Evidence/Test ordering is reversed between files, and Step 210's own boxed conclusion contradicts Step 210's own tuple
rows.statement: Step 209's tail agenda for 210 orders Invariant->Owner->EnforcementPoint->Test->Evidence->FailureMode; Step 210's own Section 210.1 tuple orders enforcement, monitoring, test, failure (test before the implied evidence); but Step 210's own boxed Section 210.40 conclusion states Invariant->Owner->Enforcement->Evidence->Test->Assurance (evidence before test); Step 211 Section 211.2 (boxed) and Step 214 Section 214.2 (boxed) both revert to Test before Evidence. Four sources agree that Test precedes Evidence; Step 210's one boxed conclusion disagrees with all of them, including with its own tuple -- the direction matters (Evidence->Test means evidence licenses the test; Test->Evidence means the test produces the evidence, which is what Steps 212-214 assume throughout). This is Contradiction #5.

rows.anchor: Tuple arity drift: 'the ledger' alone is specified at five different arities across two files
rows.statement: Machine-tabulated arity drift across the band: V_i verification tuple is 6-ary (210.1) but realized at arity 3 in the matrix (210.25); AAG is previewed as a 5-tuple but delivered as a 2-part graph with 6 node classes (211.1); the assurance vector A is 6-ary (211.9) while an AI artifact A is 7-ary (211.21); I_KOS has 8 members (209.42) vs I1-I15 has 15 (210.25, 212.4); the ledger EL_i is specified at arity 10 (214.1), then 15 (214.6), then 8 (214 tail), then again at 8 and 20 columns in Step 215 (215.5, 215.29) -- five arities for one object ('the ledger') across two files. R(S_i) is 5-ary for 6 declared questions (215.1).

rows.anchor: CONTRADICTION #8 — F/D/P/U mandated in Step 213, applied zero times across Steps 213-215
rows.statement: Step 213 Section 213.26 mandates that every important statement during reconstruction carry an [F]/[D]/[P]/[U] label ('our editorial control system'). A machine count of applied labels in Steps 213, 214, and 215 finds 4, 0, 0 respectively, and all four occurrences in 213 are the legend itself. Zero of the hundreds of statements in the three files that mandate the labels carry one, even though Section 213.26 explicitly scopes the requirement to these reconstruction documents themselves. Severity HIGH; this is a performative contradiction.

rows.anchor: CONTRADICTION #9 — Step 214's self-assessment table violates Step 214's own boxed evidentiary rule eight lines later
rows.statement: Step 214 Section 214.32 boxes 'no architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it.' Step 214 Section 214.33's final row states 'Risk of overclaiming | Explicitly controlled' -- a claim about the corpus's own overclaiming risk with zero supporting evidence, in a table that also self-awards 'Very strong' on five dimensions in a file containing no evidence at all. Severity MEDIUM-HIGH.

rows.anchor: CONTRADICTION #10 — Three incompatible ledger arities inside Step 214
rows.statement: Step 214 Section 214.1 boxes a 10-tuple EL_i=(Step,Artifact,Observation,Fact,Derivation,Decision,Architecture,Invariant,Evidence,Status); Section 214.6 gives a 15-field schema table; the Section 214 tail (line 1095) gives an 8-column matrix header whose columns barely overlap the 10-tuple's. Three incompatible schemas for 'the Evidence Ledger' in one file, with no reconciliation and no statement of which is normative. Severity MEDIUM.

rows.anchor: Total new identifiers minted in this band: 162

rows.anchor: STEP 214 load-bearing boxed claims: no claim stronger than its evidence (violated 8 lines later), EL as an empty union, NegativeKnowledge

aliases: Distributed Knowledge, Merge, Convergence and Consistency

sources.note: S0904's Step 25L: extends the S0903 closure/state-machine model to multiple independent producers, establishing a convergence theorem candidate, CRDT-analogy for event-history union, and bounded-context-relative ontology/metaknowledge treatment; distinct from but directly dependent on knowledge-state-closure-algebra (S0903) and knowledge-identity-atma-algebra (S0901).

rows.anchor: Merge(K_A,K_B,K_C) becomes fundamental
rows.statement: Extends the model to multiple knowledge producers (KnowledgeOS instances A, B and a Human/Agent C each observing different parts of the world), requiring a general Merge(K_A,K_B,K_C) operation.

rows.anchor: K_A: Nexus=3.69, K_B: Nexus=3.70 ... merge must determine Equivalent? TemporalEvolution? Contradiction? IndependentEvidence? Authority?
rows.statement: Rejects a naive 'A+B=combined knowledge' model: differing values require the merge to determine equivalence, temporal evolution, contradiction, independent-evidence status, and authority rather than arbitrarily picking one.

rows.anchor: Merge(K_A,K_B) must not flatten everything into one anonymous record ... assertion/support/provenance/temporal relations/conflicts
rows.statement: Requires merged knowledge to retain Origin(K_A) and Origin(K_B) rather than flattening into an anonymous record, illustrated with a structured merged-knowledge sketch (assertion, support per source, provenance, temporal relations, conflicts).

rows.anchor: RecordID_A\neq RecordID_B ... Evidence_A\neq Evidence_B ... KAID_A=KAID_B ... exactly why we introduced Knowledge Meaning Identity
rows.statement: Independent systems reaching the same conclusion have different RecordIDs and Evidence but may share Knowledge Atma meaning identity (KAID_A=KAID_B) — explicitly the reason the Meaning/Record identity split was introduced.

rows.anchor: Merge can unify semantic identity (KAID_A=KAID_B) while preserving multiple epistemic records (Record_A\neq Record_B) ... correct model for independent corroboration
rows.statement: States merge has two simultaneous effects: unifying semantic identity while preserving multiple distinct epistemic records — 'the correct model for independent corroboration.'

rows.anchor: Semantic deduplication must not mean provenance deduplication ... statistically this can be disastrous
rows.statement: Warns that naive deduplication discarding provenance loses the fact that two independent observations supported an assertion — statistically disastrous — 'semantic deduplication must not mean provenance deduplication.'

rows.anchor: H_{merge}=H_A\cup H_B ... K_{merge}=Derive(H_{merge},\Omega,EC,M) ... much cleaner than directly merging opaque states
rows.statement: Proposes merging at the event-history level (H_merge=H_A∪H_B, subject to identity/causal rules) then deriving K_merge=Derive(H_merge,Omega,EC,M), 'much cleaner than directly merging opaque states.'

rows.anchor: EventID ... E_1=E_2 can be detected ... EventIdentity\rightarrow DuplicateDetection
rows.statement: Requires EventID (global unique or deterministic content-derived identity) to detect duplicate event transmission — EventIdentity -> DuplicateDetection.

rows.anchor: identical events are not necessarily independent ... Independent(E_1,E_2)=False ... Replication is not new evidence
rows.statement: Warns that a replicated copy of an event is not independent evidence: Independent(E1,E2)=False when E2 is a replica of E1 — 'replication is not new evidence' — requiring OriginEventID preservation through replication.

rows.anchor: E_1\rightarrow E_2 causal ... Observation->LLM interpretation->Human decision ... A merge must preserve them
rows.statement: Worked example of a causal event chain (observation -> LLM interpretation -> human decision) that a merge must preserve as causally related, not merely temporally ordered.

rows.anchor: E_1\prec E_2 causally precedes ... stronger than Timestamp(E_1)<Timestamp(E_2)
rows.statement: Distinguishes causal ordering (E1≺E2) from wall-clock timestamp ordering, since distributed clocks can differ; suggests CausalRelation or logical clocks as needed.

rows.anchor: event IDs; causal ordering; logical clocks; append-only event streams; idempotent consumers; version vectors ... epistemic model sits on top of these mechanisms
rows.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS does not need to reinvent distributed systems — it reuses established mechanisms (event IDs, causal ordering, logical clocks, append-only streams, idempotent consumers, version vectors), with the epistemic model layered on top — 'another important architectural result.'

rows.anchor: K_A'\equiv K_B' provided both have received the same relevant information and use the same \Omega,EC,M ... convergence
rows.statement: Defines convergence: after synchronization, K_A'≡K_B' provided both nodes share the same Omega, EC, M and relevant event information.

rows.anchor: H_A=H_B and \Omega_A=\Omega_B and EC_A=EC_B and M_A=M_B implies Derive(H_A,...)\equiv Derive(H_B,...) ... extremely desirable
rows.statement: States a candidate convergence theorem: identical event sets, ontology, contract, and assessment model across two instances implies semantically equivalent derived KnowledgeStates — 'extremely desirable,' and separately argues it means KnowledgeOS does not require 'one magical central brain,' fitting enterprise architecture with independently-maintained-then-converging bounded contexts.

rows.anchor: Node A: H_A={E1,E2}, Node B: H_B={E2,E3} ... H_A'=H_B'={E1,E2,E3} ... K_A'=K_B'
rows.statement: Worked example: two nodes with partially overlapping event sets converge to the same union and, under a deterministic derivation model, the same derived knowledge state.

rows.anchor:
E_1\vdash A and E_2\vdash
eg A ... both should converge to Conflict(A,
eg A) ... AgreementOnEpistemicState, not AgreementOnTruth ... Convergence
eq Consensus
rows.statement: States that conflict does not prevent convergence: both nodes eventually receiving both contradictory events should converge to the same Conflict(A,¬A) state; convergence means AgreementOnEpistemicState, not AgreementOnTruth, giving Convergence ≠ Consensus — 'exactly appropriate for epistemic systems,' distinct from distributed-systems consensus (deciding which assertion is true).

rows.anchor: Merge\rightarrow\{Agreement,Conflict,Unresolved,Independent\}
rows.statement: Defines four possible merged-relationship outcomes: Agreement (mutually supported), Conflict (A⊥B), Unresolved relation (insufficient semantics to determine), and Independent.

rows.anchor: H_1\sqcup H_2=H_1\cup H_2 ... commutative, associative, idempotent ... CRDT-like thinking
rows.statement: Draws a CRDT analogy: an append-only immutable event set behaves like a grow-only structure under union, satisfying idempotence (H∪H=H), commutativity (H1∪H2=H2∪H1), and associativity ((H1∪H2)∪H3=H1∪(H2∪H3)) — 'extremely attractive,' contrasted with S0902's explicit refusal to grant these properties to knowledge-merge in general.

lineage_claims.target: S0902 25J.45-47 (commutativity/associativity as open questions for Merge_K)
lineage_claims.quote: Although H may have these excellent algebraic properties, K=Derive(H) may not behave like a simple CRDT.

rows.anchor: EventHistory can be monotonic while DerivedKnowledge can be non-monotonic ... This is actually ideal
rows.statement: Restates and reinforces the event-history/derived-knowledge separation in the distributed setting: EventHistory can be monotonic (CRDT-like union) while DerivedKnowledge (incorporating temporal state, retractions, conflict resolution, authority, policy, model versions) can be non-monotonic — 'this is actually ideal' since it separates distributed convergence from epistemic semantics.

lineage_claims.target: S0903 25K.13 History is monotonic; CurrentState need not be
lineage_claims.quote: EventHistory can be monotonic while DerivedKnowledge can be non-monotonic.

rows.anchor: A records E_1:Version=3.70, later E_2:Retract(E_1) ... K_A may say Retracted while K_B still says Supported ... not necessarily inconsistency
rows.statement: Worked distributed-retraction example: a node that has not yet received a retraction event legitimately differs from one that has, without this being inconsistency — convergence follows once the retraction event propagates.

rows.anchor: Consistent(K) does not imply Complete(K) ... KnowledgeState plus KnowledgeCompleteness
rows.statement: Introduces KnowledgeCompleteness as distinct from KnowledgeState: a node can be internally consistent while lacking events (Consistent(K) does not imply Complete(K)).

rows.anchor: Node A: Nexus=3.69, Node B: Nexus=3.70 ... Neither is necessarily internally inconsistent ... LocalConsistency\neq GlobalCompleteness
rows.statement: Worked example: two nodes each internally consistent but holding differing values simply have different information — 'LocalConsistency ≠ GlobalCompleteness,' called 'very important.'

rows.anchor: Frontier(K) ... Frontier_A\neq Frontier_B ... Synchronization expands the frontier
rows.statement: Defines Frontier(K) as the set of knowledge/events currently known to a node; synchronization expands the frontier — 'useful for distributed KnowledgeOS.'

rows.anchor: Infrastructure BC, Security BC, Architecture BC ... each bounded context owns its local semantics ... much healthier than one global ubiquitous model
rows.statement: Maps the model onto DDD bounded contexts: Infrastructure/Security/Architecture each own local knowledge semantics, with cross-context integration through explicit contracts/events rather than one global ubiquitous model.

rows.anchor: Approved could mean technically validated; architecture approved; security approved; legally approved ... Context must be part of semantic identity. Confirms our earlier decision
rows.statement: Worked example: 'Approved' means different things across bounded contexts, reconfirming that Context must be part of semantic identity (consistent with the canonical assertion tuple's Context field).

rows.anchor: resist creating OneOntologyForEverything ... \Omega_{Infrastructure}, \Omega_{Security}, \Omega_{Architecture} ... textbook DDD thinking applied to epistemic architecture
rows.statement: Rejects one universal ontology, proposing per-bounded-context ontologies (Omega_Infrastructure, Omega_Security, Omega_Architecture, etc.) with explicit cross-context mappings — 'textbook DDD thinking applied to epistemic architecture.'

rows.anchor: Map: \Omega_A\rightarrow\Omega_B ... Infrastructure:InstalledVersion maps to Architecture:TechnologyVersion ... that mapping itself is knowledge/governance and needs provenance
rows.statement: Worked example of a cross-ontology mapping (Infrastructure:InstalledVersion -> Architecture:TechnologyVersion) that is itself knowledge/governance requiring provenance — 'Mapping is an epistemic object too.'

rows.anchor: Knowledge\rightarrow KnowledgeAboutKnowledge. This is metaknowledge ... recursively self-describing
rows.statement: Notes an interesting architectural consequence: KnowledgeOS can hold KnowledgeMappings as knowledge about knowledge (e.g. recording which Architecture Board decision established a cross-context mapping) — the architecture becomes 'recursively self-describing... metaknowledge.'

rows.anchor: should also not assume Evidence_A\perp Evidence_B ... Vendor document -> Security / Architecture ... Independence must be derived from provenance, not organizational ownership
rows.statement: Warns that two bounded contexts consuming the same upstream source (e.g. a vendor document read by both Security and Architecture) produce correlated, not independent, evidence — 'Independence must be derived from provenance, not organizational ownership,' called 'a very important statistical result.'

rows.anchor: Merge(A,B): 1. Union event histories ... 10. Record unresolved integration issues ... computationally implementable
rows.statement: Presents a concrete ten-step distributed merge algorithm (union event histories; deduplicate identical events; preserve provenance; establish causal relationships; resolve ontology/version compatibility; re-derive assertions; detect equivalence/refinement/conflict; recalculate assessments; recalculate current KnowledgeState; record unresolved integration issues) — 'computationally implementable.'

rows.anchor: union/deduplication O(n) with hash indexing ... the expensive problem is semantic interpretation, not distributed merging itself
rows.statement: Analyzes merge complexity: union/deduplication over n events is approximately O(n) with hash indexing; 'the expensive problem is semantic interpretation, not distributed merging itself.'

rows.anchor: Falsification test 1: duplicate replication ... History_B contains one logical event. PASS.
rows.statement: Falsification Test 1: sending the same event twice results in one logical event in the receiver's history — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: Duplicate transmission should not create a second logical event.
experiment.setup: A sends E1 to B twice.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply event-identity duplicate detection
experiment.interpretation: Confirms EventIdentity->DuplicateDetection.

rows.anchor: 25L — PASS ... Convergence means epistemic state convergence, not forced agreement
